Trade and commerce
------------------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/Ostersund.JPG/250px-Ostersund.JPG)](./File:Ostersund.JPG)

Prästgatan

Like the rest of Jämtland Östersund is heavily dominated by many [small businesses](./Small_business "Small business"). The city is the centre of trade and commerce in Jämtland County and has more than 300 shops. The [retail trade](./Retailing "Retailing")'s [turnover](./Revenue "Revenue") is 30 per cent higher than it ought to be, given the number of inhabitants the city has.[[40]](./Östersund#cite_note-40) Trade in the central business district (*Staden* – 'the city') is mostly concentrated on the shopping and pedestrian street Prästgatan where large local shopping malls such as Kärnan and Mittpunkten along with department stores such as [Åhléns](./Åhléns "Åhléns") are located. There are large clothing companies such as [H&M](./H&M "H&M") and [Lindex](./Lindex "Lindex") and smaller ones like [WESC](./WESC "WESC"), approximately 50 restaurants, shoe stores, sporting goods retailers like Stadium and [Intersport](./Intersport "Intersport"), several supermarkets (Östersund has rather few convenience stores), etc. Storgatan, the street that runs parallel with Prästgatan, is also lined with shops, restaurants and coffeehouses. Unlike Prästgatan this street is not a pedestrian street. Östersund is the city in Sweden with the most square metres of window display per capita.[[41]](./Östersund#cite_note-41) The most prominent figure in Östersund's business life throughout the 20th century was the car salesman (who started out selling horses) [Sven O. Persson](./Sven_O._Persson?action=edit&redlink=1 "Sven O. Persson"), founder of [Persson Invest](./Persson_Invest?action=edit&redlink=1 "Persson Invest"), [Byggelit](./Byggelit?action=edit&redlink=1 "Byggelit") and [Bilbolaget](./Bilbolaget?action=edit&redlink=1 "Bilbolaget").[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] A significant real estate owner was [Maths O. Sundqvist](./Maths_O._Sundqvist "Maths O. Sundqvist") (1950–2012).

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/Storgatan_i_%C3%96stersund.jpg/250px-Storgatan_i_%C3%96stersund.jpg)](./File:Storgatan_i_Östersund.jpg)

Storgatan in late afternoon.

Östersund has had a long history as a [marketplace](./Marketplace "Marketplace") with the already mentioned ancient Gregorie market, tracing its lineage back to the 11th century, held in early March.[[42]](./Östersund#cite_note-42) Despite being banned in 1914, it continued to be held for a couple of years. In 1950, the market was reborn shortly and was completely resurrected in 1986, when the city celebrated its 200th anniversary, and has been held yearly since then.[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] In 1948, when the markets were non-existent, visions to restore Östersund's market traditions in a modern version were brought up. The result was the [trade fair](./Trade_fair "Trade fair") [Expo Norr](./Expo_Norr?action=edit&redlink=1 "Expo Norr"), initiated in 1950 in order to strengthen Östersund as a leading centre of trade in the northern parts of Sweden. The trade fair is an annual event just like Gregorie market, though Expo Norr is held during the summer and not during the winter. Expo Norr is usually attended by 30,000 individuals every year.

Like many other county capitals in Sweden the [county council](./Jämtland_County_Council?action=edit&redlink=1 "Jämtland County Council") and the municipality are among the largest employers.

Besides trading and [public services](./Public_services "Public services") Östersund has some larger companies such as [Solectron](./Solectron "Solectron"), [Cybercom](./Cybercom_AB?action=edit&redlink=1 "Cybercom AB"), [Volex](./Volex?action=edit&redlink=1 "Volex"), [Husqvarna AB](./Husqvarna_AB "Husqvarna AB"), [Swedbank](./Swedbank "Swedbank")'s telephone bank and [Telia](./Telia_(company) "Telia (company)").[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] Companies such as the dairy cooperation [Milko](./Milko_(Swedish_cooperative) "Milko (Swedish cooperative)") and [Inlandsbanan AB](./Inlandsbanan_AB?action=edit&redlink=1 "Inlandsbanan AB") have located their [corporate headquarters](./Corporate_headquarters "Corporate headquarters") in the city.

A national survey done by the [Confederation of Swedish Enterprise](./Confederation_of_Swedish_Enterprise "Confederation of Swedish Enterprise") shows that out of every company in Östersund Municipality 52 per cent are "very positive towards [globalization](./Globalization "Globalization")", thus ranking Östersund at number eight in Sweden as the most globalization-friendly municipality (2008).[[43]](./Östersund#cite_note-43)

Culture
-------

### Cultural venues

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/Thom%C3%A9e.jpg/250px-Thom%C3%A9e.jpg)](./File:Thomée.jpg)

S/S *Thomée* moored in the harbour.

Östersund is the cultural centre of Jämtland County and home to the prize winning museum [Jamtli](./Jamtli "Jamtli"). The museum has both an indoor exhibition area and an outdoor area which contains a number of historical buildings from all over the county, depicting the old lives of peasants, the early city of Östersund and the Scandinavian inland herding. The museum exhibition hosts an interesting set of tapestries, the *[Överhogdal tapestries](./Överhogdal_tapestries "Överhogdal tapestries")*, showing a rich imagery of both Norse and Christian origin from the [Viking Age](./Viking_Age "Viking Age"). The mythical [Storsjöodjuret](./Storsjöodjuret "Storsjöodjuret") (Great Lake Monster) has an exhibit of its own. Another remnant from the Viking Age is [Frösöstenen](./Frösöstenen "Frösöstenen"), one of the world's most northerly rune stones located on Frösön, the island of [Freyr](./Freyr "Freyr").

The county library, Jämtlands läns bibliotek, is located in the city. It is the oldest county library in Sweden, being founded in 1816 by the will of professor [Carl Zetterström](./Carl_Zetterström?action=edit&redlink=1 "Carl Zetterström"). As the library grew it was moved to a bigger facility. The older building is now situated beside the old church in Kyrkparken.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d7/Moose_Zoo_%C3%96stersund.jpg/250px-Moose_Zoo_%C3%96stersund.jpg)](./File:Moose_Zoo_Östersund.jpg)

Moose Garden

Lake Storsjön has been trafficked for a long time and the [steamships](./Steamship "Steamship") [S/S Thomée](./S/S_Thomée?action=edit&redlink=1 "S/S Thomée") and [S/S Östersund](./S/S_Östersund?action=edit&redlink=1 "S/S Östersund") are still in operation every summer. Unlike most boats, they are seen as male and not female. S/S Thomée is the only one that sets sail from Östersund's harbour. S/S Östersund sails from Arvesund, located at Storsjön's western shore but makes visits to Jamtli's steamboat jetty.

[Frösö Zoo](./Frösö_Zoo "Frösö Zoo") was one of Sweden's largest [zoological gardens](./Zoological_garden "Zoological garden") with [exotic animals](./Exotic_animal "Exotic animal"). Prior to its closing in 2019, it had roughly 700 animals[[44]](./Östersund#cite_note-44) including [Siberian tigers](./Siberian_tiger "Siberian tiger"), lions, [polar wolves](./Polar_wolf "Polar wolf"), and monkeys. Frösö Zoo also had a tropical house, a biological museum and an [amusement park](./Amusement_park "Amusement park"). Outside of Östersund in the village of [Orrviken](./Orrviken "Orrviken") there is a moose zoo called [Moose Garden](./Moose_Garden?action=edit&redlink=1 "Moose Garden"), allowing close encounters with tame moose.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/F%C3%A4rgfabriken_norr%2C_%C3%96stersund.jpg/250px-F%C3%A4rgfabriken_norr%2C_%C3%96stersund.jpg)](./File:Färgfabriken_norr,_Östersund.jpg)

Färgfabriken Norr

Färgfabriken ('the paint factory') is a centre for experimental culture based in Stockholm that portrays itself as a laboratory of contemporary art. A branch named *Färgfabriken Norr* was established in Östersund between April 2008 and January 2011.[[45]](./Östersund#cite_note-45)

[Gaaltije](./Gaaltije?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gaaltije"), the centre for [South Sami](./South_Sami "South Sami") culture, opened in 1999 and is a living source of knowledge for South Sami culture, history and business.

[Gamla Tingshuset](./Gamla_Tingshuset?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gamla Tingshuset") holds a small cinema, a café, a small venue and practice halls. It is usually a meeting place for the town's youth.

### Events

* The city festival [Storsjöyran](./Storsjöyran "Storsjöyran") (referred to as simply *Yran*, literally meaning: *[The Great Lake](./Storsjön "Storsjön") Giddy Festival*), the oldest city festival in [Scandinavia](./Scandinavia "Scandinavia") and with 55,000 visitors every year the largest in Sweden. Storsjöyran is held in the middle of Östersund the last weekend of July. Although the event starts the weekend before with the opening of Krogstråket when regional bars and restaurants gather near the lake.
* Jamtli Christmas Market is well attended market taking place the second weekend of [Advent](./Advent "Advent").
* [Expo Norr](./Expo_Norr?action=edit&redlink=1 "Expo Norr"), Sweden's oldest merchandise [trade fair](./Trade_fair "Trade fair") held in June with roughly 400 exhibitors.[[46]](./Östersund#cite_note-46)
* Vinterparken ('The Winter Park'), with seasonal lakeside events.

Media
-----

The largest daily newspaper in Östersund is *[Östersunds-Posten](./Östersunds-Posten "Östersunds-Posten")* (ÖP) with a circulation of 30,000 copies[[47]](./Östersund#cite_note-press-47) and the second largest is *[Länstidningen Östersund](./Länstidningen_Östersund?action=edit&redlink=1 "Länstidningen Östersund")* (LT) with a circulation of 15,000 copies[[47]](./Östersund#cite_note-press-47) (2006 for both). Like most Swedish newspaper they each have a political [editorial page](./Editorial_page "Editorial page"), views of the [Centre Party](./Centre_Party_(Sweden) "Centre Party (Sweden)") are expressed in ÖP and views of the [Swedish Social Democratic Party](./Swedish_Social_Democratic_Party "Swedish Social Democratic Party") are expressed in LT. *Länstidningen* is unique in Sweden, as it is the only Swedish newspaper with [press support](./Press_support "Press support") that has ever made itself non-dependent on state subsidy. [*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] Much of the paper's success is ascribed to the then editor-in-chief awarded with the [Grand Journalism Award](./Stora_Journalistpriset "Stora Journalistpriset") (*Stora Journalistpriset*).[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] Since 2006 the newspaper has been dependent on state subsidy. The media group [Mittmedia](./Mittmedia?action=edit&redlink=1 "Mittmedia") has owned both newspapers since 2005.[[48]](./Östersund#cite_note-48)

Two [free daily newspapers](./Free_daily_newspaper "Free daily newspaper") exist in the city, *[100 procent Östersund](./100_procent_Östersund?action=edit&redlink=1 "100 procent Östersund")* and *[Lokaltidningen Storsjön](./Lokaltidningen_Storsjön?action=edit&redlink=1 "Lokaltidningen Storsjön")*.

Local radio stations include [Radio Jämtland](./Radio_Jämtland?action=edit&redlink=1 "Radio Jämtland") (a part of [Sveriges Radio](./Sveriges_Radio "Sveriges Radio")), [One FM](./One_FM_(Sweden)?action=edit&redlink=1 "One FM (Sweden)") and [Modern Times Group](./Modern_Times_Group "Modern Times Group")'s [Rix FM](./Rix_FM?action=edit&redlink=1 "Rix FM").

Education
---------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/Mittuniversitetet_%C3%96stersund.jpg/250px-Mittuniversitetet_%C3%96stersund.jpg)](./File:Mittuniversitetet_Östersund.jpg)

Mid Sweden university in Östersund

Östersund recently[*[when?](./Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")*] became a university city and the [Mid Sweden University](./Mid_Sweden_University "Mid Sweden University") has its largest campus site in Östersund with well over 7,000 students. The Mid Sweden University was a [university college](./University_college#Sweden_and_Norway "University college") (*[högskola](./Högskola "Högskola")*) named *Mitthögskolan* until it was granted university status in 2005, making it the youngest university in Sweden. Mitthögskolan was the result of the merger between the University College of Sundsvall/[Härnösand](./Härnösand "Härnösand") (*Högskolan i Sundsvall/Härnösand*) and the University College of Östersund (*Högskolan i Östersund*)[[49]](./Östersund#cite_note-49)

Östersund is a centre for the research in social sciences ([business administration](./Business_Administration "Business Administration"), [psychology](./Psychology "Psychology"), sociology and [political science](./Political_Science "Political Science")) and social work, whilst the research in Health Sciences is split between Östersund and Sundsvall.

The city has several secondary schools (*[gymnasieskolor](./Gymnasium_(school) "Gymnasium (school)")*) of which [Palmcrantzskolan](./Palmcrantzskolan?action=edit&redlink=1 "Palmcrantzskolan") (PC) and [Wargentinsskolan](./Wargentinsskolan?action=edit&redlink=1 "Wargentinsskolan") (Wargen) are the two largest. Among the smaller are Storsjögymnasiet, Östersund's gymnasieskola and Dille Gård Naturbruksgymnasium.

Sports
------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/%C3%96stersunds_skidstadion_Biathlon_WC_2008.JPG/250px-%C3%96stersunds_skidstadion_Biathlon_WC_2008.JPG)](./File:Östersunds_skidstadion_Biathlon_WC_2008.JPG)

The ski stadium of Östersund

Östersund is marketed as the *Winter City* and has a long history of winter sports. It is internationally perhaps most known as one of the regular [Biathlon World Cup](./Biathlon_World_Cup "Biathlon World Cup") hosts in late-November and early-December. World Cup competitions have been held there since 1989.[[50]](./Östersund#cite_note-50) The [Biathlon World Championship 1970](./Biathlon_World_Championship_1970 "Biathlon World Championship 1970") were hosted in Östersund in [1970](./Biathlon_World_Championship_1970 "Biathlon World Championship 1970"), [2008](./Biathlon_World_Championships_2008 "Biathlon World Championships 2008") and [2019](./Biathlon_World_Championships_2019 "Biathlon World Championships 2019").

The cross-country skiing stadium is located two kilometres (1.2 miles) from the city centre and is one of the most well-equipped and spectator friendly ski stadiums in Sweden. The stadium is also internationally renowned due to the topography of its ski tracks, the compact track-system and the fact that Östersund is usually quite a reliable locality for snow during the winter months. A number of [biathlon](./Biathlon "Biathlon") world cup races have been held at the stadium as well as several national championships in cross-country skiing.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Vy_%C3%B6ver_%C3%96stersund_fr%C3%A5n_Gustavsbergsbacken_p%C3%A5_Fr%C3%B6s%C3%B6n.jpg/250px-Vy_%C3%B6ver_%C3%96stersund_fr%C3%A5n_Gustavsbergsbacken_p%C3%A5_Fr%C3%B6s%C3%B6n.jpg)](./File:Vy_över_Östersund_från_Gustavsbergsbacken_på_Frösön.jpg)

Östersund seen from the piste Gustavsbergsbacken

*Nationellt Vintersportcentrum* (NVC, Swedish Winter Sports Research Centre) is a research and training project run by the sports movement, the university, the municipality and the county council. The [Swedish Olympic Committee](./Swedish_Olympic_Committee "Swedish Olympic Committee") (SOC) use its lab for various tests.

Östersund, in association with the neighboring municipality of [Åre](./Åre "Åre"), had plans to be the candidate of Sweden for the organization of the [XXII Olympic Winter Games](./2014_Winter_Olympics "2014 Winter Olympics"), the [2014 Winter Olympics](./2014_Winter_Olympics "2014 Winter Olympics"), but the candidacy proposal was rejected by the government. It would have been the fourth attempt of this city (after [1994](./1994_Winter_Olympics "1994 Winter Olympics") where Östersund lost [the bid](./Bids_for_Olympic_Games "Bids for Olympic Games") with the score 45–39 to [Lillehammer](./Lillehammer "Lillehammer") in the final round, [1998](./1998_Winter_Olympics "1998 Winter Olympics") and [2002](./2002_Winter_Olympics "2002 Winter Olympics")).

Östersund has a basketball team in Sweden's highest division ([Ligan](./Ligan_(basketball) "Ligan (basketball)")), [Jämtland Basket](./Jämtland_Basket "Jämtland Basket").

Östersund's Fallskärmsklubb is the oldest of Sweden's drop zones and was formed in 1958. The very first civilian parachute jump was done actually on the ice of Storsjön in February 1956. The jumpers were officers from the Swedish Parachute rangers regiment that also wanted to jump on their spare time. Östersund's Fallskärmsklubb is today localized to Optand's airfields, approximately 13 km (8 mi) south from Östersund where the education of students and skydiving for experienced jumpers are carried out year-round with the exception of late autumn until early winter.

Other sports clubs include:

* [IFK Östersund](./IFK_Östersund "IFK Östersund")
* [Ope IF](./Ope_IF "Ope IF")
* [Östersunds FK](./Östersunds_FK "Östersunds FK")
* [Fältjägarnas IF](./Fältjägarnas_IF "Fältjägarnas IF")

### 2021 Special Olympics World Winter Games

Östersund along with [Åre](./Åre "Åre") were originally to host the [2021 Special Olympics World Winter Games](./2021_Special_Olympics_World_Winter_Games "2021 Special Olympics World Winter Games"). It would have marked the first time that Sweden had ever hosted the Special Olympics.[[51]](./Östersund#cite_note-51) However, due to lack of funding on 19 December 2019, the event did not take place in Sweden.[[52]](./Östersund#cite_note-52) Instead it was to take place in [Kazan](./Kazan "Kazan"), Russia and was delayed to 2022 but was cancelled following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

**Trondheim** ([UK](./British_English "British English"): [/ˈtrɒn(d)haɪm/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [*TRON(D)-hyme*](./Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"), [US](./American_English "American English"): [/ˈtrɒnheɪm/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [*TRON-haym*](./Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key");[[6]](./Trondheim#cite_note-6)[[7]](./Trondheim#cite_note-7) Urban East Norwegian: [[ˈtrɔ̂nː(h)æɪm]](./Help:IPA/Norwegian "Help:IPA/Norwegian"); [Southern Sami](./Southern_Sami_language "Southern Sami language"): *Tråante*), historically **Kaupangen**, **[Nidaros](./Nidaros "Nidaros")**, and **Trondhjem** (locally [[ˈtrɔ̂nːjæm]](./Help:IPA "Help:IPA") [ⓘ](/wiki/File:Trondheim.ogg "File:Trondheim.ogg")), is a city and [municipality](./List_of_municipalities_of_Norway "List of municipalities of Norway") in [Trøndelag](./Trøndelag "Trøndelag") county, [Norway](./Norway "Norway"). As of 2025, it had a population of 216,518.[[8]](./Trondheim#cite_note-8) Trondheim is the third most populous municipality in Norway, and is the [fourth largest](./List_of_continuously_built-up_areas_in_Norway_by_population "List of continuously built-up areas in Norway by population") [urban area](./Urban_area "Urban area"). Trondheim lies on the south shore of [Trondheim Fjord](./Trondheim_Fjord "Trondheim Fjord") at the mouth of the River [Nidelva](./Nidelva "Nidelva"). Among the significant technology-oriented institutions headquartered in Trondheim are the [Norwegian University of Science and Technology](./Norwegian_University_of_Science_and_Technology "Norwegian University of Science and Technology") (NTNU), the [Foundation for Scientific and Industrial Research (SINTEF)](./SINTEF "SINTEF"), the [Geological Survey of Norway](./Geological_Survey_of_Norway "Geological Survey of Norway") (NGU), and [St. Olavs University Hospital](./St._Olavs_University_Hospital "St. Olavs University Hospital").

The settlement was founded in 997 as a trading post and served as the capital of Norway through the [Viking Age](./Viking_Age "Viking Age") until 1217. From 1152 to 1537, the city was the seat of the Catholic [Archdiocese of Nidaros](./Archdiocese_of_Nidaros "Archdiocese of Nidaros"); it then became, and has remained, the seat of the Lutheran [Diocese of Nidaros](./Diocese_of_Nidaros "Diocese of Nidaros") and the site of the [Nidaros Cathedral](./Nidaros_Cathedral "Nidaros Cathedral"). The city was incorporated in 1838. The current municipality was formed in 1964, when Trondheim merged with [Byneset Municipality](./Byneset_Municipality "Byneset Municipality"), [Leinstrand Municipality](./Leinstrand_Municipality "Leinstrand Municipality"), [Strinda Municipality](./Strinda_Municipality "Strinda Municipality"), and [Tiller Municipality](./Tiller_Municipality "Tiller Municipality"), and further expanded on 1 January 2020, when Trondheim merged with [Klæbu Municipality](./Klæbu_Municipality "Klæbu Municipality").

Trondheim has a mild climate for its northerly latitude, resulting in moderate summers and winters that often remain above the freezing point in seaside areas. At higher elevations, though, the [microclimate](./Microclimate "Microclimate") is colder and snowier.

The city functions as the seat of the County Mayor of [Trøndelag](./Trøndelag "Trøndelag") county but not as its administrative centre (which is [Steinkjer](./Steinkjer_(town) "Steinkjer (town)")). This is designed to avoid making the county administration too [centralized](./Centralized "Centralized").

Trondheim is home to [football](./Association_football "Association football") club [Rosenborg](./Rosenborg_BK "Rosenborg BK"), Norway's most successful football club, and [Granåsen Ski Centre](./Granåsen_Ski_Centre "Granåsen Ski Centre"), which has hosted the World Championship in [Nordic Skiing](./Nordic_Skiing "Nordic Skiing").

Names and etymology
-------------------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Flag_of_Trondheim.svg/250px-Flag_of_Trondheim.svg.png)](./File:Flag_of_Trondheim.svg)

The [flag of Trondheim](./Flag_of_Trondheim "Flag of Trondheim") is one of the few Norwegian municipal flags that is not the banner of arms of the municipal [coat of arms](./Coat_of_arms "Coat of arms").



See also: [Names of Trondheim in different languages](./Names_of_Trondheim_in_different_languages "Names of Trondheim in different languages")

The city was established in 997 by [Olav Tryggvason](./Olav_Tryggvason "Olav Tryggvason") and it was originally named *Nidaros* ([Old Norse](./Old_Norse_language "Old Norse language"): *Niðaróss*). The first element of the name was the local river [Nid](./Nidelva "Nidelva"). The last element of the name was *[óss](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/óss#Old_Norse "wikt:óss")* which meant "the mouth of a river". Thus the name meant "the outlet of the river [Nid](./Nidelva "Nidelva")". Although the formal name was Nidaros, the city was commonly known as *[kaupangr](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/kaupangr#Old_Norse "wikt:kaupangr")*, which means "city" or "marketplace", or more specifically *kaupangr í Þróndheimi* which means "the city in Trondheim". Trondheim ([Old Norse](./Old_Norse_language "Old Norse language"): *Þróndheimr*) was the historic name for the whole district which is now known as [Trøndelag](./Trøndelag "Trøndelag"). This is the area where the people were known as Trønder (*[þróndr](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/þróndr#Old_Norse "wikt:þróndr")*). This district name Trondheim meant "the home of the Trønder people" (literally "Trønder-home") and Trøndelag ([Old Norse](./Old_Norse_language "Old Norse language"): *Þrǿndalǫg*) originally meant the "law area of the Trønder people" (literally "Trønder-law"). The name of the Trønder people derives from the [Old Norse](./Old_Norse "Old Norse") word *[þróndr](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/þróndr#Old_Norse "wikt:þróndr")* which is an old present participle of the verb *[þróask](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/þróask#Old_Norse "wikt:þróask")* which means "to grow" or "to thrive".[[9]](./Trondheim#cite_note-9)[[10]](./Trondheim#cite_note-10)

During the late [Middle Ages](./Middle_Ages "Middle Ages"), the city name was commonly shortened to **Þróndheimr**, dropping the *kaupanger* part, and over time the name became *Trondhjem*, using the [Dano-Norwegian](./Dano-Norwegian "Dano-Norwegian") spelling rather than the [Old Norse](./Old_Norse "Old Norse") spelling since the city was part of the Kingdom of [Denmark-Norway](./Denmark-Norway "Denmark-Norway") for centuries.

On 21 December 1917, a [royal resolution](./Royal_decree "Royal decree") enacted the [1917 Norwegian language reforms](./Norwegian_language_conflict "Norwegian language conflict"). Around the time, many municipalities and cities had their names changed to "Norwegianize" the spelling and make them look less [Danish](./Danish_language "Danish language"). On 1 January 1919, the name of the local [Church of Norway](./Church_of_Norway "Church of Norway") diocese was changed from **Trondhjem stift** to **Nidaros bispedømme** (English: [Diocese of Nidaros](./Diocese_of_Nidaros "Diocese of Nidaros")).[[11]](./Trondheim#cite_note-11) In 1924, the name of the Norwegian capital city was changed from *Kristiania* to [Oslo](./Oslo "Oslo"), removing the name referencing a Danish King in favor of the very old name Oslo. In 1928, a [referendum](./Referendum "Referendum") in Trondhjem was held on whether to keep the current name or to bring back the original name of *Nidaros*. The vote resulted in 17,163 votes in favour of *Trondhjem* and only 1,508 votes in favour of Nidaros.[[12]](./Trondheim#cite_note-12) Despite this result, the [Storting](./Storting "Storting") voted in 1929 to make some changes. The [Trondhjem Cathedral](./Nidaros_Cathedral "Nidaros Cathedral") would be changed to [Nidaros Cathedral](./Nidaros_Cathedral "Nidaros Cathedral") effective on 1 July 1929[[13]](./Trondheim#cite_note-13) and the name of the city would change to *Nidaros* starting on 1 January 1930.[[14]](./Trondheim#cite_note-14) This change caused public outrage and even [riots](./Riot "Riot") during 1930. This forced the [Storting](./Storting "Storting") to reconsider this change. On 6 March 1931, the name was formally changed to *Trondheim*, using the medieval Norwegian spelling instead of the Danish version *Trondhjem*. The name of the diocese and cathedral, however, continued using the name Nidaros.[[15]](./Trondheim#cite_note-15)

Trondheim was briefly named **Drontheim** during the [Second World War](./Second_World_War "Second World War") as a [German exonym](./German_exonyms "German exonyms").

History
-------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Lykkens_Portal%2C_Gamble_Bybro%2C_Trondheim%2C_West_view_20150605_1.jpg/250px-Lykkens_Portal%2C_Gamble_Bybro%2C_Trondheim%2C_West_view_20150605_1.jpg)](./File:Lykkens_Portal,_Gamble_Bybro,_Trondheim,_West_view_20150605_1.jpg)

The [Old Town Bridge](./Old_Town_Bridge "Old Town Bridge") of Trondheim



For the ecclesiastical history, see [Archiepiscopate of Nidaros](./Archiepiscopate_of_Nidaros "Archiepiscopate of Nidaros").

Trondheim was named Kaupangen (English: market place or trading place) by [Viking](./Viking "Viking") [King](./King_of_Norway "King of Norway") [Olav Tryggvason](./Olav_Tryggvason "Olav Tryggvason") in 997 CE.[[16]](./Trondheim#cite_note-16) Shortly after that, it came to be called *[Nidaros](./Nidaros "Nidaros")*. Initially, it was frequently used as a military retainer ([Old Norse](./Old_Norse "Old Norse"): "hird"-man) of King Olav I. It was also frequently used as the king's seat and was Norway's capital until 1217.

People have lived in the area for thousands of years, as evidenced by the [rock carvings in central Norway](./Rock_carvings_in_Central_Norway "Rock carvings in Central Norway"), the [Nøstvet and Lihult cultures](./Nøstvet_and_Lihult_cultures "Nøstvet and Lihult cultures"), and the [Corded Ware culture](./Corded_Ware_culture "Corded Ware culture"). In ancient times, the [kings of Norway](./List_of_Norwegian_monarchs "List of Norwegian monarchs") were hailed in Trondheim at [Øretinget](./Øretinget "Øretinget"), the place for the assembly of all free men by the mouth of the River [Nidelva](./Nidelva "Nidelva"). [Harald Fairhair](./Harald_Fairhair "Harald Fairhair") (865–933) was hailed as the king here, as was his son, [Haakon I](./Haakon_I_of_Norway "Haakon I of Norway"), called 'the Good.' The battle of *[Kalvskinnet](./Kalvskinnet "Kalvskinnet")* took place in Trondheim in 1179: King [Sverre Sigurdsson](./Sverre_Sigurdsson "Sverre Sigurdsson") and his *[Birkebeiner](./Birkebeiner "Birkebeiner")* warriors were victorious against [Erling Skakke](./Erling_Skakke "Erling Skakke") (a rival to the throne). Some scholars believe that the famous [Lewis chessmen](./Lewis_chessmen "Lewis chessmen"), 12th-century chess pieces carved from walrus ivory that were found in the [Hebrides](./Hebrides "Hebrides") and are now at the [British Museum](./British_Museum "British Museum"), may have been made in Trondheim.[[17]](./Trondheim#cite_note-17)

From 1152, Trondheim was the seat of the [Archbishop of Nidaros](./Roman_Catholic_Archdiocese_of_Nidaros "Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Nidaros") for Norway, which operated from the [Archbishop's Palace](./Archbishop's_Palace,_Trondheim "Archbishop's Palace, Trondheim"). Due to the introduction of [Lutheran](./Lutheranism "Lutheranism") Protestantism in 1537, the last archbishop, [Olav Engelbrektsson](./Olav_Engelbrektsson "Olav Engelbrektsson"), had to flee from the city to the [Netherlands](./Seventeen_Provinces "Seventeen Provinces"); he died in what today is [Lier, Belgium](./Lier,_Belgium "Lier, Belgium").

From the 16th through the 19th centuries, the city was repeatedly ravaged by fires that caused widespread damage since many of its buildings were made of wood. The worst occurred in 1598, 1651, 1681, 1708, 1717 (twice), 1742, 1788, 1841 and 1842. The 1651 fire destroyed 90% of all buildings within the city limits. After the "[Horneman Fire](./1681_Trondheim_fire "1681 Trondheim fire")" in 1681, there was an almost total reconstruction of the city, overseen by General [Johan Caspar von Cicignon](./Johan_Caspar_von_Cicignon "Johan Caspar von Cicignon"), originally from [Luxembourg](./Luxembourg "Luxembourg"). Broad avenues, such as Munkegata, were created, without regard for private property rights, to limit the damage from future fires. At the time, the city had a population of under 10,000 inhabitants, with most living in the downtown area.[[18]](./Trondheim#cite_note-18)[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

After the [Treaty of Roskilde](./Treaty_of_Roskilde "Treaty of Roskilde") on 26 February 1658, Trondheim and the rest of [Trøndelag](./Trøndelag "Trøndelag") became Swedish territory briefly. [However, after a three-month long siege](./Siege_of_Trondheim "Siege of Trondheim"), the area was reconquered 10 months later.[[19]](./Trondheim#cite_note-19) The conflict was finally settled by the [Treaty of Copenhagen](./Treaty_of_Copenhagen_(1660) "Treaty of Copenhagen (1660)") on 27 May 1660.

Plan of Trondheim, 1942

During the [Second World War](./Second_World_War "Second World War"), Trondheim was occupied by [Nazi Germany](./Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany") from 9 April 1940, the first day of the [invasion of Norway](./Operation_Weserübung "Operation Weserübung"), until the end of the war in Europe, [8 May 1945](./VE_Day "VE Day"). The German invasion force consisted of the [German cruiser Admiral Hipper](./German_cruiser_Admiral_Hipper "German cruiser Admiral Hipper"), 4 destroyers and 1700 Austrian Mountain troops. Except for a coastal battery that opened fire, there was no resistance to the invasion, which began on 9 April at 5 AM. On 14 and 17 April, British and French forces landed near Trondheim in a failed attempt to liberate Trondheim, as part of the [Namsos Campaign](./Namsos_Campaign "Namsos Campaign").[[20]](./Trondheim#cite_note-20) During the occupation, Trondheim was the home of the notorious Norwegian Gestapo agent, [Henry Rinnan](./Henry_Rinnan "Henry Rinnan"), who operated from a nearby villa and infiltrated Norwegian resistance groups. The city and its citizens were subjected to harsh treatment by the occupying power, including the imposition of [martial law](./Martial_law_in_Trondheim_in_1942 "Martial law in Trondheim in 1942") in October 1942. During this time, the Germans turned the city and its environs into a major base for submarines (which included building the large submarine base and bunker [DORA I](./Dora_I "Dora I")), and contemplated a scheme to build a new city for 300,000 inhabitants, *[Nordstern](./Nordstern_(city) "Nordstern (city)")* ("Northern Star"), centred 15 kilometres (9 miles) southwest of Trondheim, near the wetlands of [Øysand](./Øysand "Øysand") on the outskirts of [Melhus](./Melhus_Municipality "Melhus Municipality") municipality. This new metropolis was to be accompanied by a massively expanded version of the already existing naval base, which was intended to become the future primary stronghold of the German [Kriegsmarine](./Kriegsmarine "Kriegsmarine"). A start was made on this enormous construction project, but it was far from completed when the war ended, and today, there are few physical remains of it.[[21]](./Trondheim#cite_note-21)

### Municipal history

The city of Trondheim was established on 1 January 1838 (see [formannskapsdistrikt](./Formannskapsdistrikt "Formannskapsdistrikt") law). On 1 January 1864, part of [Strinda Municipality](./Strinda_Municipality "Strinda Municipality") (population: 1,229) was amalgamated with Trondheim. Then, on 1 January 1893, another part of Strinda Municipality (population: 4,097) was transferred to Trondheim Municipality. On 1 January 1952, the [Lade](./Lade,_Trondheim "Lade, Trondheim") area of Strinda Municipality (population: 2,230) was transferred to Trondheim Municipality. On 1 January 1964, a major municipal merger took place: [Leinstrand Municipality](./Leinstrand_Municipality "Leinstrand Municipality") (population: 4,193), [Byneset Municipality](./Byneset_Municipality "Byneset Municipality") (population: 2,049), Strinda Municipality (population: 44,600), and [Tiller Municipality](./Tiller_Municipality "Tiller Municipality") (population: 3,595) were all merged with the city of Trondheim (population: 56,982), which nearly doubled the population of the municipality.[[22]](./Trondheim#cite_note-22) On 1 January 2020, the neighboring [Klæbu Municipality](./Klæbu_Municipality "Klæbu Municipality") (population: 6,050) was merged with Trondheim Municipality.[[23]](./Trondheim#cite_note-23)

### Coat of arms and seal

See also: [Flag of Trondheim](./Flag_of_Trondheim "Flag of Trondheim")

The [coat of arms](./Coat_of_arms "Coat of arms") dates back to the 13th century. To the left, there is an [archbishop](./Archbishop "Archbishop") with his staff and [mitre](./Mitre "Mitre") in a church archway. On the right, a crowned king holding scales in a castle archway. These two pictures rest on a base which forms an arch. Underneath that arch, are three male heads which symbolise the city's rank as Norway's first capital and the archbishop's place of residence. The scales symbolise justice and the [motif](./Motif_(visual_arts) "Motif (visual arts)") is based on the political philosophy of the 13th century, where the balance of power between king and church was an important issue. The three heads at the bottom may symbolise the city council. The motif is unique in Norwegian municipal heraldry, but similar motifs are found in bishopric cities on the continent. The design of the coat-of-arms that was adopted in 1897, and is still used today, was made by Håkon Thorsen.[[24]](./Trondheim#cite_note-24)

Geography
---------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/13/Nidelva-Trondheim-foliage.JPG/250px-Nidelva-Trondheim-foliage.JPG)](./File:Nidelva-Trondheim-foliage.JPG)

Autumn [foliage](./Foliage "Foliage") along Nidelva; October 2009

Trondheim is situated where the River Nidelva meets [Trondheim Fjord](./Trondheim_Fjord "Trondheim Fjord") with an excellent harbour and sheltered condition. In the Middle Ages the river was deep enough to be navigable by most boats. However, in the mid–17th century, an avalanche of mud and stones made it less navigable, and partly ruined the harbour. The municipality's highest elevation is the [Storheia](./Storheia "Storheia") hill, 565 metres (1,854 ft) [above sea level](./Above_mean_sea_level "Above mean sea level"). At the summer [solstice](./Solstice "Solstice"), the sun rises at 03:00 and sets at 23:40, and then stays just below the horizon. Between 23 May and 19 July, when the sky is cloud-free, it remains light enough at night that no artificial lighting is needed outdoors.[[25]](./Trondheim#cite_note-25) At the winter solstice, the sun rises at 10:01, stays very low above the horizon (at midday its altitude is slightly more than 3 degrees over the horizon), and sets at 14:31.

### Climate

Trondheim city has an [oceanic climate](./Oceanic_climate "Oceanic climate") ([Cfb](./Köppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification")) or [humid continental climate](./Humid_continental_climate "Humid continental climate") (Dfb), depending on the winter threshold used (−3 °C or 0 °C). Winters are fairly cold and summers are mild. The part of the municipality further away from the fjord has slightly colder winters, while the part close to the fjord has the mildest winters. Trondheim is mostly sheltered from the strong south and southwesterly winds which can occur along the outer seaboard but is more exposed to northwesterly winds. As with the rest of Norway, the weather is dependent on the weather pattern. High pressure over Central Norway or to the east can last for weeks, while Atlantic Lows from the west also can dominate for weeks. Such stuck opposite weather patterns was evident in 2020, when May saw northwesterlies with cold air even bringing some snowfall, while the following June was warm and sunny. Trondheim experiences moderate snowfall from November to March,[[26]](./Trondheim#cite_note-26) but mixed with mild weather and rainfall. There is often more snow and later snowmelt in suburban areas at a higher elevation, with good skiing conditions in [Bymarka](./Bymarka "Bymarka"). All the monthly record lows are from 1955 or older, with half of them from before 1920. The last overnight frost in June was in 1958. The all-time low −26 °C (−14.8 °F) was recorded February 1899. The all-time high 35 °C (95 °F) was recorded 22 July 1901.
The earliest weather stations were located closer to the city centre, from 1945 onwards the weather station has been located at a higher elevation (Voll, 127 m and Tyholt, 113 m), therefore being slightly colder.
A new sunrecorder was established in the city by met.no at [Gløshaugen](./Gløshaugen "Gløshaugen") (NTNU campus) December 2015, recording more sunhours than the earlier sunrecorder, which had terrain blocking issues.[[27]](./Trondheim#cite_note-27) There are on average 229 sunhours in July (based 2016–2020).[[28]](./Trondheim#cite_note-28) Trondheim recorded 197 sunhours in October 2016 beating the previous national record for October. In April 2019, Trondheim recorded 308 sunhours, setting a new national record for April.[[29]](./Trondheim#cite_note-29)[[30]](./Trondheim#cite_note-30) In contrast, December 2016 only recorded 10 sunhours.

Located at 63 degrees north, Trondheim experience "white nights" with only civil twilight during the height of summer. This light allow for normal daytime activities at night, such as reading a book.

### Fauna

The city has various wetland [habitats](./Habitat "Habitat"). among which there is the *Gaulosen.* The observation tower accommodates for birdwatching and providing information about birdlife.[[34]](./Trondheim#cite_note-34)

Though Trondheim is Norway's third largest city, wild animals are regularly seen. [Otters](./European_otter "European otter") and [beavers](./European_beaver "European beaver") thrive in Nidelva and Bymarka.[[35]](./Trondheim#cite_note-35) [Badgers](./Eurasian_badger "Eurasian badger") and [red foxes](./Red_fox "Red fox") are not uncommon sights. [Moose](./Moose "Moose") and [deer](./Deer "Deer") are common in the hills surrounding the city, and might wander into the city, especially in May when the one-year-olds are chased away by their mothers, or in late winter when food grows scarce in the snow-covered higher regions. From 2002 until 2017, a [wolverine](./Wolverine "Wolverine") lived in Bymarka.[[36]](./Trondheim#cite_note-36)[[37]](./Trondheim#cite_note-37)

[DORA 1](./DORA_1 "DORA 1") is a [German submarine](./U-boat "U-boat") base that housed the [13th U-boat Flotilla](./13th_U-boat_Flotilla "13th U-boat Flotilla") during the Second World War occupation of Norway. Today the bunker houses various archives, among them the city archives, the university and state archives. More recently, DORA has been used as a concert venue.

[Kristiansten Fortress](./Kristiansten_Fortress "Kristiansten Fortress"), built 1681–1684, is located on a hill east of Trondheim. It repelled the invading [Swedes](./Sweden "Sweden") in 1718, but was decommissioned in 1816 by Crown Prince Regent [Charles John](./Charles_XIV_John_of_Sweden "Charles XIV John of Sweden").

A [statue of Olav Tryggvason](./Olav_Tryggvason_(statue) "Olav Tryggvason (statue)"), the founder of Trondheim, is located in the city's central square, mounted on top of an obelisk. The statue base is also a [sun dial](./Sun_dial "Sun dial"), but it is calibrated to UTC+1 so that the reading is inaccurate by one hour in the summer.

The islet Munkholmen is a popular tourist attraction and recreation site. The islet has served as a place of execution, a [monastery](./Monastery "Monastery"), a [fortress](./Fortress "Fortress"), [prison](./Prison "Prison"), and a Second World War [anti-aircraft](./Anti-aircraft "Anti-aircraft") gun station.

[Stiftsgården](./Stiftsgården "Stiftsgården") is the royal residence in Trondheim, originally constructed in 1774 by [Cecilie Christine Schøller](./Cecilie_Christine_Schøller "Cecilie Christine Schøller"). At 140 rooms constituting 4,000 square metres (43,056 sq ft), it is possibly the largest wooden building in [Northern Europe](./Northern_Europe "Northern Europe") and has been used by royals and their guests since 1800.

A statue of [Leif Ericson](./Leif_Ericson "Leif Ericson") is located at the seaside, close to the old Customs Building, the cruise ship facilities and the new swimming hall. The statue is a replica, the original being located at a Seattle [marina](./Marina "Marina").

### Shopping

Most of Trondheim's city centre is scattered with small speciality shops. However, the city centre's main shopping area is concentrated around the pedestrianised streets *Nordre gate* (English: Northern street), *Olav Tryggvasons gate* and *Thomas Angells gate* even though the rest of the city centre is provided with everything from old, well-established companies to new, hip and trendy shops.

In the mid-to-late 1990s, the area surrounding the old [drydock](./Drydock "Drydock") and ship construction buildings of the defunct [Trondhjems mekaniske Værksted](./Trondhjems_mekaniske_Værksted "Trondhjems mekaniske Værksted") shipbuilding company at the [Nedre Elvehavn](./Nedre_Elvehavn "Nedre Elvehavn") was renovated and old industrial buildings were torn down to make way for condominiums. A shopping centre was also built, known as Solsiden (The Sunny Side). This is a popular residential and shopping area, especially for young people.

Larger multi-mall shopping areas are located in the eastern suburb of Lade-Strindheim along the *Haakon VIIs gate* and *Bromstadvegen* streets, and in the southern suburb of Tiller (The latter centred around [City Syd](./City_Syd "City Syd")). Swedish store chains are widely present throughout the areas, especially in the DIY and clothing store fields, including [IKEA](./IKEA "IKEA"), [Biltema](./Biltema "Biltema"), and [Clas Ohlson](./Clas_Ohlson "Clas Ohlson").

### Nidaros Cathedral

The [Nidaros Cathedral](./Nidaros_Cathedral "Nidaros Cathedral") and the Archbishop's Palace are located side by side in the middle of the city centre. The cathedral, built from 1070 on, is the most important [Gothic](./Gothic_architecture "Gothic architecture") monument in Norway and was Northern Europe's most important Christian [pilgrimage](./Pilgrimage "Pilgrimage") site during the Middle Ages,[[38]](./Trondheim#cite_note-38) with pilgrimage routes leading to it from [Oslo](./Oslo "Oslo") in southern Norway and from the [Jämtland](./Jämtland "Jämtland") and [Värmland](./Värmland "Värmland") regions of Sweden. Today, it is the northernmost medieval cathedral in the world, and the second-largest in [Scandinavia](./Scandinavia "Scandinavia").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/Nidaros_cathedral_front.jpg/250px-Nidaros_cathedral_front.jpg)](./File:Nidaros_cathedral_front.jpg)

West front of [Nidaros Cathedral](./Nidaros_Cathedral "Nidaros Cathedral")

During the Middle Ages, and again after independence was restored in 1814, the Nidaros Cathedral was the [coronation](./Coronation "Coronation") church of the Norwegian kings. [King Haakon VII](./Haakon_VII_of_Norway "Haakon VII of Norway") was the last monarch to be crowned there, in 1906. Starting with [King Olav V](./Olav_V_of_Norway "Olav V of Norway") in 1957, coronation was replaced by [consecration](./Consecration "Consecration"). In 1991, the present [King Harald V](./Harald_V_of_Norway "Harald V of Norway") and [Queen Sonja](./Queen_Sonja_of_Norway "Queen Sonja of Norway") were consecrated in the cathedral.[[39]](./Trondheim#cite_note-39) On 24 May 2002, their daughter [Princess Märtha Louise](./Princess_Märtha_Louise_of_Norway "Princess Märtha Louise of Norway") married the writer [Ari Behn](./Ari_Behn "Ari Behn") in the cathedral.[[40]](./Trondheim#cite_note-40)

The [Pilgrim's Route](./Pilgrim's_Route "Pilgrim's Route") (*Pilegrimsleden*) to the site of Saint Olufs's tomb at [Nidaros](./Nidaros "Nidaros") Cathedral, has recently been re-instated. Also known as St. Olav's Way, (*Sankt Olavs vei*), the main route, which is approximately 640 kilometres (400 mi) long, starts in [Oslo](./Oslo "Oslo") and heads North, along Lake [Mjøsa](./Mjøsa "Mjøsa"), up the valley [Gudbrandsdalen](./Gudbrandsdalen "Gudbrandsdalen"), over the mountain range [Dovrefjell](./Dovrefjell "Dovrefjell") and down the [Oppdal](./Oppdal_Municipality "Oppdal Municipality") valley to end at [Nidaros Cathedral](./Nidaros_Cathedral "Nidaros Cathedral") in Trondheim. There is a Pilgrim's Office in Oslo which gives advice to pilgrims and a Pilgrim Centre in Trondheim, under the [aegis](./Aegis "Aegis") of the cathedral, which awards certificates to successful [pilgrims](./Pilgrims "Pilgrims") upon the completion of their journey.[[41]](./Trondheim#cite_note-41)[[42]](./Trondheim#cite_note-42)

### Other churches

The Lutheran [Church of Norway](./Church_of_Norway "Church of Norway") has 21 churches within the municipality of Trondheim. They are all a part of the [Diocese of Nidaros](./Diocese_of_Nidaros "Diocese of Nidaros"), which is based in Trondheim at the [Nidaros Cathedral](./Nidaros_Cathedral "Nidaros Cathedral"). Many of the churches are several hundred years old, with a couple which were built almost 1,000 years ago.

The [Roman Catholic](./Roman_Catholic "Roman Catholic") [Sankt Olav domkirke](./St._Olav's_Cathedral,_Trondheim "St. Olav's Cathedral, Trondheim") is the [cathedral](./Cathedral "Cathedral") episcopal see of the exempt [Territorial Prelature of Trondheim](./Territorial_Prelature_of_Trondheim "Territorial Prelature of Trondheim"). Being located across the street from the Nidaros Cathedral, the two of them form an unofficial religious quarter along with a [synagogue](./Synagogue "Synagogue"), a Baptist church, a [Salvation Army](./Salvation_Army "Salvation Army") office, and the 8-auditorium [cinema](./Movie_theater "Movie theater") *Prinsen kinosenter*.

### Museums

[Sverresborg](./Sverresborg "Sverresborg"), also named [Zion](./Zion "Zion") after [King David](./King_David "King David")'s castle in [Jerusalem](./Jerusalem "Jerusalem"), was a fortification built by [Sverre Sigurdsson](./Sverre_Sigurdsson "Sverre Sigurdsson"). It is now an open-air museum, consisting of more than 60 buildings. The castle was originally built in 1182–1183, but did not last for long as it was burned down in 1188. However, the [Sverresaga](./Sverresaga "Sverresaga") indicates it had been restored by 1197.[[43]](./Trondheim#cite_note-43)[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

The Trondheim Science Center ([Norwegian](./Norwegian_language "Norwegian language"): *Vitensenteret i Trondheim*) is a scientific hands-on experience center. The [NTNU University Museum](./NTNU_University_Museum "NTNU University Museum") (Norwegian: NTNU Vitenskapsmuseet) is part of the [Norwegian University of Science and Technology](./Norwegian_University_of_Science_and_Technology "Norwegian University of Science and Technology"). There are also a variety of small history, science and [natural history](./Natural_history "Natural history") museums, such as the [Trondheim Maritime Museum](./Trondheim_Maritime_Museum?action=edit&redlink=1 "Trondheim Maritime Museum"), the *Armoury*, adjacent to the Archbishops's Palace, Kristiansten Fortress, the music and musical instrument museum [Ringve National Museum](./Ringve_National_Museum "Ringve National Museum"), [Ringve Botanical Garden](./Ringve_Botanical_Garden?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ringve Botanical Garden"), the [Trondheim Tramway Museum](./Trondheim_Tramway_Museum "Trondheim Tramway Museum"), and the [Jewish Museum](./Jewish_Museum_of_Trondheim?action=edit&redlink=1 "Jewish Museum of Trondheim"), co-located with the city's synagogue, which is among the northernmost in the world.

[Rockheim](./Rockheim "Rockheim") ([Norwegian](./Norwegian_language "Norwegian language"): *Det nasjonale opplevelsessenteret for pop og rock*, The National Discovery Center for Pop and Rock) opened at the Pier in August 2010. It is located inside an old warehouse, but characterised by an easily recognisable roof in the shape of a box. "The box" is decorated by thousands of tiny lights that change in a variety of colours and patterns, and is a landmark in the cityscape – especially on dark winter evenings.

### Prison

Vollan District Jail ([Norwegian](./Norwegian_language "Norwegian language"): *Vollan kretsfengsel*) was a [jail](./Jail "Jail") during the [nazi occupation of Norway](./Nazi_occupation_of_Norway "Nazi occupation of Norway") and was used to imprison both prisoners of war and criminals. Vollan was not considered a [concentration camp](./Concentration_camp "Concentration camp").[[44]](./Trondheim#cite_note-NOU1998-44) In a summary of prisoners of war in Norway, numerous prisoners were registered at Vollan. One of its roles was as a [transit camp](./Internment "Internment") for [political prisoners](./Political_prisoners "Political prisoners"). Many prisoners were taken from Vollan to [Kristiansten Fortress](./Kristiansten_Fortress "Kristiansten Fortress") and shot. The prisoners at Vollan were interrogated at the Mission Hotel in Trondheim. Some were also interrogated by [Henry Rinnan](./Henry_Rinnan "Henry Rinnan") and his gang.[[44]](./Trondheim#cite_note-NOU1998-44) It was closed in 1971 after the opening of Trondheim Prison at Tunga.

Trondheim Prison (Norwegian: *Trondheim fengsel*) is a prison that belongs to the Northern Region of the [Norwegian Correctional Services](./Norwegian_Correctional_Services "Norwegian Correctional Services").[[45]](./Trondheim#cite_note-45) The prison can house 184 [inmates](./Inmates "Inmates").

It consists of four main departments:

* Nermarka ("Tunga") – closed department
* Detention department (no: *Forvaringsavdelingen*) at Nermarka
* Leira – open division. Through joint positive activities, the individual inmate on certain conditions teaches to be responsible with other people.[[46]](./Trondheim#cite_note-46)
* division Kongens gt. – halfway house, located in downtown Trondheim.

### Attractions

The [water park](./Water_park "Water park") and [public pool](./Public_pool "Public pool") [Pirbadet](./Pirbadet "Pirbadet") is located on the northernmost shore of the Brattøra district, within walking distance of the central station.

### Wider urban area

Trondheim forms the centre of the [Trondheim Region](./Trondheim_Region "Trondheim Region"), and is a common commuting point for work, shopping, and healthcare. Although the official list of [metropolitan regions of Norway](./Metropolitan_regions_of_Norway "Metropolitan regions of Norway") defines the region very broadly, the area of two-way commuting where Trondheim residents too would head outwards for transport, shopping, and [upper secondary schools](./Upper_secondary_school "Upper secondary school"), consists roughly of Trondheim, [Malvik](./Malvik_Municipality "Malvik Municipality"), downtown [Stjørdal](./Stjørdal "Stjørdal") (incl. [Værnes](./Værnes "Værnes")), downtown [Melhus](./Melhus_Municipality "Melhus Municipality"), [Skaun](./Skaun_Municipality "Skaun Municipality"), and the lower sections of [Vanvikan](./Vanvikan "Vanvikan") in [Indre Fosen](./Indre_Fosen "Indre Fosen").[[47]](./Trondheim#cite_note-47)

Government
----------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/R%C3%A5dhuset_i_Trondheim_sett_fra_Bispegata%2C_2023.jpg/250px-R%C3%A5dhuset_i_Trondheim_sett_fra_Bispegata%2C_2023.jpg)](./File:Rådhuset_i_Trondheim_sett_fra_Bispegata,_2023.jpg)

Trondheim's town hall.

Trondheim Municipality is responsible for [primary education](./Primary_education "Primary education") (through 10th grade), outpatient [health services](./Health_care "Health care"), [senior citizen](./Old_age "Old age") services, [welfare](./Welfare_spending "Welfare spending") and other [social services](./Social_work "Social work"), [zoning](./Zoning "Zoning"), [economic development](./Economic_development "Economic development"), and municipal [roads](./Road "Road") and utilities. The municipality is governed by a [municipal council](./Municipal_council_(Norway) "Municipal council (Norway)") of [directly elected](./Direct_election "Direct election") representatives. The [mayor](./Mayor "Mayor") is [indirectly elected](./Indirect_election "Indirect election") by a vote of the municipal council.[[48]](./Trondheim#cite_note-ks-48) The municipality is under the jurisdiction of the [Trøndelag District Court](./Trøndelag_District_Court "Trøndelag District Court") and the [Frostating Court of Appeal](./Frostating_Court_of_Appeal "Frostating Court of Appeal").

On 1 January 2005, the city was reorganized from five [boroughs](./Borough "Borough") into four, with each of these having separate social services offices.[[49]](./Trondheim#cite_note-49) The current boroughs are [Midtbyen](./Midtbyen,_Trondheim "Midtbyen, Trondheim") (44,967 inhabitants), [Østbyen](./Østbyen "Østbyen") (42,707 inhabitants), [Lerkendal](./Lerkendal,_Trondheim "Lerkendal, Trondheim") (46,603 inhabitants) and [Heimdal](./Heimdal "Heimdal") (30,744) inhabitants. The Population statistics listed are as of 1 January 2008. [Prior to 2005](./List_of_boroughs_in_Trondheim_prior_to_2005 "List of boroughs in Trondheim prior to 2005"), Trondheim was divided into the boroughs *Sentrum*, *Strinda*, *Nardo*, *Byåsen* and *Heimdal*.

See also: [List of mayors of Trondheim](./List_of_mayors_of_Trondheim "List of mayors of Trondheim")

Education and research
----------------------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/Hovedbygningen_Gl%C3%B8shaugen_Trondheim_2022-08-18_03.jpg/250px-Hovedbygningen_Gl%C3%B8shaugen_Trondheim_2022-08-18_03.jpg)](./File:Hovedbygningen_Gløshaugen_Trondheim_2022-08-18_03.jpg)

NTNU's main building

:   *See also the [list of primary schools in Trondheim](./Okstad_School "Okstad School")*.

Trondheim is home to both the [Norwegian University of Science and Technology](./Norwegian_University_of_Science_and_Technology "Norwegian University of Science and Technology") (NTNU) with its many technical lab facilities and disciplines, and BI-Trondheim, a satellite campus for the Norwegian Business School (BI).[[77]](./Trondheim#cite_note-77) Both universities welcome a number of international students on a yearly basis and offer various scholarships.[[78]](./Trondheim#cite_note-78)

[St. Olav's University Hospital](./St._Olavs_University_Hospital "St. Olavs University Hospital"), a regional hospital for Central Norway, is located in downtown Trondheim. St. Olav's is a teaching hospital and cooperates closely with the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) on both research and medical education.

[SINTEF](./SINTEF "SINTEF"), a large independent research organisation in [Scandinavia](./Scandinavia "Scandinavia"), has 1,800 employees with 1,300 of these located in Trondheim.[[79]](./Trondheim#cite_note-79) The Air Force Academy of the [Royal Norwegian Air Force](./Royal_Norwegian_Air_Force "Royal Norwegian Air Force") is located at Kuhaugen in Trondheim.

The [Geological Survey of Norway](./Geological_Survey_of_Norway "Geological Survey of Norway") is located at Lade in Trondheim and is a major geoscientific institution with 220 employees of which 70% are scientists.

There are 11 high schools in the city. [Trondheim katedralskole](./Trondheim_katedralskole "Trondheim katedralskole") ("Trondheim Cathedral School") was founded in 1152 and is the oldest upper secondary school ([gymnasium](./Gymnasium_(school) "Gymnasium (school)")) in Norway, while [Charlottenlund videregående skole](./Charlottenlund_videregående_skole?action=edit&redlink=1 "Charlottenlund videregående skole") is the largest in Sør-Trøndelag with its 1,100 students and 275 employees. Brundalen Skole, has big festivals each year, and is building out to increase space.

Ila skole was founded in 1770 and is the oldest primary school in Trondheim.[[80]](./Trondheim#cite_note-80)

Media
-----

[Adresseavisen](./Adresseavisen "Adresseavisen") is the largest regional newspaper and the oldest active newspaper in Norway, having been established in 1767. The two headquarters of the Norwegian Broadcasting Corporation (NRK) are located at [Tyholt](https://no.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRK%20Tyholt "no:NRK Tyholt") in Trondheim, and in Oslo.[[81]](./Trondheim#cite_note-81) On 31 December 2019 the fully digital and local newspaper Nidaros was launched as a competitor to Adresseavisen.[[82]](./Trondheim#cite_note-82) The student press of Trondheim features three types of media. [Under Dusken](./Under_Dusken "Under Dusken") is the student paper, [Radio Revolt](./Radio_Revolt "Radio Revolt") is the student radio, and Student-TV broadcasts videos online.

Radio stations established in Trondheim include Trøndelag-focused opt-out feeds of [NRK P1](./NRK_P1 "NRK P1") and [NRK P1+](./NRK_P1+ "NRK P1+"), a local version of NRK [Yr](./Yr.no "Yr.no")'s radio station, and Radio Revolt. Along with Norway's national radio stations, they can be listened to on [DAB+](./Digital_audio_broadcasting "Digital audio broadcasting") across most of Trøndelag, as well as on [internet radio](./Internet_radio "Internet radio"). As of 2017, the commercial stations Radio Trondheim and Radio 247 also broadcast from within Trondheim,[[83]](./Trondheim#cite_note-83) but as of May 2025 there are no commercial local stations that broadcast from within Trondheim Municipality proper, but intra-regional stations like [Nea Radio](./Nea_Radio?action=edit&redlink=1 "Nea Radio"), [Radio Trøndelag](./Radio_Trøndelag?action=edit&redlink=1 "Radio Trøndelag"), and P5 Fosen (Not to be mistaken for the national P5 Hits) are fully available on DAB+ in Trondheim.

Culture
-------

### Visual arts

The [Trondheim Art Museum](./Trondheim_Art_Museum "Trondheim Art Museum") has Norway's third largest public art collection, mainly Norwegian art from the last 150 years.[[84]](./Trondheim#cite_note-84)

The [National Museum of Decorative Arts and Design](./National_Museum_of_Decorative_Arts_and_Design,_Trondheim?action=edit&redlink=1 "National Museum of Decorative Arts and Design, Trondheim") [[no](https://no.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordenfjeldske%20Kunstindustrimuseum "no:Nordenfjeldske Kunstindustrimuseum")] boasts a large collection of [decorative arts](./Decorative_arts "Decorative arts") and design, including a great number of tapestries from the Norwegian tapestry artist [Hannah Ryggen](./Hannah_Ryggen "Hannah Ryggen"), as well as Norway's only permanent exhibibition of Japanese [arts and crafts](./Handicraft "Handicraft").[[85]](./Trondheim#cite_note-85)

[Trøndelag senter for samtidskunst](./Trøndelag_senter_for_samtidskunst?action=edit&redlink=1 "Trøndelag senter for samtidskunst") (English: Trøndelag Centre for Contemporary Art, TSSK) was established in 1976.[[86]](./Trondheim#cite_note-86)

There are two artist-run spaces, [Galleri Blunk](./Galleri_Blunk?action=edit&redlink=1 "Galleri Blunk") [[no](https://no.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galleri%20Blunk "no:Galleri Blunk")], that was founded by students of the [Trondheim Academy of Fine Art](./Trondheim_Academy_of_Fine_Art "Trondheim Academy of Fine Art") in 2002, and [Babel](./Babel_visningsrom_for_kunst?action=edit&redlink=1 "Babel visningsrom for kunst"), that was founded by Lademoen Kunstnerverksteder (English: Lademoen Artist Workshops, LKV) in 2006.[[87]](./Trondheim#cite_note-87)

[Kunsthall Trondheim](./Kunsthall_Trondheim "Kunsthall Trondheim") was inaugurated at its permanent premises on Kongens gate in October 2016.[[88]](./Trondheim#cite_note-88)[[89]](./Trondheim#cite_note-89)

The [PoMo Museum](./Trondheim_PoMo_Museum?action=edit&redlink=1 "Trondheim PoMo Museum") [[no](https://no.wikipedia.org/wiki/PoMo "no:PoMo")], dedicated to [modern](./Modern_art "Modern art") and [contemporary art](./Contemporary_art "Contemporary art"), opened on Dronningens gate in February 2025.[[90]](./Trondheim#cite_note-90)[[91]](./Trondheim#cite_note-91)

### Stage

The main regional theatre, [Trøndelag Teater](./Trøndelag_Teater "Trøndelag Teater"), is situated in Trondheim. Built in 1816, the theatre is the oldest theatre still in use in Scandinavia.[[92]](./Trondheim#cite_note-92) The city also features an alternative theatre house [Teaterhuset Avant Garden](./Teaterhuset_Avant_Garden?action=edit&redlink=1 "Teaterhuset Avant Garden"), and the theatre company Teater Fusentast.[[93]](./Trondheim#cite_note-93)

### Music

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Ringve_botaniske_hage_1_%2815100598877%29.jpg/250px-Ringve_botaniske_hage_1_%2815100598877%29.jpg)](./File:Ringve_botaniske_hage_1_(15100598877).jpg)

The [Ringve Museum](./Ringve_Museum "Ringve Museum") is a museum devoted to music

Trondheim has a broad music scene, and is known for its strong communities committed to rock, [jazz](./Jazz "Jazz") and [classical music](./European_classical_music "European classical music"). The city's interest in Jazz and classical music are spearheaded by the [music conservatory](./Music_conservatory "Music conservatory") at [NTNU](./Norwegian_University_of_Science_and_Technology "Norwegian University of Science and Technology") which has been called one of the most innovative in the world,[[94]](./Trondheim#cite_note-94) and the municipal music school, *Trondheim Kommunale Musikk- og Kulturskole*.[[95]](./Trondheim#cite_note-95) The [Trondheim Symphony Orchestra](./Trondheim_Symphony_Orchestra "Trondheim Symphony Orchestra") and the [Trondheim Soloists](./Trondheim_Soloists "Trondheim Soloists") are well-known. The city hosts a yearly Jazz festival, and is home to [Trondheim Jazz Orchestra](./Trondheim_Jazz_Orchestra "Trondheim Jazz Orchestra").[[96]](./Trondheim#cite_note-96) The [Fjordgata Records](./Fjordgata_Records "Fjordgata Records") label is also hosted in Trondheim.

Classical artists hailing from Trondheim include violinist [Arve Tellefsen](./Arve_Tellefsen "Arve Tellefsen"), [Elise Båtnes](./Elise_Båtnes "Elise Båtnes") and [Marianne Thorsen](./Marianne_Thorsen "Marianne Thorsen"). Also the [Nidaros Cathedral Boys' Choir](./Nidaros_Cathedral_Boys'_Choir "Nidaros Cathedral Boys' Choir").

[Thomas Bergersen](./Thomas_Bergersen "Thomas Bergersen"), a Norwegian self-taught composer, multi-instrumentalist, and the co-founder of the production music company Two Steps From Hell, was born in Trondheim.

Pop/rock artists and bands associated with Trondheim include [Åge Aleksandersen](./Åge_Aleksandersen "Åge Aleksandersen"), [Margaret Berger](./Margaret_Berger "Margaret Berger"), [DumDum Boys](./DumDum_Boys "DumDum Boys"), [Lasse Marhaug](./Lasse_Marhaug "Lasse Marhaug"), [Gåte](./Gåte "Gåte"), [Keep Of Kalessin](./Keep_Of_Kalessin "Keep Of Kalessin"), [Lumsk](./Lumsk "Lumsk"), [Motorpsycho](./Motorpsycho_(band) "Motorpsycho (band)"), [Kari Rueslåtten](./Kari_Rueslåtten "Kari Rueslåtten"), [the 3rd and the Mortal](./The_3rd_and_the_Mortal "The 3rd and the Mortal"), [TNT](./TNT_(Norwegian_band) "TNT (Norwegian band)"), [Tre Små Kinesere](./Tre_Små_Kinesere "Tre Små Kinesere"), [the Kids](./The_Kids_(Norwegian_band) "The Kids (Norwegian band)"), [Bokassa](./Bokassa_(band) "Bokassa (band)"), Casino Steel (of [the Boys](./The_Boys_(UK_band) "The Boys (UK band)")), Atrox, Bloodthorn, Manes, child prodigy [Malin Reitan](./Malin_Reitan "Malin Reitan") and [Aleksander With](./Aleksander_With "Aleksander With"). The most popular punk scene is [UFFA](./UFFA "UFFA").

[Georg Kajanus](./Georg_Kajanus "Georg Kajanus"), creator of the bands [Eclection](./Eclection "Eclection"), [Sailor](./Sailor_(band) "Sailor (band)") and [DATA](./DATA_(band) "DATA (band)"), was born in Trondheim. The music production team [Stargate](./Stargate_(production_team) "Stargate (production team)") started out in Trondheim.

Trondheim is also home to Rockheim, the national museum of popular music, which is responsible for collecting, preserving and sharing Norwegian popular music from the 1950s to the present day.[[97]](./Trondheim#cite_note-97)[[98]](./Trondheim#cite_note-98)[[99]](./Trondheim#cite_note-99)

### Film

Trondheim features a lively film scene, including three filmfests: Minimalen Short Film Fest and [Kosmorama International Film Fest](./Kosmorama "Kosmorama") in March, and [Trondheim Documentarfestival](./Trondheim_Documentarfestival?action=edit&redlink=1 "Trondheim Documentarfestival") in November. Trondheim has two cinemas in the center of the city, Prinsen Kino and Nova kino [Prinsen Kinosenter](./Prinsen_Kinosenter?action=edit&redlink=1 "Prinsen Kinosenter"), [Nova Kinosenter](./Nova_Kinosenter "Nova Kinosenter")

### Student culture

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Studentersamfundet_i_Trondhjem_from_South-West.jpg/250px-Studentersamfundet_i_Trondhjem_from_South-West.jpg)](./File:Studentersamfundet_i_Trondhjem_from_South-West.jpg)

The building of the [Studentersamfundet i Trondhjem](./Studentersamfundet_i_Trondhjem "Studentersamfundet i Trondhjem")

With students comprising almost a fifth of the population, the city of Trondheim is heavily influenced by student culture. Most noticeable is [Studentersamfundet i Trondhjem](./Studentersamfundet_i_Trondhjem "Studentersamfundet i Trondhjem"), the city's student society. Its characteristic round, red building from 1929 sits at the head of the bridge crossing the river southwards from the city centre. As the largest university in Norway, the [Norwegian University of Science and Technology](./Norwegian_University_of_Science_and_Technology "Norwegian University of Science and Technology") (NTNU) is the host of some 36,000 students.[[100]](./Trondheim#cite_note-100)

Student culture in Trondheim is characterised by a long-standing tradition of volunteer work. The student society is for example run by more than 1,200 volunteers.[[101]](./Trondheim#cite_note-101) [NTNUI](./NTNUI "NTNUI"), Norway's largest sports club, is among the other volunteer organisations that dominate student culture in Trondheim. Students in Trondheim are also behind two major Norwegian culture festivals, [UKA](./UKA_(festival) "UKA (festival)") and [The International Student Festival in Trondheim](./Isfit "Isfit") (ISFiT). NTNU lists over 200 student organisations with registered web pages on its servers alone.[[102]](./Trondheim#cite_note-102)

### In popular culture

Trondheim culture is parodied on the [Monty Python](./Monty_Python "Monty Python") album *[Another Monty Python Record](./Another_Monty_Python_Record "Another Monty Python Record")* in the form of the fictitious Trondheim Hammer Dance.[[103]](./Trondheim#cite_note-103)

Trondheim is also a key location in the *[Command & Conquer: Tiberian Sun](./Command_&_Conquer:_Tiberian_Sun "Command & Conquer: Tiberian Sun")* universe, as it is a critical battleground for both factions.

Trondheim was the name of a planet in the Hundred Worlds of the [*Ender's Game* novel series](./Ender's_Game_(novel_series) "Ender's Game (novel series)").

Trondheim likely serves as an inspiration for the fictional city Tronjheim in [The Inheritance Cycle](./The_Inheritance_Cycle "The Inheritance Cycle").

Sports and recreation
---------------------

[Granåsen Ski Centre](./Granåsen_Ski_Centre "Granåsen Ski Centre"), a [Nordic skiing](./Nordic_skiing "Nordic skiing") venue located in Byåsen, regularly hosts World Cup competitions in [ski jumping](./Ski_jumping "Ski jumping"), [biathlon](./Biathlon "Biathlon") and [cross-country skiing](./Cross-country_skiing_(sport) "Cross-country skiing (sport)"), as well as the [1997](./1997_FIS_Nordic_World_Ski_Championships "1997 FIS Nordic World Ski Championships") and [2025 FIS Nordic World Ski Championships](./FIS_Nordic_World_Ski_Championships_2025 "FIS Nordic World Ski Championships 2025"). Trondheim [attempted but failed](./Trondheim_bid_for_the_2018_Winter_Olympics "Trondheim bid for the 2018 Winter Olympics") to become the Norwegian candidate for the [2018 Winter Olympics](./2018_Winter_Olympics "2018 Winter Olympics"). Hiking and recreational skiing is available around the city, particularly in [Bymarka](./Bymarka "Bymarka"), which can be reached by the tramway. Trondheim Golfklubb, one of the oldest golf clubs in Norway, has a nine-hole golf course in Byåsen. Byneset Golfklubb has a full 18 hole par 72 course, which has hosted the [Norwegian Challenge](./Norwegian_Challenge "Norwegian Challenge") of the [Challenge Tour](./Challenge_Tour "Challenge Tour") in 2012, as well as a short and easy 9 hole course, located at Spongdal. Klæbu Golfklubb in Klæbu has another 9 hole course, albeit with artificial greens. There's also a public (no golf experience of course required) 9 hole par 3 course with a nice view overlooking the city centre at Byåsen.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/Lerkendal_stadion_panorama_-_august_2018.jpg/250px-Lerkendal_stadion_panorama_-_august_2018.jpg)](./File:Lerkendal_stadion_panorama_-_august_2018.jpg)

[Rosenborg](./Rosenborg_BK "Rosenborg BK")'s Lerkendal Stadium.

[Rosenborg BK](./Rosenborg_BK "Rosenborg BK") is the city's only top flight football club. They play their home matches at [Lerkendal Stadion](./Lerkendal_Stadion "Lerkendal Stadion"). They have won the [Norwegian Premier League](./Norwegian_Premier_League "Norwegian Premier League") 26 times between 1967 and 2018, have reached the [UEFA Champions League](./UEFA_Champions_League "UEFA Champions League") group stage 12 times, and made it to the last 8 [on one occasion](./1996–97_UEFA_Champions_League "1996–97 UEFA Champions League"). [Ranheim Fotball](./Ranheim_Fotball "Ranheim Fotball") was promoted from the [Norwegian First Division](./Norwegian_First_Division "Norwegian First Division") to join [Eliteserien](./Eliteserien "Eliteserien") in 2018. They finished seventh in their first season in the top flight, but finished last the following season and was relegated. They have played in the first division since the 2020 season. Ranheim's home ground is the [EXTRA Arena](./EXTRA_Arena "EXTRA Arena").

[Byåsen IL](./Byåsen_IL "Byåsen IL") plays in [the women's handball league](./Eliteserien_(women's_handball) "Eliteserien (women's handball)"), and used to be a regular in the [EHF Women's Champions League](./EHF_Women's_Champions_League "EHF Women's Champions League"), whereas [Kolstad Håndball](./Kolstad_Håndball "Kolstad Håndball") plays in [the men's handball league](./Eliteserien_(men's_handball) "Eliteserien (men's handball)") and have played in the [2023–24](./2023–24_EHF_Champions_League "2023–24 EHF Champions League") and [2024–25](./2024–25_EHF_Champions_League "2024–25 EHF Champions League") seasons of the [EHF Champions League](./EHF_Champions_League "EHF Champions League"). The 2 teams variably play their home games at [Trondheim Spektrum](./Trondheim_Spektrum "Trondheim Spektrum") and [Kolstad Arena](./Kolstad_Arena?action=edit&redlink=1 "Kolstad Arena") [[nb](https://no.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolstad%20Arena "nb:Kolstad Arena")] depending on expected attendances and economic viability.

Trondheim and Trøndelag is also regarded as the home of the [basse](./Basse_(game) "Basse (game)") game, a game played using a ball made from tightly bound rubber bands.

Main article: [Public Transport in Trondheim](./Public_Transport_in_Trondheim "Public Transport in Trondheim")

Trondheim has an international airport, [Trondheim Airport, Værnes](./Trondheim_Airport,_Værnes "Trondheim Airport, Værnes"), situated in [Stjørdal](./Stjørdal "Stjørdal") 32 kilometres (20 mi) away, which is Norway's fourth largest airport in terms of passenger traffic. Værnes has non-stop connections to cities such as [London](./London "London"), [Amsterdam](./Amsterdam "Amsterdam"), [Copenhagen](./Copenhagen "Copenhagen"), and [Stockholm](./Stockholm "Stockholm"), among others. The domestic route Trondheim – Oslo is among the [busiest air routes](./List_of_busiest_passenger_air_routes "List of busiest passenger air routes") in Europe with around 2 million passengers annually.

Trondheim boasts the world's only bicycle lift, *[Trampe](./Trampe_bicycle_lift "Trampe bicycle lift")*.

### Bus

The bus network, operated by [AtB](./AtB "AtB"), runs throughout most of the city and its suburbs. A new metro line system went public 3 August 2019. The new transportation system covers the Trondheim area (Trondheim, Malvik, and Melhus). The three metro lines and the city lines that link the city across. The new public transport system becomes flexible, with buses running more often and accommodating more passengers. Fewer travelers must take a detour through the center of Trondheim, but relies more on bus transits.

In addition, the Nattbuss (Night Bus) service ensures cheap and effective transport for those enjoying nightlife in the city centre during the weekends. The Nattbus has other and more expensive prices than ordinary buses.

### Boats

The Coastal Express ships ([Hurtigruten](./Hurtigruten "Hurtigruten"): Covering the [Bergen](./Bergen "Bergen")–[Kirkenes](./Kirkenes "Kirkenes") stretch of the coast) call at Trondheim, as do many [cruise ships](./Cruise_ship "Cruise ship") during the summer season. Every morning the Hurtigruten ships have one southbound and one northbound arrival and departure in Trondheim.

Since 1994 there is also a fast commuter boat service to [Kristiansund](./Kristiansund "Kristiansund") (via [Brekstad](./Brekstad "Brekstad")), the closest coastal city to the southwest; there is also a second commuter boat service to [Vanvikan](./Vanvikan "Vanvikan").

A [car ferry route](./Flakk–Rørvik_Ferry "Flakk–Rørvik Ferry") from the port of Flakk in the northwest of the municipality, connects Trondheim with [Fosen](./Fosen "Fosen").

### Rail transport

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Trondheim_tram_2.jpg/250px-Trondheim_tram_2.jpg)](./File:Trondheim_tram_2.jpg)

A tram in Trondheim in 2006

Major railway connections are the northbound [Nordland Line](./Nordland_Line "Nordland Line"), the eastbound [Meråker Line](./Meråker_Line "Meråker Line") to [Åre](./Åre "Åre") and [Östersund](./Östersund "Östersund") in Sweden, and two southbound connections to Oslo, the [Røros Line](./Røros_Line "Røros Line") and [Dovre Line](./Dovre_Line "Dovre Line").

Trondheim also boasts the northernmost (since closure of [Arkhangelsk](./Arkhangelsk "Arkhangelsk") tram in 2004) [tramway](./Tram "Tram") line in the world: the [Gråkallen Line](./Gråkallen_Line "Gråkallen Line"), the last remaining segment of the [Trondheim Tramway](./Trondheim_Tramway "Trondheim Tramway"), is an 8.8 kilometres (5.5 mi) route (which is mostly single-track outside the innermost parts of the city; except the stretch between Breidablikk and Nordre Hoem stations) which runs from the city centre, through the [Byåsen](./Byåsen "Byåsen") district, and up to Lian, in the large recreation area [Bymarka](./Bymarka "Bymarka").

### Roads

Norway's longest road, the [European route E6](./European_route_E6 "European route E6") north-south [motorway](./Motorway "Motorway"), passes through Trondheim mostly southeast of the major districts, except a long section between Tiller and Sluppen just north of Nidelva. The eastern terminus for [European route E39](./European_route_E39 "European route E39") is at Klett narrowly within the municipality border, which heads west to [Møre og Romsdal](./Møre_og_Romsdal "Møre og Romsdal").

The later built National Road 706, *Nordre avlastningsvei*, is an alternate bypass that heads northwest instead of northeast at Sluppen, passing through Ila, Piren, and northern Strindheim before rejoining European Route E6 northeast of IKEA. This bypass is slower and has various [roundabout](./Roundabout "Roundabout") crosses.

Various bridge projects over the Trondheim Fjord to replace the car ferry have been planned, but none have begun construction.
