|\\n\\nCityscape\\n---------\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1f/Draak_%C3%96stersund_22jul2006.jpg/250px-Draak_%C3%96stersund_22jul2006.jpg)](./File:Draak_Östersund_22jul2006.jpg)\\n\\n[Storsjöodjuret](./Storsjöodjuret \"Storsjöodjuret\") (the Great lake monster) is a [cryptid](./Cryptid \"Cryptid\") said to inhabit lake [Storsjön](./Storsjön \"Storsjön\"). This figure has often been used as a symbol for Östersund, along with the moose (see above).\\n\\nÖstersund was laid out with roads spanning from north to south countered by several [alleys](./Alley \"Alley\") from east to west, which is why an alley in Östersund is synonymous with a road leading down towards Storsjön. From the inner city one may gaze upon Storsjön, Frösön and the Jamtish [fell](./Fell \"Fell\") region with snow-clad mountains. This was made possible due to the [topography](./Topography \"Topography\") and the [grid plan](./Grid_plan \"Grid plan\").\\n\\nThe regularity in Östersund\\'s road system and the slanting alleys leading from higher altitudes down towards Storsjön have created the \"windows to the west\" characteristic and unique to Östersund as a city.[[17]](./Östersund#cite_note-17) The alleys, often seen as rather steep, have created the illusion that the houses in the city core are climbing to higher grounds. These houses were conformed upon their construction to fit with the slopes.\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/%C3%96stersund_badhusparken.jpg/250px-%C3%96stersund_badhusparken.jpg)](./File:Östersund_badhusparken.jpg)\\n\\nBadhusparken\\n\\nThe first city plan of Östersund was made with several large segments in the core being reserved as [green areas](./Green \"Green\"). Östersund was thus planned as a green city and special lots, e.g. *kryddgårdstomter* \\'spice garden lots\\' were created along with construction lots. These lots shifted with a construction lot alternating with a spice garden lot. The garden lots are no longer existent since they too have been constructed upon. Many of the fences that separated each lot from another with trees and verdure were left intact. The large green areas are still present, with parks such as Kyrkparken, Österängsparken and Badhusparken being the most prominent. Badhusparken was once the location of a large [bath house](./Public_bathing \"Public bathing\") (hence the name *Badhus*-) though it was torn down in 1881 when the railway was constructed. A new larger two-storey pompous bath house was later built on poles a few metres from the shore, enabling the population to bathe in the waters of Storsjön during summers. This house was also torn down when a new bath house with heated water was founded in 1938.[[18]](./Östersund#cite_note-18)\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/%C3%96stersund_winter_festival.jpg/250px-%C3%96stersund_winter_festival.jpg)](./File:Östersund_winter_festival.jpg)\\n\\nThe national romantic Sparbanken building illuminated during the Winter Festival.\\n\\nWhen Östersund started to grow as a city in the late 19th century the houses consisted predominantly of wood, though stone had become popular in the central parts. These houses were heavily characterized by [Neo-Gothicism](./Gothic_Revival_architecture \"Gothic Revival architecture\") and [Neo-Renaissance](./Neo-Renaissance \"Neo-Renaissance\") architecture.[[19]](./Östersund#cite_note-19) A very common feature of these houses were [towers](./Tower \"Tower\"), some even resembling those on old castles like the one on [Hotell Grand](./Hotell_Grand?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Hotell Grand\") at the main square. In the early 20th century a new age had come and in the main road, Prästgatan, the new age came fiercely. The wooden houses were replaced by stone buildings, because a city\\'s well-being was measured in how many stone buildings it had. At the same time [military barracks](./Military_barracks \"Military barracks\") were constructed in connection to the older settlement.[[20]](./Östersund#cite_note-20) [Jugendstil](./Jugendstil \"Jugendstil\") became popular too as an addition to the [National Romantic style](./National_Romantic_style \"National Romantic style\") architecture.\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3c/Storgatan_in_%C3%96stersund.jpg/250px-Storgatan_in_%C3%96stersund.jpg)](./File:Storgatan_in_Östersund.jpg)\\n\\nStorgatan in Östersund with an alley, a window to the west, down towards the Storsjön lake.\\n\\nIn the 1930s, the [functionalistic style](./Functionalism_(architecture) \"Functionalism (architecture)\") made itself apparent in Östersund\\'s outskirts, which were growing. In the 1940s, the city was made more car-friendly and the city was first and foremost planned for cars.[[21]](./Östersund#cite_note-21) Later sanitation issues were brought up, which resulted in the construction of a [sewage treatment works](./Sewage_treatment_works \"Sewage treatment works\") and waste water was no longer flushed directly into Storsjön. Östersund was also affected by the [Million Programme](./Million_Programme \"Million Programme\"), though to a lesser extent than other cities. During the same period older buildings such as Hotell Grand (to make room for Storsjöteatern), Cellfängelset (a jail located at the beginning of Prästgatan), Flickskolan (the girl school next to the city hall, where the current county library is located) and Västra stationen (at Badhusparken) were torn down. The local media described it as \"demolishing madness\".[[22]](./Östersund#cite_note-22) When the Good Templar house was threatened in order to widen Rådhusgatan the city\\'s inhabitants had had enough and the building was saved.\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/Storgatan_%C3%96stersund.jpg/250px-Storgatan_%C3%96stersund.jpg)](./File:Storgatan_Östersund.jpg)\\n\\nStorgatan with a \"spice garden lot\" to the left.\\n\\nThe buildings along Storgatan (literally: \\'the large street\\') with entire segments intact since the 1880s are considered one of the best preserved city settlements in Sweden. The wooden façades are rich with details and the house are relatively low, short and slim. A great amount of work was put down on creating a balance between details and entirety. Parallel with Storgatan lies Prästgatan – \\'the priest street\\', Östersund\\'s main shopping street. The buildings between the two streets are often connected and the streets create small rooms mostly inaccessible for keen winds. These so-called rooms also stimulate the social life on the streets.[*[clarification needed](./Wikipedia:Please_clarify \"Wikipedia:Please clarify\")*]\\n\\nStortorget – the main [town square](./Town_square \"Town square\") in central Östersund is one of six \"closed squares\" built in Sweden, the others being the ones in [Uppsala](./Uppsala \"Uppsala\"), [Karlstad](./Karlstad \"Karlstad\"), [Vimmerby](./Vimmerby \"Vimmerby\"), [Piteå](./Piteå \"Piteå\") and [Haparanda](./Haparanda \"Haparanda\"). It was created through indentation in four different blocks to deliberately create an open air room with openings to every direction, a style deriving from how cities were planned during [the Renaissance](./The_Renaissance \"The Renaissance\"). However the town square lost its original shape when it was opened up and expanded towards the lake. Stortorget has long been the city\\'s main market place and core; it is also here that the thousand-year-old market *[Gregorie market](./Gregorie_market?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Gregorie market\")* is held each year in March. The city festival *[Storsjöyran](./Storsjöyran \"Storsjöyran\")* has Stortorget as its main centre.\\n\\n### Districts and housing estates\\n\\nBefore Östersund was established the population in the area was very scarce. In [Odensala](./Odensala?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Odensala\") and [Torvalla](./Torvalla \"Torvalla\") older settlements existed; the name Odensala can be derived from the Viking age and the Halls of [Odin](./Odin \"Odin\") (though Torvalla means \\'dry wealds\\' with no reference to [Thor](./Thor \"Thor\")). These two villages were later incorporated into Östersund and are today two major urban districts. Besides them the urban districts of [Staden](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staden,%20Östersund \"sv:Staden, Östersund\"), [Norr](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norr,%20Östersund \"sv:Norr, Östersund\"), [Söder](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Söder,%20Östersund \"sv:Söder, Östersund\"), [Odenslund](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odenslund \"sv:Odenslund\"), [Karlslund](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karlslund,%20Östersund \"sv:Karlslund, Östersund\"), [Körfältet](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Körfältet \"sv:Körfältet\"), [Odenskog](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odenskog \"sv:Odenskog\"), [Lugnvik](./Lugnvik \"Lugnvik\") are found on the mainland of Östersund. On the island Frösön are the six urban districts [Hornsberg](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hornsberg,%20Östersund \"sv:Hornsberg, Östersund\"), [Östberget](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Östberget \"sv:Östberget\"), [Frösödal](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frösödal \"sv:Frösödal\"), [Mjälle](./Mjälle?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Mjälle\"), [Valla](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valla,%20Östersund \"sv:Valla, Östersund\") and [Härke](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Härke \"sv:Härke\").\\n\\nThe central parts of Östersund are a part of the urban district *[Staden](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staden,%20Östersund \"sv:Staden, Östersund\")* – \\'the city\\', which has become synonymous with Östersund for many people living in the nearby villages and towns. As Östersund is the only city in the area and nearest city for many it is common to call it *Stan*, though the [dative form](./Dative_case \"Dative case\") *Staa* has increasingly grown unusual. The residents of Östersund are referred to as *östersundare*, though local people in rural areas call them *stassbon* \\'towners\\', and *stassbo* \\'towner\\', in [singular](./Grammatical_number \"Grammatical number\").\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/%C3%96stersund_panorama.jpg/1920px-%C3%96stersund_panorama.jpg)](./File:Östersund_panorama.jpg \"View of district Norr and Staden during early spring, as seen from the hill Östberget in district Hornsberg on the island of Frösön.\")\\n\\nView of district Norr and Staden during early spring, as seen from the hill Östberget in district Hornsberg on the island of Frösön.\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Arctura_natt1.jpg/250px-Arctura_natt1.jpg)](./File:Arctura_natt1.jpg)\\n\\n*Arctura*\\n\\n### Landmarks\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/Ostersund_city_hall.jpg/250px-Ostersund_city_hall.jpg)](./File:Ostersund_city_hall.jpg)\\n\\nÖstersund City Hall\\n\\nThe most well-known landmark of Östersund is the national romantic [Östersund City Hall](./Östersund_City_Hall?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Östersund City Hall\")\\xa0[[sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Östersunds%20rådhus \"sv:Östersunds rådhus\")] (*Östersunds rådhus*). It is 51 meters tall, contains 136 rooms and opened in 1912. It is the greatest constructional symbol of the National Romantic architecture in Östersund.[[23]](./Östersund#cite_note-23) The city hall looks almost like a fortress and has a particular connection to the local art of Jämtland. The [bell tower](./Bell_tower \"Bell tower\") is of typical Jamtish design, shaped like an [onion](./Onion_dome \"Onion dome\"). Local sculptor [Olof Ahlberg](./Olof_Ahlberg \"Olof Ahlberg\") (1876–1956) made most of the sculptural details and the ornaments are made from Jamtish [limestone](./Limestone \"Limestone\").[[24]](./Östersund#cite_note-24)\\n\\nÖstersund City Hall was designed by [Frans Bertil Wallberg](./Frans_Bertil_Wallberg?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Frans Bertil Wallberg\")\\xa0[[sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frans%20Bertil%20Wallberg \"sv:Frans Bertil Wallberg\")] (1862–1935) and was seen by contemporary colleagues as the best of modern Swedish architecture.[[25]](./Östersund#cite_note-25) The main part of the building is accentuated by a grand tower and a monumental stairway. It is accompanied by only one wing, the north wing, as the second, south wing, was torn down in the 1970s.[[26]](./Östersund#cite_note-26)[*[failed verification](./Wikipedia:Verifiability \"Wikipedia:Verifiability\")*]\\n\\nA recently built landmark is *Arctura*, named after Jämtland\\'s provincial star [Arcturus](./Arcturus \"Arcturus\"), a large hot water accumulator tank. Due to its appearance it is referred to as *Termosen* (\\'the [Thermos](./Vacuum_flask \"Vacuum flask\")\\'). At night the 65-meter building is illuminated with various lights to give the appearance of sunrise and the [Aurora Borealis](./Aurora_(astronomy) \"Aurora (astronomy)\"), for example.\\n\\nHistory\\n-------\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/Fr%C3%B6s%C3%B6stenen.jpg/250px-Fr%C3%B6s%C3%B6stenen.jpg)](./File:Frösöstenen.jpg)\\n\\nThe Frösö Runestone is situated on Frösön in Östersund.\\n\\n\\n\\nMain article: [History of Östersund](./History_of_Östersund \"History of Östersund\")\\n\\nLake Storsjön\\'s shores have long been inhabited. The area where Östersund is situated was for a very long time Frösön\\'s link to the east mainland. Frösön, the island of the [Norse god](./Norse_god \"Norse god\") [Freyr](./Freyr \"Freyr\"), was originally the centre of the region and it was here the only inland Scandinavian [hill fort](./Hill_fort \"Hill fort\"), [Mjälleborgen](./Mjälleborgen?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Mjälleborgen\"), was built around 300 AD. The ancient [Scandinavian thing](./Thing_(assembly) \"Thing (assembly)\") [Jamtamót](./Jamtamót \"Jamtamót\") was held on this island, the christening of Jämtland begun here and it was here the world\\'s northernmost raised runestone, [Frösö Runestone](./Frösö_Runestone \"Frösö Runestone\"), was raised.\\n\\nPlans regarding the foundation of a [Swedish city](./Stad_(Sweden) \"Stad (Sweden)\") or *[köping](./Köping \"Köping\")* (market town, \\'Chipping\\') in Jämtland existed among governmental officials already after the previously Norwegian province was ceded from [Denmark-Norway](./Denmark-Norway \"Denmark-Norway\") in 1645. [Queen Christina](./Christina_of_Sweden \"Christina of Sweden\") demanded the establishment of a [sconce](./Sconce_(fortification) \"Sconce (fortification)\") on [Andersön](./Andersön?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Andersön\") shortly after the province became Swedish; this sconce would together with [Frösö sconce](./Frösö_sconce?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Frösö sconce\") secure Swedish control of Jämtland.[[27]](./Östersund#cite_note-27) Christina\\'s intention was to locate the \"Jamts\\' city\" within this [fortification](./Fortification \"Fortification\"). In order to construct the sconce the local inhabitants were coerced into [forced labour](./Forced_labour \"Forced labour\") 1651 but after protests and lack of [capital](./Capital_(economics) \"Capital (economics)\") the project was ended in 1654.\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/Old_%C3%96stersund.png/250px-Old_%C3%96stersund.png)](./File:Old_Östersund.png)\\n\\nÖstersund in the mid-19th century, the church in the picture was the first church in Östersund. When the houses were smaller it dominated the cityscape.\\n\\nIn 1758, the plans were brought back up through an initiative from the chief financial director [Pehr Schissler](./Pehr_Schissler?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Pehr Schissler\") and the proposition did however initiate a new debate whether or not a city was to be established in Jämtland, in order to counteract the trading and [faring traditions](./Jämtland#Provincial_character \"Jämtland\") of Jämtland\\'s farmers.[[5]](./Östersund#cite_note-found-5) Several other attempts at concentration had previously been taken, and deemed unsatisfactory.[[28]](./Östersund#cite_note-28) Östersund was founded and given its charter by Monarch [Gustav III of Sweden](./Gustav_III_of_Sweden \"Gustav III of Sweden\") on 23 October 1786, shortly after the outskirt of the Odensala farmers\\' lands were bought for the purpose. Several other places had been suggested, like [Huså](./Huså?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Huså\"), the then-largest settlement in Jämtland, along with [Krokom](./Krokom \"Krokom\"), [Sunne](./Sunne_(Jämtland)?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Sunne (Jämtland)\") and Ede outside of [Brunflo](./Brunflo \"Brunflo\"). Frösön was also a candidate but the lot fell on Östersund, as it was deemed most favourable.[[5]](./Östersund#cite_note-found-5) The only things actually located in the area at the time were the main road and the bridge to Frösön. Östersund was upon its foundation freed from taxes for a period of 20 years and completely liberated from trade regulations and [guild](./Guild \"Guild\") order.[[5]](./Östersund#cite_note-found-5) In other remote locations of the [Nordic region](./Nordic_region \"Nordic region\"), similar cities were founded, like [Reykjavík](./Reykjavík \"Reykjavík\") in Iceland the very same year, [Tromsø](./Tromsø \"Tromsø\") (1794) in [Northern Norway](./Northern_Norway \"Northern Norway\") and [Tampere](./Tampere \"Tampere\") (1775) and [Kuopio](./Kuopio \"Kuopio\") (1782) in the Finnish [inland](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/inland \"wikt:inland\"). Östersund is however the only city in present-day Sweden to have been founded in the 18th century.[[29]](./Östersund#cite_note-29)\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/%C3%96stersunds_centralstation_01.jpg/250px-%C3%96stersunds_centralstation_01.jpg)](./File:Östersunds_centralstation_01.jpg)\\n\\nThe main railway station was built in 1879\\n\\nThe city developed poorly and had to struggle in its infancy.[[30]](./Östersund#cite_note-30) The state tried to persuade the Jamtish traders on Frösön to migrate to the new city but they had no intentions of leaving such a rich parish with the fertile soils Frösön consisted of in favour of the swamp and marshes across the strait. During its first 50 years the city\\'s population only grew by an average of eight people per year.[[31]](./Östersund#cite_note-Rum-31) The city became the county seat of the newly founded county consisting of the provinces Jämtland and [Härjedalen](./Härjedalen \"Härjedalen\") in 1810, and a county council was established.[[31]](./Östersund#cite_note-Rum-31) Though, Östersund remained a de facto farming village with fewer than 400 inhabitants in 1820.[[32]](./Östersund#cite_note-32) An upswing occurred in the 1850s, as trade was liberalized and the logging industry developed.\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/05/%C3%96stersund%2C_gamla_teatern.jpg/250px-%C3%96stersund%2C_gamla_teatern.jpg)](./File:Östersund,_gamla_teatern.jpg)\\n\\n\"The Old Theatre\", originally built as an [IOGT](./IOGT \"IOGT\") assembly house in 1884. Now a hotel and a restaurant.\\n\\nIt took until the construction of the railroad in 1879 before Östersund became a real city and actually gained the status as Jämtland\\'s centre, at Frösön\\'s expense. Thanks to the \"farmer chieftain\" [Nils Larson i Tullus](./Nils_Larson_i_Tullus?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Nils Larson i Tullus\"), the railroad came to pass through the city itself instead of outside it, as planned. The railway from coast to coast across the then-union between [Sweden and Norway](./Sweden_and_Norway \"Sweden and Norway\") was finished in 1882, connecting Östersund more closely to [Trondheim](./Trondheim \"Trondheim\") and Sundsvall. Östersund then came to grow faster than any other Swedish city. After ten years it had passed 20 Swedish cities in population.[[33]](./Östersund#cite_note-33) The city attracted immigrants, a slight majority from the Jamtish countryside, though still with a high number of settlers from southern Sweden.[[34]](./Östersund#cite_note-34) While Östersund was in its most intense state of growth, [popular movements](./Social_movement \"Social movement\") emerged among the inhabitants. In Jämtland and Härjedalen the [Good Templar movement](./IOGT \"IOGT\") (a part of the [temperance movement](./Temperance_movement \"Temperance movement\")) came to dominate completely. In 1883, 700 of the city\\'s total population of 3,000 were organized Good Templars. The greatest symbol of the movements grandeur was the Order House constructed in 1885 in the city, *Östersunds-Goodtemplars-Ordenshus*. When one of the most prominent leaders, [Joseph Malins](./Joseph_Malins \"Joseph Malins\"), visited the city he announced that it was the world\\'s largest order house.[[35]](./Östersund#cite_note-35)\\n\\nMany of the leading people behind the popular movements in Östersund saw industrialization as a significant threat to the native districts and the old village and farming community. The work from the movements made the city and its centre-right governance extremely hostile to industry. Instead they wanted to portray Östersund as a centre of [outdoor activities](./Outdoor_activity \"Outdoor activity\"), culture, education and tourism. Industry was not allowed to threaten the good environment and [cultural history](./Cultural_history \"Cultural history\") traditions.\\n\\nIn 1917 when the [Great War](./World_War_I \"World War I\") was fought on the continent and with the [February Revolution](./February_Revolution \"February Revolution\") in Russia, the beginning of the [Russian Revolution](./Russian_Revolution_(1917) \"Russian Revolution (1917)\") also affected Östersund. Rationing led to lack of supplies and a revolution was feared. Some of the citizens, primarily soldiers, went on hunger strikes and at the first of May that year 4,000 demonstrators gathered in front of the city hall demanding lower prices on milk and wood. The year after, the [Spanish flu](./Spanish_flu \"Spanish flu\") spread the world. The [city doctor](./City_physician \"City physician\") in Östersund noted that \"Östersund ought without objection to have been more haunted by the flu than any other Swedish city\", which is why Östersund was referred to by locals as *spanska sjukans huvudstad*, \\'capital of the Spanish flu\\'.[[36]](./Östersund#cite_note-36)\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Stora_kyrkan_%C3%96stersund_march_2012.jpg/250px-Stora_kyrkan_%C3%96stersund_march_2012.jpg)](./File:Stora_kyrkan_Östersund_march_2012.jpg)\\n\\nThe large brick church was built in 1940.\\n\\nDespite the [Great Depression](./Great_Depression \"Great Depression\") and several crises resulting in a very high unemployment rate, Östersund continued to grow in the [interwar period](./Interwar_period \"Interwar period\"). In 1918 the Odenslund area was [incorporated](./Municipal_corporation \"Municipal corporation\"). The business sector remained largely unaffected and Östersund continued to be one of the least industrialized cities in Sweden. Instead Östersund continued to focus on wholesale trade and became a centre for it in northern and north-central Sweden. The city\\'s central position was strengthened when the [Inlandsbanan](./Inlandsbanan \"Inlandsbanan\") railway was constructed through Jämtland from the north to the south. The first scheduled bus route was created in the 1920s between Östersund and the nearby town of [Brunflo](./Brunflo \"Brunflo\"). In the next decade well over 40 bus routes were functioning in Östersund. The dairy was located west of the bus square, Gustav III:s torg, at the current site of the shopping mall Kärnan. This square naturally become a central part of the city.\\n\\nÖstersund continued to grow after the [Second World War](./Second_World_War \"Second World War\"). Lugnvik was incorporated into the city in 1954 and Östersund was, like the rest of Jämtland, affected by the [Rehn-Meidner-model](./Rehn-Meidner-model \"Rehn-Meidner-model\"), though not in the same way. The Swedish [Keynesian](./Keynesian \"Keynesian\") policy was launched in order to improve the mobility of the labour force. Jämtland was struck hard by this when the people moved from the countryside to cities, from inland to coast and from the north to the south.[[37]](./Östersund#cite_note-37) As an urban area Östersund was affected by the [Million Programme](./Million_Programme \"Million Programme\") and urban districts like [Körfältet](./Körfältet?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Körfältet\") were created.\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/09/Unofficial_Flag_of_Jamtland.svg/250px-Unofficial_Flag_of_Jamtland.svg.png)](./File:Unofficial_Flag_of_Jamtland.svg)\\n\\nÖstersund became the capital of the Republic of Jamtland. Its [flag](./Flag_of_the_Republic_of_Jamtland \"Flag of the Republic of Jamtland\") can be seen throughout the year at the main town square.\\n\\nThe negative view towards industry changed when the [Social Democrats](./Swedish_Social_Democratic_Party \"Swedish Social Democratic Party\") came to power for the first time in the city\\'s history in 1952. Industries were enticed to Östersund through the national localization policy and industrial areas were created in Odenskog and Lugnvik. Development was not, as already mentioned, as good in the rest of Jämtland as it was in Östersund and as a counter to the governmental policy, the [Republic of Jamtland](./Republic_of_Jamtland \"Republic of Jamtland\") was established in 1963.[[38]](./Östersund#cite_note-38) Östersund became the capital of the tongue-in-cheek republic and the home of the freedom festival [Storsjöyran](./Storsjöyran \"Storsjöyran\").\\n\\nÖstersund continued to grow and in 1970 [Frösö köping](./Frösö_köping?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Frösö köping\") was made part of Östersund. In 1971 a major reform occurred in Sweden creating large municipalities replacing all the older institutions; the new large municipality was named after the city. As in the rest of Sweden, the public sector greatly expanded at this time. In 1960 the public sector of Sweden constituted about 30 per cent of Sweden\\'s total gross domestic product; by the mid-1980s the number had grown to 65 per cent. At the time jobs were growing in the county council, the government and in the new municipality. The main reasons for the large expansion were the expanded [transfer payment](./Transfer_payment \"Transfer payment\") to the households that occurred along with growing interest and public consumption.[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*] Everything was financed by heavy tax increases. The entirety of the 1970s was a period of expansion. Besides the new industrial complex the [Frösö bridge](./Frösö_bridge?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Frösö bridge\") was constructed, a new police station, Z-kupolen (burned to the ground in 1989), Storsjöteatern, [Folkets hus](./Folkets_hus \"Folkets hus\"), neighborhood churches, malls, etc. The county administrative office and the hospital were expanded and large residential areas grew up in the aforementioned Körfältet and Lugnvik areas, as well as in Odensala.\\n\\nAs early as the 1940s, the city tried to have a [humanities](./Humanities \"Humanities\") [university college](./University_college \"University college\") located on Frösön. Opposition between cities in Norrland was great and it was Umeå that finally emerged victorious in 1962. Östersund did, however, get a university college for social workers ([socialhögskola](./Socialhögskola?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Socialhögskola\")\\xa0[[sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialhögskola \"sv:Socialhögskola\")]) in 1971. Since 2005 Östersund has been one of the main campus sites of the [Mid Sweden University](./Mid_Sweden_University \"Mid Sweden University\") (Mittuniversitetet). A number of governmental offices have also been built in the city in recent years.[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*]\\n\\nGarrison town\\n-------------\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/F4tva%29.JPG/250px-F4tva%29.JPG)](./File:F4tva).JPG)\\n\\n[Hangar](./Hangar \"Hangar\") on Frösön\\n\\nÖstersund became a [garrison town](./Garrison \"Garrison\") when the [Norrland Artillery Regiment](./Norrland_Artillery_Regiment \"Norrland Artillery Regiment\") (A 4) was founded in the city in 1892, followed by the upgrading of the [Jämtland Ranger Corps](./Jämtland_Ranger_Corps \"Jämtland Ranger Corps\") to the [Jämtland Ranger Regiment](./Jämtland_Ranger_Corps \"Jämtland Ranger Corps\") (I 23). This was done with the growing fear of a Russian assault whereas Jämtland-Trøndelag and [Norrbotten](./Norrbotten \"Norrbotten\") became the most prioritized defense regions. The [dissolution of the union between Sweden and Norway](./Dissolution_of_the_union_between_Norway_and_Sweden_in_1905 \"Dissolution of the union between Norway and Sweden in 1905\") contributed by enhancing Östersund as a military city and strengthening its presence; the Jämtland Ranger Regiment was located in the city in 1910 and the [Jämtland Wing](./Jämtland_Wing \"Jämtland Wing\") (F 4) came to Frösön in 1926.\\n\\nÖstersund\\'s importance as a garrison town grew when the city was connected to the [Boden Fortress](./Boden_Fortress \"Boden Fortress\"), following the construction of the Inlandsbanan railway.\\n\\nAfter the fall of the [Iron Curtain](./Iron_Curtain \"Iron Curtain\"), the destruction of the [Berlin Wall](./Berlin_Wall \"Berlin Wall\") in 1989 and the [Dissolution of the USSR](./History_of_the_Soviet_Union_(1985–1991)#Dissolution_of_the_USSR \"History of the Soviet Union (1985–1991)\") in 1991 Sweden had lost its national threat and the demand for a strong defense organization was deemed unnecessary. The issue was debated throughout the 1990s and the final decision came in 2004 where all military presence in Östersund was ended. Upon delivering the message the [Swedish Minister for Defence](./Minister_for_Defence_(Sweden) \"Minister for Defence (Sweden)\") [Leni Björklund](./Leni_Björklund \"Leni Björklund\") was publicly [booed](./Booing \"Booing\") by the city\\'s inhabitants.\\n\\nThe ending of Östersund\\'s status as a garrison town has however created larger enthusiasm regarding the city\\'s future[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*] as the [private sector](./Private_sector \"Private sector\") has grown larger and more companies are being established, much of which is due to the financial compensation offered by the state. The older areas reserved for military activities have been opened up and two more urban districts were made available.\\n\\nPolitics and governance\\n-----------------------\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/00/Stadsvapensflagga_framf%C3%B6r_%C3%96stersunds_r%C3%A5dhus.jpg/250px-Stadsvapensflagga_framf%C3%B6r_%C3%96stersunds_r%C3%A5dhus.jpg)](./File:Stadsvapensflagga_framför_Östersunds_rådhus.jpg)\\n\\nÖstersund Municipality is governed from the city hall.\\n\\n\\n\\nMain article: [Östersund Municipality](./Östersund_Municipality \"Östersund Municipality\")\\n\\nÖstersund is the capital of Jämtland County and thus, the county governor [Britt Bohlin Ohlsson](./Britt_Bohlin_Ohlsson?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Britt Bohlin Ohlsson\") resides in the city. Bohlin Ohlsson is the head of [Jämtland County Administrative Board](./County_Administrative_Boards_of_Sweden \"County Administrative Boards of Sweden\") (*Länsstyrelsen i Jämtlands län*), an administrative entity appointed by the [Swedish Government](./Government_of_Sweden \"Government of Sweden\").\\n\\nÖstersund is also the seat of [Jämtland County Council](./Jämtland_County_Council?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Jämtland County Council\") (*Jämtlands läns landsting*). The County Council is the elected assembly of Jämtland County. The County Council\\'s responsibilities lie primarily within the [public health care](./Publicly_funded_health_care \"Publicly funded health care\") system and transportation between the municipalities.\\n\\nÖstersund is the seat of [Östersund Municipality](./Östersund_Municipality \"Östersund Municipality\") (*Östersunds kommun*). The legislative body of the municipality is the 67-member municipal assembly (*[kommunfullmäktige](./Kommunfullmäktige \"Kommunfullmäktige\")*), elected by proportional representation for a four-year term. The assembly appoints the municipality\\'s main governing body, the 15-member executive committee (*kommunstyrelsen*). The executive committee is headed by the Mayor (*kommunstyrelsens ordförande*). Östersund has historically been dominated by [the Conservatives](./Moderate_Party \"Moderate Party\"), [the freeminded](./Liberalism_and_centrism_in_Sweden \"Liberalism and centrism in Sweden\") (later on [Liberal People\\'s Party](./Liberal_People\\'s_Party_(Sweden) \"Liberal People\\'s Party (Sweden)\")) and the [Social Democrats](./Swedish_Social_Democratic_Party \"Swedish Social Democratic Party\"). Though contrary to Sweden on a national level, Östersund\\'s centre-right parties long remained in majority. The situation changed only in 1952 when the Social Democrats were included and they won an absolute majority in 1962. In 1966 the [agrarian and rural](./Nordic_Agrarian_parties \"Nordic Agrarian parties\") [Centre Party](./Centre_Party_(Sweden) \"Centre Party (Sweden)\") entered the scene, along with the minor [Christian Democrat](./Christian_Democrats_(Sweden) \"Christian Democrats (Sweden)\") and [Communist](./Left_Party_(Sweden) \"Left Party (Sweden)\") parties. A new centre-right municipal government was appointed and the Centre Party became the largest party in that coalition in 1970. However, since the 1980s the Social Democratic Party has been in power (excluding a term in the 1990s) supported by the communists (now Left Party) and occasionally the [Green Party](./Green_Party_(Sweden) \"Green Party (Sweden)\") (entered in 1982).\\nJens Nilsson from the Social Democratic Party is the mayor of Östersund and has been so since 1997.[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*]\\n\\nTransport\\n---------\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/%C3%85re_%C3%B6stersund_flygplats.jpg/250px-%C3%85re_%C3%B6stersund_flygplats.jpg)](./File:Åre_östersund_flygplats.jpg)\\n\\nIn 2006 [Åre](./Åre \"Åre\") was included in the airport\\'s name, in order to emphasize its role as a gateway to Sweden\\'s largest ski resort.[[39]](./Östersund#cite_note-39)\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/Fr%C3%B6s%C3%B6bron.jpg/250px-Fr%C3%B6s%C3%B6bron.jpg)](./File:Frösöbron.jpg)\\n\\nFrösö Bridge\\n\\nThe airport is situated 11\\xa0km (7\\xa0mi) outside the city centre, on the island of Frösön. [Åre Östersund Airport](./Åre_Östersund_Airport \"Åre Östersund Airport\") (previously named *Östersunds flygplats*) is an [international airport](./International_airport \"International airport\") and the ninth biggest in Sweden with roughly 390,000 passengers in 2005. The airport is one of few Swedish airports with incoming foreign charter traffic and the only one with considerable economic growth in that sector.[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*]\\n\\nThe [European route E14](./European_route_E14 \"European route E14\") runs through Östersund from Trondheim to [Sundsvall](./Sundsvall \"Sundsvall\") and briefly merges with the [European route E45](./European_route_E45 \"European route E45\") (referred to as [Inlandsvägen](./Inlandsvägen \"Inlandsvägen\") locally) coming from the north. The two roads are later split in [Brunflo](./Brunflo \"Brunflo\") where E14 continues heading east and E45 turns south again.\\n\\nÖstersund has passenger rail services to and from, mainly, Sundsvall and Stockholm. [Norrtåg](./Norrtåg \"Norrtåg\") operates [Mittbanan](./Mittbanan \"Mittbanan\") from [Storlien](./Storlien \"Storlien\") to Sundsvall. [Inlandsbanan](./Inlandsbanan \"Inlandsbanan\") runs in the same directions as European Route 45. Östersund is connected to Stockholm via long distance [SJ 3000](./SJ_3000 \"SJ 3000\") ([higher-speed trains](./Higher-speed_rail \"Higher-speed rail\")), [InterCity](./InterCity \"InterCity\") and night train. There are overnight services to and from [Gothenburg](./Gothenburg \"Gothenburg\") and, seasonally, [Malmö](./Malmö \"Malmö\"). Local company Stadsbussarna i Östersund (literally: \\'the City Buses in Östersund\\') has nine routes in the city.\\n\\nAs Östersund is located on the shores of Storsjön, (English: \\'the great lake\\'), it also has a [harbour](./Harbour \"Harbour\"). There is also a harbour on the Frösö side of the strait. Several bridges span across Storsjön connecting Östersund with communities nearby, [Frösöbron](./Frösöbron?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Frösöbron\") across Östersundet, [Vallsundsbron](./Vallsundsbron?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Vallsundsbron\") from Frösön across Vallsundet to *Annersia* \\'the other side\\' and [Rödöbron](./Rödöbron?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Rödöbron\") from Frösön to Rödön in Krokom Municipality.\\n\\n* [![Östersund\\'s harbour](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/%C3%96stersund_harbour2.jpg/120px-%C3%96stersund_harbour2.jpg)](./File:Östersund_harbour2.jpg \"Östersund\\'s harbour\")\\n\\n  Östersund\\'s harbour\\n* [![City bus](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/Stadsbuss_%C3%B6stersund_2007.jpg/120px-Stadsbuss_%C3%B6stersund_2007.jpg)](./File:Stadsbuss_östersund_2007.jpg \"City bus\")\\n\\n  City bus\\n* [![A train (before 2013) on the line between Östersund and Trondheim](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Mittnabot%C3%A5get_regina.JPG/120px-Mittnabot%C3%A5get_regina.JPG)](./File:Mittnabotåget_regina.JPG \"A train (before 2013) on the line between Östersund and Trondheim\")\\n\\n  A train (before 2013) on the line between Östersund and Trondheim\\n* [![Airport terminal](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/%C3%96stersunds_flygplats%2C_terminal.jpg/120px-%C3%96stersunds_flygplats%2C_terminal.jpg)](./File:Östersunds_flygplats,_terminal.jpg \"Airport terminal\")\\n\\n  Airport terminal\\n\\nTrade and commerce\\n------------------\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/Ostersund.JPG/250px-Ostersund.JPG)](./File:Ostersund.JPG)\\n\\nPrästgatan\\n\\nLike the rest of Jämtland Östersund is heavily dominated by many [small businesses](./Small_business \"Small business\"). The city is the centre of trade and commerce in Jämtland County and has more than 300 shops. The [retail trade](./Retailing \"Retailing\")\\'s [turnover](./Revenue \"Revenue\") is 30 per cent higher than it ought to be, given the number of inhabitants the city has.[[40]](./Östersund#cite_note-40) Trade in the central business district (*Staden* – \\'the city\\') is mostly concentrated on the shopping and pedestrian street Prästgatan where large local shopping malls such as Kärnan and Mittpunkten along with department stores such as [Åhléns](./Åhléns \"Åhléns\") are located. There are large clothing companies such as [H&M](./H&M \"H&M\") and [Lindex](./Lindex \"Lindex\") and smaller ones like [WESC](./WESC \"WESC\"), approximately 50 restaurants, shoe stores, sporting goods retailers like Stadium and [Intersport](./Intersport \"Intersport\"), several supermarkets (Östersund has rather few convenience stores), etc. Storgatan, the street that runs parallel with Prästgatan, is also lined with shops, restaurants and coffeehouses. Unlike Prästgatan this street is not a pedestrian street. Östersund is the city in Sweden with the most square metres of window display per capita.[[41]](./Östersund#cite_note-41) The most prominent figure in Östersund\\'s business life throughout the 20th century was the car salesman (who started out selling horses) [Sven O. Persson](./Sven_O._Persson?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Sven O. Persson\"), founder of [Persson Invest](./Persson_Invest?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Persson Invest\"), [Byggelit](./Byggelit?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Byggelit\") and [Bilbolaget](./Bilbolaget?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Bilbolaget\").[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*] A significant real estate owner was [Maths O. Sundqvist](./Maths_O._Sundqvist \"Maths O. Sundqvist\") (1950–2012).\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/Storgatan_i_%C3%96stersund.jpg/250px-Storgatan_i_%C3%96stersund.jpg)](./File:Storgatan_i_Östersund.jpg)\\n\\nStorgatan in late afternoon.\\n\\nÖstersund has had a long history as a [marketplace](./Marketplace \"Marketplace\") with the already mentioned ancient Gregorie market, tracing its lineage back to the 11th century, held in early March.[[42]](./Östersund#cite_note-42) Despite being banned in 1914, it continued to be held for a couple of years. In 1950, the market was reborn shortly and was completely resurrected in 1986, when the city celebrated its 200th anniversary, and has been held yearly since then.[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*] In 1948, when the markets were non-existent, visions to restore Östersund\\'s market traditions in a modern version were brought up. The result was the [trade fair](./Trade_fair \"Trade fair\") [Expo Norr](./Expo_Norr?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Expo Norr\"), initiated in 1950 in order to strengthen Östersund as a leading centre of trade in the northern parts of Sweden. The trade fair is an annual event just like Gregorie market, though Expo Norr is held during the summer and not during the winter. Expo Norr is usually attended by 30,000 individuals every year.\\n\\nLike many other county capitals in Sweden the [county council](./Jämtland_County_Council?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Jämtland County Council\") and the municipality are among the largest employers.\\n\\nBesides trading and [public services](./Public_services \"Public services\") Östersund has some larger companies such as [Solectron](./Solectron \"Solectron\"), [Cybercom](./Cybercom_AB?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Cybercom AB\"), [Volex](./Volex?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Volex\"), [Husqvarna AB](./Husqvarna_AB \"Husqvarna AB\"), [Swedbank](./Swedbank \"Swedbank\")\\'s telephone bank and [Telia](./Telia_(company) \"Telia (company)\").[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*] Companies such as the dairy cooperation [Milko](./Milko_(Swedish_cooperative) \"Milko (Swedish cooperative)\") and [Inlandsbanan AB](./Inlandsbanan_AB?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Inlandsbanan AB\") have located their [corporate headquarters](./Corporate_headquarters \"Corporate headquarters\") in the city.\\n\\nA national survey done by the [Confederation of Swedish Enterprise](./Confederation_of_Swedish_Enterprise \"Confederation of Swedish Enterprise\") shows that out of every company in Östersund Municipality 52 per cent are \"very positive towards [globalization](./Globalization \"Globalization\")\", thus ranking Östersund at number eight in Sweden as the most globalization-friendly municipality (2008).[[43]](./Östersund#cite_note-43)\\n\\nCulture\\n-------\\n\\n### Cultural venues\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/Thom%C3%A9e.jpg/250px-Thom%C3%A9e.jpg)](./File:Thomée.jpg)\\n\\nS/S *Thomée* moored in the harbour.\\n\\nÖstersund is the cultural centre of Jämtland County and home to the prize winning museum [Jamtli](./Jamtli \"Jamtli\"). The museum has both an indoor exhibition area and an outdoor area which contains a number of historical buildings from all over the county, depicting the old lives of peasants, the early city of Östersund and the Scandinavian inland herding. The museum exhibition hosts an interesting set of tapestries, the *[Överhogdal tapestries](./Överhogdal_tapestries \"Överhogdal tapestries\")*, showing a rich imagery of both Norse and Christian origin from the [Viking Age](./Viking_Age \"Viking Age\"). The mythical [Storsjöodjuret](./Storsjöodjuret \"Storsjöodjuret\") (Great Lake Monster) has an exhibit of its own. Another remnant from the Viking Age is [Frösöstenen](./Frösöstenen \"Frösöstenen\"), one of the world\\'s most northerly rune stones located on Frösön, the island of [Freyr](./Freyr \"Freyr\").\\n\\nThe county library, Jämtlands läns bibliotek, is located in the city. It is the oldest county library in Sweden, being founded in 1816 by the will of professor [Carl Zetterström](./Carl_Zetterström?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Carl Zetterström\"). As the library grew it was moved to a bigger facility. The older building is now situated beside the old church in Kyrkparken.\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d7/Moose_Zoo_%C3%96stersund.jpg/250px-Moose_Zoo_%C3%96stersund.jpg)](./File:Moose_Zoo_Östersund.jpg)\\n\\nMoose Garden\\n\\nLake Storsjön has been trafficked for a long time and the [steamships](./Steamship \"Steamship\") [S/S Thomée](./S/S_Thomée?action=edit&redlink=1 \"S/S Thomée\") and [S/S Östersund](./S/S_Östersund?action=edit&redlink=1 \"S/S Östersund\") are still in operation every summer. Unlike most boats, they are seen as male and not female. S/S Thomée is the only one that sets sail from Östersund\\'s harbour. S/S Östersund sails from Arvesund, located at Storsjön\\'s western shore but makes visits to Jamtli\\'s steamboat jetty.\\n\\n[Frösö Zoo](./Frösö_Zoo \"Frösö Zoo\") was one of Sweden\\'s largest [zoological gardens](./Zoological_garden \"Zoological garden\") with [exotic animals](./Exotic_animal \"Exotic animal\"). Prior to its closing in 2019, it had roughly 700 animals[[44]](./Östersund#cite_note-44) including [Siberian tigers](./Siberian_tiger \"Siberian tiger\"), lions, [polar wolves](./Polar_wolf \"Polar wolf\"), and monkeys. Frösö Zoo also had a tropical house, a biological museum and an [amusement park](./Amusement_park \"Amusement park\"). Outside of Östersund in the village of [Orrviken](./Orrviken \"Orrviken\") there is a moose zoo called [Moose Garden](./Moose_Garden?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Moose Garden\"), allowing close encounters with tame moose.\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/F%C3%A4rgfabriken_norr%2C_%C3%96stersund.jpg/250px-F%C3%A4rgfabriken_norr%2C_%C3%96stersund.jpg)](./File:Färgfabriken_norr,_Östersund.jpg)\\n\\nFärgfabriken Norr\\n\\nFärgfabriken (\\'the paint factory\\') is a centre for experimental culture based in Stockholm that portrays itself as a laboratory of contemporary art. A branch named *Färgfabriken Norr* was established in Östersund between April 2008 and January 2011.[[45]](./Östersund#cite_note-45)\\n\\n[Gaaltije](./Gaaltije?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Gaaltije\"), the centre for [South Sami](./South_Sami \"South Sami\") culture, opened in 1999 and is a living source of knowledge for South Sami culture, history and business.\\n\\n[Gamla Tingshuset](./Gamla_Tingshuset?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Gamla Tingshuset\") holds a small cinema, a café, a small venue and practice halls. It is usually a meeting place for the town\\'s youth.\\n\\n### Events\\n\\n* The city festival [Storsjöyran](./Storsjöyran \"Storsjöyran\") (referred to as simply *Yran*, literally meaning: *[The Great Lake](./Storsjön \"Storsjön\") Giddy Festival*), the oldest city festival in [Scandinavia](./Scandinavia \"Scandinavia\") and with 55,000 visitors every year the largest in Sweden. Storsjöyran is held in the middle of Östersund the last weekend of July. Although the event starts the weekend before with the opening of Krogstråket when regional bars and restaurants gather near the lake.\\n* Jamtli Christmas Market is well attended market taking place the second weekend of [Advent](./Advent \"Advent\").\\n* [Expo Norr](./Expo_Norr?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Expo Norr\"), Sweden\\'s oldest merchandise [trade fair](./Trade_fair \"Trade fair\") held in June with roughly 400 exhibitors.[[46]](./Östersund#cite_note-46)\\n* Vinterparken (\\'The Winter Park\\'), with seasonal lakeside events.\\n\\nMedia\\n-----\\n\\nThe largest daily newspaper in Östersund is *[Östersunds-Posten](./Östersunds-Posten \"Östersunds-Posten\")* (ÖP) with a circulation of 30,000 copies[[47]](./Östersund#cite_note-press-47) and the second largest is *[Länstidningen Östersund](./Länstidningen_Östersund?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Länstidningen Östersund\")* (LT) with a circulation of 15,000 copies[[47]](./Östersund#cite_note-press-47) (2006 for both). Like most Swedish newspaper they each have a political [editorial page](./Editorial_page \"Editorial page\"), views of the [Centre Party](./Centre_Party_(Sweden) \"Centre Party (Sweden)\") are expressed in ÖP and views of the [Swedish Social Democratic Party](./Swedish_Social_Democratic_Party \"Swedish Social Democratic Party\") are expressed in LT. *Länstidningen* is unique in Sweden, as it is the only Swedish newspaper with [press support](./Press_support \"Press support\") that has ever made itself non-dependent on state subsidy. [*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*] Much of the paper\\'s success is ascribed to the then editor-in-chief awarded with the [Grand Journalism Award](./Stora_Journalistpriset \"Stora Journalistpriset\") (*Stora Journalistpriset*).[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*] Since 2006 the newspaper has been dependent on state subsidy. The media group [Mittmedia](./Mittmedia?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Mittmedia\") has owned both newspapers since 2005.[[48]](./Östersund#cite_note-48)\\n\\nTwo [free daily newspapers](./Free_daily_newspaper \"Free daily newspaper\") exist in the city, *[100 procent Östersund](./100_procent_Östersund?action=edit&redlink=1 \"100 procent Östersund\")* and *[Lokaltidningen Storsjön](./Lokaltidningen_Storsjön?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Lokaltidningen Storsjön\")*.\\n\\nLocal radio stations include [Radio Jämtland](./Radio_Jämtland?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Radio Jämtland\") (a part of [Sveriges Radio](./Sveriges_Radio \"Sveriges Radio\")), [One FM](./One_FM_(Sweden)?action=edit&redlink=1 \"One FM (Sweden)\") and [Modern Times Group](./Modern_Times_Group \"Modern Times Group\")\\'s [Rix FM](./Rix_FM?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Rix FM\").\\n\\nFilms shot in Östersund\\n-----------------------\\n\\nThe following feature films have been shot in Östersund:\\n\\n* *[Bitter Flowers](./Bitter_Flowers_(2007_film) \"Bitter Flowers (2007 film)\")*\\n* *[Dunderklumpen](./Dunderklumpen \"Dunderklumpen\")*\\n* *[Marianne](./Marianne_(2011_film) \"Marianne (2011 film)\")*\\n* *[The American](./The_American_(2010_film) \"The American (2010 film)\")*\\n\\nEducation\\n---------\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/Mittuniversitetet_%C3%96stersund.jpg/250px-Mittuniversitetet_%C3%96stersund.jpg)](./File:Mittuniversitetet_Östersund.jpg)\\n\\nMid Sweden university in Östersund\\n\\nÖstersund recently[*[when?](./Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items \"Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers\")*] became a university city and the [Mid Sweden University](./Mid_Sweden_University \"Mid Sweden University\") has its largest campus site in Östersund with well over 7,000 students. The Mid Sweden University was a [university college](./University_college#Sweden_and_Norway \"University college\") (*[högskola](./Högskola \"Högskola\")*) named *Mitthögskolan* until it was granted university status in 2005, making it the youngest university in Sweden. Mitthögskolan was the result of the merger between the University College of Sundsvall/[Härnösand](./Härnösand \"Härnösand\") (*Högskolan i Sundsvall/Härnösand*) and the University College of Östersund (*Högskolan i Östersund*)[[49]](./Östersund#cite_note-49)\\n\\nÖstersund is a centre for the research in social sciences ([business administration](./Business_Administration \"Business Administration\"), [psychology](./Psychology \"Psychology\"), sociology and [political science](./Political_Science \"Political Science\")) and social work, whilst the research in Health Sciences is split between Östersund and Sundsvall.\\n\\nThe city has several secondary schools (*[gymnasieskolor](./Gymnasium_(school) \"Gymnasium (school)\")*) of which [Palmcrantzskolan](./Palmcrantzskolan?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Palmcrantzskolan\") (PC) and [Wargentinsskolan](./Wargentinsskolan?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Wargentinsskolan\") (Wargen) are the two largest. Among the smaller are Storsjögymnasiet, Östersund\\'s gymnasieskola and Dille Gård Naturbruksgymnasium.\\n\\nSports\\n------\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/%C3%96stersunds_skidstadion_Biathlon_WC_2008.JPG/250px-%C3%96stersunds_skidstadion_Biathlon_WC_2008.JPG)](./File:Östersunds_skidstadion_Biathlon_WC_2008.JPG)\\n\\nThe ski stadium of Östersund\\n\\nÖstersund is marketed as the *Winter City* and has a long history of winter sports. It is internationally perhaps most known as one of the regular [Biathlon World Cup](./Biathlon_World_Cup \"Biathlon World Cup\") hosts in late-November and early-December. World Cup competitions have been held there since 1989.[[50]](./Östersund#cite_note-50) The [Biathlon World Championship 1970](./Biathlon_World_Championship_1970 \"Biathlon World Championship 1970\") were hosted in Östersund in [1970](./Biathlon_World_Championship_1970 \"Biathlon World Championship 1970\"), [2008](./Biathlon_World_Championships_2008 \"Biathlon World Championships 2008\") and [2019](./Biathlon_World_Championships_2019 \"Biathlon World Championships 2019\").\\n\\nThe cross-country skiing stadium is located two kilometres (1.2 miles) from the city centre and is one of the most well-equipped and spectator friendly ski stadiums in Sweden. The stadium is also internationally renowned due to the topography of its ski tracks, the compact track-system and the fact that Östersund is usually quite a reliable locality for snow during the winter months. A number of [biathlon](./Biathlon \"Biathlon\") world cup races have been held at the stadium as well as several national championships in cross-country skiing.\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Vy_%C3%B6ver_%C3%96stersund_fr%C3%A5n_Gustavsbergsbacken_p%C3%A5_Fr%C3%B6s%C3%B6n.jpg/250px-Vy_%C3%B6ver_%C3%96stersund_fr%C3%A5n_Gustavsbergsbacken_p%C3%A5_Fr%C3%B6s%C3%B6n.jpg)](./File:Vy_över_Östersund_från_Gustavsbergsbacken_på_Frösön.jpg)\\n\\nÖstersund seen from the piste Gustavsbergsbacken\\n\\n*Nationellt Vintersportcentrum* (NVC, Swedish Winter Sports Research Centre) is a research and training project run by the sports movement, the university, the municipality and the county council. The [Swedish Olympic Committee](./Swedish_Olympic_Committee \"Swedish Olympic Committee\") (SOC) use its lab for various tests.\\n\\nÖstersund, in association with the neighboring municipality of [Åre](./Åre \"Åre\"), had plans to be the candidate of Sweden for the organization of the [XXII Olympic Winter Games](./2014_Winter_Olympics \"2014 Winter Olympics\"), the [2014 Winter Olympics](./2014_Winter_Olympics \"2014 Winter Olympics\"), but the candidacy proposal was rejected by the government. It would have been the fourth attempt of this city (after [1994](./1994_Winter_Olympics \"1994 Winter Olympics\") where Östersund lost [the bid](./Bids_for_Olympic_Games \"Bids for Olympic Games\") with the score 45–39 to [Lillehammer](./Lillehammer \"Lillehammer\") in the final round, [1998](./1998_Winter_Olympics \"1998 Winter Olympics\") and [2002](./2002_Winter_Olympics \"2002 Winter Olympics\")).\\n\\nÖstersund has a basketball team in Sweden\\'s highest division ([Ligan](./Ligan_(basketball) \"Ligan (basketball)\")), [Jämtland Basket](./Jämtland_Basket \"Jämtland Basket\").\\n\\nÖstersund\\'s Fallskärmsklubb is the oldest of Sweden\\'s drop zones and was formed in 1958. The very first civilian parachute jump was done actually on the ice of Storsjön in February 1956. The jumpers were officers from the Swedish Parachute rangers regiment that also wanted to jump on their spare time. Östersund\\'s Fallskärmsklubb is today localized to Optand\\'s airfields, approximately 13\\xa0km (8\\xa0mi) south from Östersund where the education of students and skydiving for experienced jumpers are carried out year-round with the exception of late autumn until early winter.\\n\\nOther sports clubs include:\\n\\n* [IFK Östersund](./IFK_Östersund \"IFK Östersund\")\\n* [Ope IF](./Ope_IF \"Ope IF\")\\n* [Östersunds FK](./Östersunds_FK \"Östersunds FK\")\\n* [Fältjägarnas IF](./Fältjägarnas_IF \"Fältjägarnas IF\")\\n\\n### 2021 Special Olympics World Winter Games\\n\\nÖstersund along with [Åre](./Åre \"Åre\") were originally to host the [2021 Special Olympics World Winter Games](./2021_Special_Olympics_World_Winter_Games \"2021 Special Olympics World Winter Games\"). It would have marked the first time that Sweden had ever hosted the Special Olympics.[[51]](./Östersund#cite_note-51) However, due to lack of funding on 19 December 2019, the event did not take place in Sweden.[[52]](./Östersund#cite_note-52) Instead it was to take place in [Kazan](./Kazan \"Kazan\"), Russia and was delayed to 2022 but was cancelled following Russia\\'s invasion of [ⓘ](/wiki/File:Trondheim.ogg \"File:Trondheim.ogg\")), is a city and [municipality](./List_of_municipalities_of_Norway \"List of municipalities of Norway\") in [Trøndelag](./Trøndelag \"Trøndelag\") county, [Norway](./Norway \"Norway\"). As of 2025, it had a population of 216,518.[[8]](./Trondheim#cite_note-8) Trondheim is the third most populous municipality in Norway, and is the [fourth largest](./List_of_continuously_built-up_areas_in_Norway_by_population \"List of continuously built-up areas in Norway by population\") [urban area](./Urban_area \"Urban area\"). Trondheim lies on the south shore of [Trondheim Fjord](./Trondheim_Fjord \"Trondheim Fjord\") at the mouth of the River [Nidelva](./Nidelva \"Nidelva\"). Among the significant technology-oriented institutions headquartered in Trondheim are the [Norwegian University of Science and Technology](./Norwegian_University_of_Science_and_Technology \"Norwegian University of Science and Technology\") (NTNU), the [Foundation for Scientific and Industrial Research (SINTEF)](./SINTEF \"SINTEF\"), the [Geological Survey of Norway](./Geological_Survey_of_Norway \"Geological Survey of Norway\") (NGU), and [St. Olavs University Hospital](./St._Olavs_University_Hospital \"St. Olavs University Hospital\").\\n\\nThe settlement was founded in 997 as a trading post and served as the capital of Norway through the [Viking Age](./Viking_Age \"Viking Age\") until 1217. From 1152 to 1537, the city was the seat of the Catholic [Archdiocese of Nidaros](./Archdiocese_of_Nidaros \"Archdiocese of Nidaros\"); it then became, and has remained, the seat of the Lutheran [Diocese of Nidaros](./Diocese_of_Nidaros \"Diocese of Nidaros\") and the site of the [Nidaros Cathedral](./Nidaros_Cathedral \"Nidaros Cathedral\"). The city was incorporated in 1838. The current municipality was formed in 1964, when Trondheim merged with [Byneset Municipality](./Byneset_Municipality \"Byneset Municipality\"), [Leinstrand Municipality](./Leinstrand_Municipality \"Leinstrand Municipality\"), [Strinda Municipality](./Strinda_Municipality \"Strinda Municipality\"), and [Tiller Municipality](./Tiller_Municipality \"Tiller Municipality\"), and further expanded on 1 January 2020, when Trondheim merged with [Klæbu Municipality](./Klæbu_Municipality \"Klæbu Municipality\").\\n\\nTrondheim has a mild climate for its northerly latitude, resulting in moderate summers and winters that often remain above the freezing point in seaside areas. At higher elevations, though, the [microclimate](./Microclimate \"Microclimate\") is colder and snowier.\\n\\nThe city functions as the seat of the County Mayor of [Trøndelag](./Trøndelag \"Trøndelag\") county but not as its administrative centre (which is [Steinkjer](./Steinkjer_(town) \"Steinkjer (town)\")). This is designed to avoid making the county administration too [centralized](./Centralized \"Centralized\").\\n\\nTrondheim is home to [football](./Association_football \"Association football\") club [Rosenborg](./Rosenborg_BK \"Rosenborg BK\"), Norway\\'s most successful football club, and [Granåsen Ski Centre](./Granåsen_Ski_Centre \"Granåsen Ski Centre\"), which has hosted the World Championship in [Nordic Skiing](./Nordic_Skiing \"Nordic Skiing\").\\n\\nNames and etymology\\n-------------------\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Flag_of_Trondheim.svg/250px-Flag_of_Trondheim.svg.png)](./File:Flag_of_Trondheim.svg)\\n\\nThe [flag of Trondheim](./Flag_of_Trondheim \"Flag of Trondheim\") is one of the few Norwegian municipal flags that is not the banner of arms of the municipal [coat of arms](./Coat_of_arms \"Coat of arms\").\\n\\n\\n\\nSee also: [Names of Trondheim in different languages](./Names_of_Trondheim_in_different_languages \"Names of Trondheim in different languages\")\\n\\nThe city was established in 997 by [Olav Tryggvason](./Olav_Tryggvason \"Olav Tryggvason\") and it was originally named *Nidaros* ([Old Norse](./Old_Norse_language \"Old Norse language\"): *Niðaróss*). The first element of the name was the local river [Nid](./Nidelva \"Nidelva\"). The last element of the name was *[óss](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/óss#Old_Norse \"wikt:óss\")* which meant \"the mouth of a river\". Thus the name meant \"the outlet of the river [Nid](./Nidelva \"Nidelva\")\". Although the formal name was Nidaros, the city was commonly known as *[kaupangr](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/kaupangr#Old_Norse \"wikt:kaupangr\")*, which means \"city\" or \"marketplace\", or more specifically *kaupangr í Þróndheimi* which means \"the city in Trondheim\". Trondheim ([Old Norse](./Old_Norse_language \"Old Norse language\"): *Þróndheimr*) was the historic name for the whole district which is now known as [Trøndelag](./Trøndelag \"Trøndelag\"). This is the area where the people were known as Trønder (*[þróndr](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/þróndr#Old_Norse \"wikt:þróndr\")*). This district name Trondheim meant \"the home of the Trønder people\" (literally \"Trønder-home\") and Trøndelag ([Old Norse](./Old_Norse_language \"Old Norse language\"): *Þrǿndalǫg*) originally meant the \"law area of the Trønder people\" (literally \"Trønder-law\"). The name of the Trønder people derives from the [Old Norse](./Old_Norse \"Old Norse\") word *[þróndr](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/þróndr#Old_Norse \"wikt:þróndr\")* which is an old present participle of the verb *[þróask](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/þróask#Old_Norse \"wikt:þróask\")* which means \"to grow\" or \"to thrive\".[[9]](./Trondheim#cite_note-9)[[10]](./Trondheim#cite_note-10)\\n\\nDuring the late [Middle Ages](./Middle_Ages \"Middle Ages\"), the city name was commonly shortened to **Þróndheimr**, dropping the *kaupanger* part, and over time the name became *Trondhjem*, using the [Dano-Norwegian](./Dano-Norwegian \"Dano-Norwegian\") spelling rather than the [Old Norse](./Old_Norse \"Old Norse\") spelling since the city was part of the Kingdom of [Denmark-Norway](./Denmark-Norway \"Denmark-Norway\") for centuries.\\n\\nOn 21 December 1917, a [royal resolution](./Royal_decree \"Royal decree\") enacted the [1917 Norwegian language reforms](./Norwegian_language_conflict \"Norwegian language conflict\"). Around the time, many municipalities and cities had their names changed to \"Norwegianize\" the spelling and make them look less [Danish](./Danish_language \"Danish language\"). On 1 January 1919, the name of the local [Church of Norway](./Church_of_Norway \"Church of Norway\") diocese was changed from **Trondhjem stift** to **Nidaros bispedømme** (English: [Diocese of Nidaros](./Diocese_of_Nidaros \"Diocese of Nidaros\")).[[11]](./Trondheim#cite_note-11) In 1924, the name of the Norwegian capital city was changed from *Kristiania* to [Oslo](./Oslo \"Oslo\"), removing the name referencing a Danish King in favor of the very old name Oslo. In 1928, a [referendum](./Referendum \"Referendum\") in Trondhjem was held on whether to keep the current name or to bring back the original name of *Nidaros*. The vote resulted in 17,163 votes in favour of *Trondhjem* and only 1,508 votes in favour of Nidaros.[[12]](./Trondheim#cite_note-12) Despite this result, the [Storting](./Storting \"Storting\") voted in 1929 to make some changes. The [Trondhjem Cathedral](./Nidaros_Cathedral \"Nidaros Cathedral\") would be changed to [Nidaros Cathedral](./Nidaros_Cathedral \"Nidaros Cathedral\") effective on 1 July 1929[[13]](./Trondheim#cite_note-13) and the name of the city would change to *Nidaros* starting on 1 January 1930.[[14]](./Trondheim#cite_note-14) This change caused public outrage and even [riots](./Riot \"Riot\") during 1930. This forced the [Storting](./Storting \"Storting\") to reconsider this change. On 6 March 1931, the name was formally changed to *Trondheim*, using the medieval Norwegian spelling instead of the Danish version *Trondhjem*. The name of the diocese and cathedral, however, continued using the name Nidaros.[[15]](./Trondheim#cite_note-15)\\n\\nTrondheim was briefly named **Drontheim** during the [Second World War](./Second_World_War \"Second World War\") as a [German exonym](./German_exonyms \"German exonyms\").\\n\\nHistory\\n-------\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Lykkens_Portal%2C_Gamble_Bybro%2C_Trondheim%2C_West_view_20150605_1.jpg/250px-Lykkens_Portal%2C_Gamble_Bybro%2C_Trondheim%2C_West_view_20150605_1.jpg)](./File:Lykkens_Portal,_Gamble_Bybro,_Trondheim,_West_view_20150605_1.jpg)\\n\\nThe [Old Town Bridge](./Old_Town_Bridge \"Old Town Bridge\") of Trondheim\\n\\n\\n\\nFor the ecclesiastical history, see [Archiepiscopate of Nidaros](./Archiepiscopate_of_Nidaros \"Archiepiscopate of Nidaros\").\\n\\nTrondheim was named Kaupangen (English: market place or trading place) by [Viking](./Viking \"Viking\") [King](./King_of_Norway \"King of Norway\") [Olav Tryggvason](./Olav_Tryggvason \"Olav Tryggvason\") in 997 CE.[[16]](./Trondheim#cite_note-16) Shortly after that, it came to be called *[Nidaros](./Nidaros \"Nidaros\")*. Initially, it was frequently used as a military retainer ([Old Norse](./Old_Norse \"Old Norse\"): \"hird\"-man) of King Olav I. It was also frequently used as the king\\'s seat and was Norway\\'s capital until 1217.\\n\\nPeople have lived in the area for thousands of years, as evidenced by the [rock carvings in central Norway](./Rock_carvings_in_Central_Norway \"Rock carvings in Central Norway\"), the [Nøstvet and Lihult cultures](./Nøstvet_and_Lihult_cultures \"Nøstvet and Lihult cultures\"), and the [Corded Ware culture](./Corded_Ware_culture \"Corded Ware culture\"). In ancient times, the [kings of Norway](./List_of_Norwegian_monarchs \"List of Norwegian monarchs\") were hailed in Trondheim at [Øretinget](./Øretinget \"Øretinget\"), the place for the assembly of all free men by the mouth of the River [Nidelva](./Nidelva \"Nidelva\"). [Harald Fairhair](./Harald_Fairhair \"Harald Fairhair\") (865–933) was hailed as the king here, as was his son, [Haakon I](./Haakon_I_of_Norway \"Haakon I of Norway\"), called \\'the Good.\\' The battle of *[Kalvskinnet](./Kalvskinnet \"Kalvskinnet\")* took place in Trondheim in 1179: King [Sverre Sigurdsson](./Sverre_Sigurdsson \"Sverre Sigurdsson\") and his *[Birkebeiner](./Birkebeiner \"Birkebeiner\")* warriors were victorious against [Erling Skakke](./Erling_Skakke \"Erling Skakke\") (a rival to the throne). Some scholars believe that the famous [Lewis chessmen](./Lewis_chessmen \"Lewis chessmen\"), 12th-century chess pieces carved from walrus ivory that were found in the [Hebrides](./Hebrides \"Hebrides\") and are now at the [British Museum](./British_Museum \"British Museum\"), may have been made in Trondheim.[[17]](./Trondheim#cite_note-17)\\n\\nFrom 1152, Trondheim was the seat of the [Archbishop of Nidaros](./Roman_Catholic_Archdiocese_of_Nidaros \"Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Nidaros\") for Norway, which operated from the [Archbishop\\'s Palace](./Archbishop\\'s_Palace,_Trondheim \"Archbishop\\'s Palace, Trondheim\"). Due to the introduction of [Lutheran](./Lutheranism \"Lutheranism\") Protestantism in 1537, the last archbishop, [Olav Engelbrektsson](./Olav_Engelbrektsson \"Olav Engelbrektsson\"), had to flee from the city to the [Netherlands](./Seventeen_Provinces \"Seventeen Provinces\"); he died in what today is [Lier, Belgium](./Lier,_Belgium \"Lier, Belgium\").\\n\\nFrom the 16th through the 19th centuries, the city was repeatedly ravaged by fires that caused widespread damage since many of its buildings were made of wood. The worst occurred in 1598, 1651, 1681, 1708, 1717 (twice), 1742, 1788, 1841 and 1842. The 1651 fire destroyed 90% of all buildings within the city limits. After the \"[Horneman Fire](./1681_Trondheim_fire \"1681 Trondheim fire\")\" in 1681, there was an almost total reconstruction of the city, overseen by General [Johan Caspar von Cicignon](./Johan_Caspar_von_Cicignon \"Johan Caspar von Cicignon\"), originally from [Luxembourg](./Luxembourg \"Luxembourg\"). Broad avenues, such as Munkegata, were created, without regard for private property rights, to limit the damage from future fires. At the time, the city had a population of under 10,000 inhabitants, with most living in the downtown area.[[18]](./Trondheim#cite_note-18)[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*]\\n\\nAfter the [Treaty of Roskilde](./Treaty_of_Roskilde \"Treaty of Roskilde\") on 26 February 1658, Trondheim and the rest of [Trøndelag](./Trøndelag \"Trøndelag\") became Swedish territory briefly. [However, after a three-month long siege](./Siege_of_Trondheim \"Siege of Trondheim\"), the area was reconquered 10 months later.[[19]](./Trondheim#cite_note-19) The conflict was finally settled by the [Treaty of Copenhagen](./Treaty_of_Copenhagen_(1660) \"Treaty of Copenhagen (1660)\") on 27 May 1660.\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/Trondheim_map_1898.jpg/250px-Trondheim_map_1898.jpg)](./File:Trondheim_map_1898.jpg)\\n\\nCity Map of Trondheim in 1898, Norwegian edition\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Plan_of_Trondheim%2C_1942.jpg/250px-Plan_of_Trondheim%2C_1942.jpg)](./File:Plan_of_Trondheim,_1942.jpg)\\n\\nPlan of Trondheim, 1942\\n\\nDuring the [Second World War](./Second_World_War \"Second World War\"), Trondheim was occupied by [Nazi Germany](./Nazi_Germany \"Nazi Germany\") from 9 April 1940, the first day of the [invasion of Norway](./Operation_Weserübung \"Operation Weserübung\"), until the end of the war in Europe, [8 May 1945](./VE_Day \"VE Day\"). The German invasion force consisted of the [German cruiser Admiral Hipper](./German_cruiser_Admiral_Hipper \"German cruiser Admiral Hipper\"), 4 destroyers and 1700 Austrian Mountain troops. Except for a coastal battery that opened fire, there was no resistance to the invasion, which began on 9 April at 5 AM. On 14 and 17 April, British and French forces landed near Trondheim in a failed attempt to liberate Trondheim, as part of the [Namsos Campaign](./Namsos_Campaign \"Namsos Campaign\").[[20]](./Trondheim#cite_note-20) During the occupation, Trondheim was the home of the notorious Norwegian Gestapo agent, [Henry Rinnan](./Henry_Rinnan \"Henry Rinnan\"), who operated from a nearby villa and infiltrated Norwegian resistance groups. The city and its citizens were subjected to harsh treatment by the occupying power, including the imposition of [martial law](./Martial_law_in_Trondheim_in_1942 \"Martial law in Trondheim in 1942\") in October 1942. During this time, the Germans turned the city and its environs into a major base for submarines (which included building the large submarine base and bunker [DORA I](./Dora_I \"Dora I\")), and contemplated a scheme to build a new city for 300,000 inhabitants, *[Nordstern](./Nordstern_(city) \"Nordstern (city)\")* (\"Northern Star\"), centred 15 kilometres (9 miles) southwest of Trondheim, near the wetlands of [Øysand](./Øysand \"Øysand\") on the outskirts of [Melhus](./Melhus_Municipality \"Melhus Municipality\") municipality. This new metropolis was to be accompanied by a massively expanded version of the already existing naval base, which was intended to become the future primary stronghold of the German [Kriegsmarine](./Kriegsmarine \"Kriegsmarine\"). A start was made on this enormous construction project, but it was far from completed when the war ended, and today, there are few physical remains of it.[[21]](./Trondheim#cite_note-21)\\n\\n### Municipal history\\n\\nThe city of Trondheim was established on 1 January 1838 (see [formannskapsdistrikt](./Formannskapsdistrikt \"Formannskapsdistrikt\") law). On 1 January 1864, part of [Strinda Municipality](./Strinda_Municipality \"Strinda Municipality\") (population: 1,229) was amalgamated with Trondheim. Then, on 1 January 1893, another part of Strinda Municipality (population: 4,097) was transferred to Trondheim Municipality. On 1 January 1952, the [Lade](./Lade,_Trondheim \"Lade, Trondheim\") area of Strinda Municipality (population: 2,230) was transferred to Trondheim Municipality. On 1 January 1964, a major municipal merger took place: [Leinstrand Municipality](./Leinstrand_Municipality \"Leinstrand Municipality\") (population: 4,193), [Byneset Municipality](./Byneset_Municipality \"Byneset Municipality\") (population: 2,049), Strinda Municipality (population: 44,600), and [Tiller Municipality](./Tiller_Municipality \"Tiller Municipality\") (population: 3,595) were all merged with the city of Trondheim (population: 56,982), which nearly doubled the population of the municipality.[[22]](./Trondheim#cite_note-22) On 1 January 2020, the neighboring [Klæbu Municipality](./Klæbu_Municipality \"Klæbu Municipality\") (population: 6,050) was merged with Trondheim Municipality.[[23]](./Trondheim#cite_note-23)\\n\\n### Coat of arms and seal\\n\\nSee also: [Flag of Trondheim](./Flag_of_Trondheim \"Flag of Trondheim\")\\n\\nThe [coat of arms](./Coat_of_arms \"Coat of arms\") dates back to the 13th century. To the left, there is an [archbishop](./Archbishop \"Archbishop\") with his staff and [mitre](./Mitre \"Mitre\") in a church archway. On the right, a crowned king holding scales in a castle archway. These two pictures rest on a base which forms an arch. Underneath that arch, are three male heads which symbolise the city\\'s rank as Norway\\'s first capital and the archbishop\\'s place of residence. The scales symbolise justice and the [motif](./Motif_(visual_arts) \"Motif (visual arts)\") is based on the political philosophy of the 13th century, where the balance of power between king and church was an important issue. The three heads at the bottom may symbolise the city council. The motif is unique in Norwegian municipal heraldry, but similar motifs are found in bishopric cities on the continent. The design of the coat-of-arms that was adopted in 1897, and is still used today, was made by Håkon Thorsen.[[24]](./Trondheim#cite_note-24)\\n\\nGeography\\n---------\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/13/Nidelva-Trondheim-foliage.JPG/250px-Nidelva-Trondheim-foliage.JPG)](./File:Nidelva-Trondheim-foliage.JPG)\\n\\nAutumn [foliage](./Foliage \"Foliage\") along Nidelva; October 2009\\n\\nTrondheim is situated where the River Nidelva meets [Trondheim Fjord](./Trondheim_Fjord \"Trondheim Fjord\") with an excellent harbour and sheltered condition. In the Middle Ages the river was deep enough to be navigable by most boats. However, in the mid–17th century, an avalanche of mud and stones made it less navigable, and partly ruined the harbour. The municipality\\'s highest elevation is the [Storheia](./Storheia \"Storheia\") hill, 565 metres (1,854\\xa0ft) [above sea level](./Above_mean_sea_level \"Above mean sea level\"). At the summer [solstice](./Solstice \"Solstice\"), the sun rises at 03:00 and sets at 23:40, and then stays just below the horizon. Between 23 May and 19 July, when the sky is cloud-free, it remains light enough at night that no artificial lighting is needed outdoors.[[25]](./Trondheim#cite_note-25) At the winter solstice, the sun rises at 10:01, stays very low above the horizon (at midday its altitude is slightly more than 3 degrees over the horizon), and sets at 14:31.\\n\\n### Climate\\n\\nTrondheim city has an [oceanic climate](./Oceanic_climate \"Oceanic climate\") ([Cfb](./Köppen_climate_classification \"Köppen climate classification\")) or [humid continental climate](./Humid_continental_climate \"Humid continental climate\") (Dfb), depending on the winter threshold used (−3\\xa0°C or 0\\xa0°C). Winters are fairly cold and summers are mild. The part of the municipality further away from the fjord has slightly colder winters, while the part close to the fjord has the mildest winters. Trondheim is mostly sheltered from the strong south and southwesterly winds which can occur along the outer seaboard but is more exposed to northwesterly winds. As with the rest of Norway, the weather is dependent on the weather pattern. High pressure over Central Norway or to the east can last for weeks, while Atlantic Lows from the west also can dominate for weeks. Such stuck opposite weather patterns was evident in 2020, when May saw northwesterlies with cold air even bringing some snowfall, while the following June was warm and sunny. Trondheim experiences moderate snowfall from November to March,[[26]](./Trondheim#cite_note-26) but mixed with mild weather and rainfall. There is often more snow and later snowmelt in suburban areas at a higher elevation, with good skiing conditions in [Bymarka](./Bymarka \"Bymarka\"). All the monthly record lows are from 1955 or older, with half of them from before 1920. The last overnight frost in June was in 1958. The all-time low −26\\xa0°C (−14.8\\xa0°F) was recorded February 1899. The all-time high 35\\xa0°C (95\\xa0°F) was recorded 22 July 1901.\\nThe earliest weather stations were located closer to the city centre, from 1945 onwards the weather station has been located at a higher elevation (Voll, 127 m and Tyholt, 113 m), therefore being slightly colder.\\nA new sunrecorder was established in the city by met.no at [Gløshaugen](./Gløshaugen \"Gløshaugen\") (NTNU campus) December 2015, recording more sunhours than the earlier sunrecorder, which had terrain blocking issues.[[27]](./Trondheim#cite_note-27) There are on average 229 sunhours in July (based 2016–2020).[[28]](./Trondheim#cite_note-28) Trondheim recorded 197 sunhours in October 2016 beating the previous national record for October. In April 2019, Trondheim recorded 308 sunhours, setting a new national record for April.[[29]](./Trondheim#cite_note-29)[[30]](./Trondheim#cite_note-30) In contrast, December 2016 only recorded 10 sunhours.\\n\\nLocated at 63 degrees north, Trondheim experience \"white nights\" with only civil twilight during the height of summer.
