| | | | | | | | | | | | |\\n\\n### Fauna\\n\\nThe city has various wetland [habitats](./Habitat \"Habitat\"). among which there is the *Gaulosen.* The observation tower accommodates for birdwatching and providing information about birdlife.[[34]](./Trondheim#cite_note-34)\\n\\nThough Trondheim is Norway\\'s third largest city, wild animals are regularly seen. [Otters](./European_otter \"European otter\") and [beavers](./European_beaver \"European beaver\") thrive in Nidelva and Bymarka.[[35]](./Trondheim#cite_note-35) [Badgers](./Eurasian_badger \"Eurasian badger\") and [red foxes](./Red_fox \"Red fox\") are not uncommon sights. [Moose](./Moose \"Moose\") and [deer](./Deer \"Deer\") are common in the hills surrounding the city, and might wander into the city, especially in May when the one-year-olds are chased away by their mothers, or in late winter when food grows scarce in the snow-covered higher regions. From 2002 until 2017, a [wolverine](./Wolverine \"Wolverine\") lived in Bymarka.[[36]](./Trondheim#cite_note-36)[[37]](./Trondheim#cite_note-37)\\n\\nCityscape and sites\\n-------------------\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/TrondheimFromRoofOfNidarosdomen-improved.jpg/250px-TrondheimFromRoofOfNidarosdomen-improved.jpg)](./File:TrondheimFromRoofOfNidarosdomen-improved.jpg)\\n\\nCentral Trondheim as seen from the tower of the Nidaros Cathedral looking towards [Trondheim Fjord](./Trondheim_Fjord \"Trondheim Fjord\") and [Munkholmen](./Munkholmen \"Munkholmen\") Island\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Torvet_i_Trondheim%2C_2020.jpg/250px-Torvet_i_Trondheim%2C_2020.jpg)](./File:Torvet_i_Trondheim,_2020.jpg)\\n\\nThe city\\'s central square (Torvet) in 2020\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/Bakklandet_in_Trondheim_4.jpg/250px-Bakklandet_in_Trondheim_4.jpg)](./File:Bakklandet_in_Trondheim_4.jpg)\\n\\nThe pavement cafes at Bakklandet\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9c/Trondheim-Drone-20160722-009.jpg/250px-Trondheim-Drone-20160722-009.jpg)](./File:Trondheim-Drone-20160722-009.jpg)\\n\\nBakke Bridge\\n\\n[DORA 1](./DORA_1 \"DORA 1\") is a [German submarine](./U-boat \"U-boat\") base that housed the [13th U-boat Flotilla](./13th_U-boat_Flotilla \"13th U-boat Flotilla\") during the Second World War occupation of Norway. Today the bunker houses various archives, among them the city archives, the university and state archives. More recently, DORA has been used as a concert venue.\\n\\n[Kristiansten Fortress](./Kristiansten_Fortress \"Kristiansten Fortress\"), built 1681–1684, is located on a hill east of Trondheim. It repelled the invading [Swedes](./Sweden \"Sweden\") in 1718, but was decommissioned in 1816 by Crown Prince Regent [Charles John](./Charles_XIV_John_of_Sweden \"Charles XIV John of Sweden\").\\n\\nA [statue of Olav Tryggvason](./Olav_Tryggvason_(statue) \"Olav Tryggvason (statue)\"), the founder of Trondheim, is located in the city\\'s central square, mounted on top of an obelisk. The statue base is also a [sun dial](./Sun_dial \"Sun dial\"), but it is calibrated to UTC+1 so that the reading is inaccurate by one hour in the summer.\\n\\nThe islet Munkholmen is a popular tourist attraction and recreation site. The islet has served as a place of execution, a [monastery](./Monastery \"Monastery\"), a [fortress](./Fortress \"Fortress\"), [prison](./Prison \"Prison\"), and a Second World War [anti-aircraft](./Anti-aircraft \"Anti-aircraft\") gun station.\\n\\n[Stiftsgården](./Stiftsgården \"Stiftsgården\") is the royal residence in Trondheim, originally constructed in 1774 by [Cecilie Christine Schøller](./Cecilie_Christine_Schøller \"Cecilie Christine Schøller\"). At 140 rooms constituting 4,000 square metres (43,056\\xa0sq\\xa0ft), it is possibly the largest wooden building in [Northern Europe](./Northern_Europe \"Northern Europe\") and has been used by royals and their guests since 1800.\\n\\nA statue of [Leif Ericson](./Leif_Ericson \"Leif Ericson\") is located at the seaside, close to the old Customs Building, the cruise ship facilities and the new swimming hall. The statue is a replica, the original being located at a Seattle [marina](./Marina \"Marina\").\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/Edificios_a_lo_largo_del_r%C3%ADo_Nidelva%2C_Trondheim%2C_Noruega%2C_2019-09-06%2C_DD_46-50_PAN.jpg/960px-Edificios_a_lo_largo_del_r%C3%ADo_Nidelva%2C_Trondheim%2C_Noruega%2C_2019-09-06%2C_DD_46-50_PAN.jpg)](./File:Edificios_a_lo_largo_del_río_Nidelva,_Trondheim,_Noruega,_2019-09-06,_DD_46-50_PAN.jpg)\\n\\nThe [Nidelva](./Nidelva \"Nidelva\") flows through Trondheim with old storehouses flanking both sides of this river. The [Old Town Bridge](./Old_Town_Bridge \"Old Town Bridge\") can be seen on the right side of this panorama.\\n\\n### Shopping\\n\\nMost of Trondheim\\'s city centre is scattered with small speciality shops. However, the city centre\\'s main shopping area is concentrated around the pedestrianised streets *Nordre gate* (English: Northern street), *Olav Tryggvasons gate* and *Thomas Angells gate* even though the rest of the city centre is provided with everything from old, well-established companies to new, hip and trendy shops.\\n\\nIn the mid-to-late 1990s, the area surrounding the old [drydock](./Drydock \"Drydock\") and ship construction buildings of the defunct [Trondhjems mekaniske Værksted](./Trondhjems_mekaniske_Værksted \"Trondhjems mekaniske Værksted\") shipbuilding company at the [Nedre Elvehavn](./Nedre_Elvehavn \"Nedre Elvehavn\") was renovated and old industrial buildings were torn down to make way for condominiums. A shopping centre was also built, known as Solsiden (The Sunny Side). This is a popular residential and shopping area, especially for young people.\\n\\nLarger multi-mall shopping areas are located in the eastern suburb of Lade-Strindheim along the *Haakon VIIs gate* and *Bromstadvegen* streets, and in the southern suburb of Tiller (The latter centred around [City Syd](./City_Syd \"City Syd\")). Swedish store chains are widely present throughout the areas, especially in the DIY and clothing store fields, including [IKEA](./IKEA \"IKEA\"), [Biltema](./Biltema \"Biltema\"), and [Clas Ohlson](./Clas_Ohlson \"Clas Ohlson\").\\n\\n### Nidaros Cathedral\\n\\nThe [Nidaros Cathedral](./Nidaros_Cathedral \"Nidaros Cathedral\") and the Archbishop\\'s Palace are located side by side in the middle of the city centre. The cathedral, built from 1070 on, is the most important [Gothic](./Gothic_architecture \"Gothic architecture\") monument in Norway and was Northern Europe\\'s most important Christian [pilgrimage](./Pilgrimage \"Pilgrimage\") site during the Middle Ages,[[38]](./Trondheim#cite_note-38) with pilgrimage routes leading to it from [Oslo](./Oslo \"Oslo\") in southern Norway and from the [Jämtland](./Jämtland \"Jämtland\") and [Värmland](./Värmland \"Värmland\") regions of Sweden. Today, it is the northernmost medieval cathedral in the world, and the second-largest in [Scandinavia](./Scandinavia \"Scandinavia\").\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/Nidaros_cathedral_front.jpg/250px-Nidaros_cathedral_front.jpg)](./File:Nidaros_cathedral_front.jpg)\\n\\nWest front of [Nidaros Cathedral](./Nidaros_Cathedral \"Nidaros Cathedral\")\\n\\nDuring the Middle Ages, and again after independence was restored in 1814, the Nidaros Cathedral was the [coronation](./Coronation \"Coronation\") church of the Norwegian kings. [King Haakon VII](./Haakon_VII_of_Norway \"Haakon VII of Norway\") was the last monarch to be crowned there, in 1906. Starting with [King Olav V](./Olav_V_of_Norway \"Olav V of Norway\") in 1957, coronation was replaced by [consecration](./Consecration \"Consecration\"). In 1991, the present [King Harald V](./Harald_V_of_Norway \"Harald V of Norway\") and [Queen Sonja](./Queen_Sonja_of_Norway \"Queen Sonja of Norway\") were consecrated in the cathedral.[[39]](./Trondheim#cite_note-39) On 24 May 2002, their daughter [Princess Märtha Louise](./Princess_Märtha_Louise_of_Norway \"Princess Märtha Louise of Norway\") married the writer [Ari Behn](./Ari_Behn \"Ari Behn\") in the cathedral.[[40]](./Trondheim#cite_note-40)\\n\\nThe [Pilgrim\\'s Route](./Pilgrim\\'s_Route \"Pilgrim\\'s Route\") (*Pilegrimsleden*) to the site of Saint Olufs\\'s tomb at [Nidaros](./Nidaros \"Nidaros\") Cathedral, has recently been re-instated. Also known as St. Olav\\'s Way, (*Sankt Olavs vei*), the main route, which is approximately 640 kilometres (400\\xa0mi) long, starts in [Oslo](./Oslo \"Oslo\") and heads North, along Lake [Mjøsa](./Mjøsa \"Mjøsa\"), up the valley [Gudbrandsdalen](./Gudbrandsdalen \"Gudbrandsdalen\"), over the mountain range [Dovrefjell](./Dovrefjell \"Dovrefjell\") and down the [Oppdal](./Oppdal_Municipality \"Oppdal Municipality\") valley to end at [Nidaros Cathedral](./Nidaros_Cathedral \"Nidaros Cathedral\") in Trondheim. There is a Pilgrim\\'s Office in Oslo which gives advice to pilgrims and a Pilgrim Centre in Trondheim, under the [aegis](./Aegis \"Aegis\") of the cathedral, which awards certificates to successful [pilgrims](./Pilgrims \"Pilgrims\") upon the completion of their journey.[[41]](./Trondheim#cite_note-41)[[42]](./Trondheim#cite_note-42)\\n\\n### Other churches\\n\\nThe Lutheran [Church of Norway](./Church_of_Norway \"Church of Norway\") has 21 churches within the municipality of Trondheim. They are all a part of the [Diocese of Nidaros](./Diocese_of_Nidaros \"Diocese of Nidaros\"), which is based in Trondheim at the [Nidaros Cathedral](./Nidaros_Cathedral \"Nidaros Cathedral\"). Trondheim](./Territorial_Prelature_of_Trondheim \"Territorial Prelature of Trondheim\"). Being located across the street from the Nidaros Cathedral, the two of them form an unofficial religious quarter along with a [synagogue](./Synagogue \"Synagogue\"), a Baptist church, a [Salvation Army](./Salvation_Army \"Salvation Army\") office, and the 8-auditorium [cinema](./Movie_theater \"Movie theater\") *Prinsen kinosenter*.\\n\\n### Museums\\n\\n[Sverresborg](./Sverresborg \"Sverresborg\"), also named [Zion](./Zion \"Zion\") after [King David](./King_David \"King David\")\\'s castle in [Jerusalem](./Jerusalem \"Jerusalem\"), was a fortification built by [Sverre Sigurdsson](./Sverre_Sigurdsson \"Sverre Sigurdsson\"). It is now an open-air museum, consisting of more than 60 buildings. The castle was originally built in 1182–1183, but did not last for long as it was burned down in 1188. However, the [Sverresaga](./Sverresaga \"Sverresaga\") indicates it had been restored by 1197.[[43]](./Trondheim#cite_note-43)[*[citation needed](./Wikipedia:Citation_needed \"Wikipedia:Citation needed\")*]\\n\\nThe Trondheim Science Center ([Norwegian](./Norwegian_language \"Norwegian language\"): *Vitensenteret i Trondheim*) is a scientific hands-on experience center. The [NTNU University Museum](./NTNU_University_Museum \"NTNU University Museum\") (Norwegian: NTNU Vitenskapsmuseet) is part of the [Norwegian University of Science and Technology](./Norwegian_University_of_Science_and_Technology \"Norwegian University of Science and Technology\"). There are also a variety of small history, science and [natural history](./Natural_history \"Natural history\") museums, such as the [Trondheim Maritime Museum](./Trondheim_Maritime_Museum?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Trondheim Maritime Museum\"), the *Armoury*, adjacent to the Archbishops\\'s Palace, Kristiansten Fortress, the music and musical instrument museum [Ringve National Museum](./Ringve_National_Museum \"Ringve National Museum\"), [Ringve Botanical Garden](./Ringve_Botanical_Garden?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Ringve Botanical Garden\"), the [Trondheim Tramway Museum](./Trondheim_Tramway_Museum \"Trondheim Tramway Museum\"), and the [Jewish Museum](./Jewish_Museum_of_Trondheim?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Jewish Museum of Trondheim\"), co-located with the city\\'s synagogue, which is among the northernmost in the world.\\n\\n[Rockheim](./Rockheim \"Rockheim\") ([Norwegian](./Norwegian_language \"Norwegian language\"): *Det nasjonale opplevelsessenteret for pop og rock*, The National Discovery Center for Pop and Rock) opened at the Pier in August 2010. It is located inside an old warehouse, but characterised by an easily recognisable roof in the shape of a box. \"The box\" is decorated by thousands of tiny lights that change in a variety of colours and patterns, and is a landmark in the cityscape – especially on dark winter evenings.\\n\\n### Prison\\n\\nVollan District Jail ([Norwegian](./Norwegian_language \"Norwegian language\"): *Vollan kretsfengsel*) was a [jail](./Jail \"Jail\") during the [nazi occupation of Norway](./Nazi_occupation_of_Norway \"Nazi occupation of Norway\") and was used to imprison both prisoners of war and criminals. Vollan was not considered a [concentration camp](./Concentration_camp \"Concentration camp\").[[44]](./Trondheim#cite_note-NOU1998-44) In a summary of prisoners of war in Norway, numerous prisoners were registered at Vollan. One of its roles was as a [transit camp](./Internment \"Internment\") for [political prisoners](./Political_prisoners \"Political prisoners\"). Many prisoners were taken from Vollan to [Kristiansten Fortress](./Kristiansten_Fortress \"Kristiansten Fortress\") and shot. The prisoners at Vollan were interrogated at the Mission Hotel in Trondheim. Some were also interrogated by [Henry Rinnan](./Henry_Rinnan \"Henry Rinnan\") and his gang.[[44]](./Trondheim#cite_note-NOU1998-44) It was closed in 1971 after the opening of Trondheim Prison at Tunga.\\n\\nTrondheim Prison (Norwegian: *Trondheim fengsel*) is a prison that belongs to the Northern Region of the [Norwegian Correctional Services](./Norwegian_Correctional_Services \"Norwegian Correctional Services\").[[45]](./Trondheim#cite_note-45) The prison can house 184 [inmates](./Inmates \"Inmates\").\\n\\nIt consists of four main departments:\\n\\n* Nermarka (\"Tunga\") – closed department\\n* Detention department (no: *Forvaringsavdelingen*) at Nermarka\\n* Leira – open division. Through joint positive activities, the individual inmate on certain conditions teaches to be responsible with other people.[[46]](./Trondheim#cite_note-46)\\n* division Kongens gt. – halfway house, located in downtown Trondheim.\\n\\n### Attractions\\n\\nThe [water park](./Water_park \"Water park\") and [public pool](./Public_pool \"Public pool\") [Pirbadet](./Pirbadet \"Pirbadet\") is located on the northernmost shore of the Brattøra district, within walking distance of the central station.\\n\\n### Wider urban area\\n\\nTrondheim forms the centre of the [Trondheim Region](./Trondheim_Region \"Trondheim Region\"), and is a common commuting point for work, shopping, and healthcare. Although the official list of [metropolitan regions of Norway](./Metropolitan_regions_of_Norway \"Metropolitan regions of Norway\") defines the region very broadly, the area of two-way commuting where Trondheim residents too would head outwards for transport, shopping, and [upper secondary schools](./Upper_secondary_school \"Upper secondary school\"), consists roughly of Trondheim, [Malvik](./Malvik_Municipality \"Malvik Municipality\"), downtown [Stjørdal](./Stjørdal \"Stjørdal\") (incl. [Værnes](./Værnes \"Værnes\")), downtown [Melhus](./Melhus_Municipality \"Melhus Municipality\"), [Skaun](./Skaun_Municipality \"Skaun Municipality\"), and the lower sections of [Vanvikan](./Vanvikan \"Vanvikan\") in [Indre Fosen](./Indre_Fosen \"Indre Fosen\").[[47]](./Trondheim#cite_note-47)\\n\\nGovernment\\n----------\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/R%C3%A5dhuset_i_Trondheim_sett_fra_Bispegata%2C_2023.jpg/250px-R%C3%A5dhuset_i_Trondheim_sett_fra_Bispegata%2C_2023.jpg)](./File:Rådhuset_i_Trondheim_sett_fra_Bispegata,_2023.jpg)\\n\\nTrondheim\\'s town hall.\\n\\nTrondheim Municipality is responsible for [primary education](./Primary_education \"Primary education\") (through 10th grade), outpatient [health services](./Health_care \"Health care\"), [senior citizen](./Old_age \"Old age\") services, [welfare](./Welfare_spending \"Welfare spending\") and other [social services](./Social_work \"Social work\"), [zoning](./Zoning \"Zoning\"), [economic development](./Economic_development \"Economic development\"), and municipal [roads](./Road \"Road\") and utilities. The municipality is governed by a [municipal council](./Municipal_council_(Norway) \"Municipal council (Norway)\") of [directly elected](./Direct_election \"Direct election\") representatives. The [mayor](./Mayor \"Mayor\") is [indirectly elected](./Indirect_election \"Indirect election\") by a vote of the municipal council.[[48]](./Trondheim#cite_note-ks-48) The municipality is under the jurisdiction of the [Trøndelag District Court](./Trøndelag_District_Court \"Trøndelag District Court\") and the [Frostating Court of Appeal](./Frostating_Court_of_Appeal \"Frostating Court of Appeal\").\\n\\nOn 1 January 2005, the city was reorganized from five [boroughs](./Borough \"Borough\") into four, with each of these having separate social services offices.[[49]](./Trondheim#cite_note-49) The current boroughs are [Midtbyen](./Midtbyen,_Trondheim \"Midtbyen, Trondheim\") (44,967 inhabitants), [Østbyen](./Østbyen \"Østbyen\") (42,707 inhabitants), [Lerkendal](./Lerkendal,_Trondheim \"Lerkendal, Trondheim\") (46,603 inhabitants) and [Heimdal](./Heimdal \"Heimdal\") (30,744) inhabitants. The Population statistics listed are as of 1 January 2008. [Prior to 2005](./List_of_boroughs_in_Trondheim_prior_to_2005 \"List of boroughs in Trondheim prior to 2005\"), Trondheim was divided into the boroughs *Sentrum*, *Strinda*, *Nardo*, *Byåsen* and *Heimdal*.\\n\\nSee also: [List of mayors of Trondheim](./List_of_mayors_of_Trondheim \"List of mayors of Trondheim\")\\n\\n### Municipal council\\n\\nThe [city council](./Municipal_council_(Norway) \"Municipal council (Norway)\") *(Bystyret)* of Trondheim Municipality is made up of 67 representatives that are elected to four year terms. research\\n----------------------\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/Hovedbygningen_Gl%C3%B8shaugen_Trondheim_2022-08-18_03.jpg/250px-Hovedbygningen_Gl%C3%B8shaugen_Trondheim_2022-08-18_03.jpg)](./File:Hovedbygningen_Gløshaugen_Trondheim_2022-08-18_03.jpg)\\n\\nNTNU\\'s main building\\n\\n:   *See also the [list of primary schools in Trondheim](./Okstad_School \"Okstad School\")*.\\n\\nTrondheim is home to both the [Norwegian University of Science and Technology](./Norwegian_University_of_Science_and_Technology \"Norwegian University of Science and Technology\") (NTNU) with its many technical lab facilities and disciplines, and BI-Trondheim, a satellite campus for the Norwegian Business School (BI).[[77]](./Trondheim#cite_note-77) Both universities welcome a number of international students on a yearly basis and offer various scholarships.[[78]](./Trondheim#cite_note-78)\\n\\n[St. Olav\\'s University Hospital](./St._Olavs_University_Hospital \"St. Olavs University Hospital\"), a regional hospital for Central Norway, is located in downtown Trondheim. St. Olav\\'s is a teaching hospital and cooperates closely with the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) on both research and medical education.\\n\\n[SINTEF](./SINTEF \"SINTEF\"), a large independent research organisation in [Scandinavia](./Scandinavia \"Scandinavia\"), has 1,800 employees with 1,300 of these located in Trondheim.[[79]](./Trondheim#cite_note-79) The Air Force Academy of the [Royal Norwegian Air Force](./Royal_Norwegian_Air_Force \"Royal Norwegian Air Force\") is located at Kuhaugen in Trondheim.\\n\\nThe [Geological Survey of Norway](./Geological_Survey_of_Norway \"Geological Survey of Norway\") is located at Lade in Trondheim and is a major geoscientific institution with 220 employees of which 70% are scientists.\\n\\nThere are 11 high schools in the city. [Trondheim katedralskole](./Trondheim_katedralskole \"Trondheim katedralskole\") (\"Trondheim Cathedral School\") was founded in 1152 and is the oldest upper secondary school ([gymnasium](./Gymnasium_(school) \"Gymnasium (school)\")) in Norway, while [Charlottenlund videregående skole](./Charlottenlund_videregående_skole?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Charlottenlund videregående skole\") is the largest in Sør-Trøndelag with its 1,100 students and 275 employees. Brundalen Skole, has big festivals each year, and is building out to increase space.\\n\\nIla skole was founded in 1770 and is the oldest primary school in Trondheim.[[80]](./Trondheim#cite_note-80)\\n\\nMedia\\n-----\\n\\n[Adresseavisen](./Adresseavisen \"Adresseavisen\") is the largest regional newspaper and the oldest active newspaper in Norway, having been established in 1767. The two headquarters of the Norwegian Broadcasting Corporation (NRK) are located at [Tyholt](https://no.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRK%20Tyholt \"no:NRK Tyholt\") in Trondheim, and in Oslo.[[81]](./Trondheim#cite_note-81) On 31 December 2019 the fully digital and local newspaper Nidaros was launched as a competitor to Adresseavisen.[[82]](./Trondheim#cite_note-82) The student press of Trondheim features three types of media. [Under Dusken](./Under_Dusken \"Under Dusken\") is the student paper, [Radio Revolt](./Radio_Revolt \"Radio Revolt\") is the student radio, and Student-TV broadcasts videos online.\\n\\nRadio stations established in Trondheim include Trøndelag-focused opt-out feeds of [NRK P1](./NRK_P1 \"NRK P1\") and [NRK P1+](./NRK_P1+ \"NRK P1+\"), a local version of NRK [Yr](./Yr.no \"Yr.no\")\\'s radio station, and Radio Revolt. Along with Norway\\'s national radio stations, they can be listened to on [DAB+](./Digital_audio_broadcasting \"Digital audio broadcasting\") across most of Trøndelag, as well as on [internet radio](./Internet_radio \"Internet radio\"). As of 2017, the commercial stations Radio Trondheim and Radio 247 also broadcast from within Trondheim,[[83]](./Trondheim#cite_note-83) but as of May 2025 there are no commercial local stations that broadcast from within Trondheim Municipality proper, but intra-regional stations like [Nea Radio](./Nea_Radio?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Nea Radio\"), [Radio Trøndelag](./Radio_Trøndelag?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Radio Trøndelag\"), and P5 Fosen (Not to be mistaken for the national P5 Hits) are fully available on DAB+ in Trondheim.\\n\\nCulture\\n-------\\n\\n### Visual arts\\n\\nThe [Trondheim Art Museum](./Trondheim_Art_Museum \"Trondheim Art Museum\") has Norway\\'s third largest public art collection, mainly Norwegian art from the last 150 years.[[84]](./Trondheim#cite_note-84)\\n\\nThe [National Museum of Decorative Arts and Trondheim\")\\xa0[[no](https://no.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordenfjeldske%20Kunstindustrimuseum \"no:Nordenfjeldske Kunstindustrimuseum\")] boasts a large collection of [decorative arts](./Decorative_arts \"Decorative arts\") and design, including a great number of tapestries from the Norwegian tapestry artist [Hannah Ryggen](./Hannah_Ryggen \"Hannah Ryggen\"), as well as Norway\\'s only permanent samtidskunst](./Trøndelag_senter_for_samtidskunst?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Trøndelag senter for samtidskunst\") (English: Trøndelag Centre for Contemporary Art, TSSK) was established in Dronningens gate in February 2025.[[90]](./Trondheim#cite_note-90)[[91]](./Trondheim#cite_note-91)\\n\\n### Stage\\n\\nThe main regional theatre, [Trøndelag Teater](./Trøndelag_Teater \"Trøndelag Teater\"), is situated in Trondheim. Built in 1816, the theatre is the oldest theatre still in use in Scandinavia.[[92]](./Trondheim#cite_note-92) The city also features an alternative theatre house [Teaterhuset Avant Garden](./Teaterhuset_Avant_Garden?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Teaterhuset Avant Garden\"), and the theatre company Teater Fusentast.[[93]](./Trondheim#cite_note-93)\\n\\n### Music\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Ringve_botaniske_hage_1_%2815100598877%29.jpg/250px-Ringve_botaniske_hage_1_%2815100598877%29.jpg)](./File:Ringve_botaniske_hage_1_(15100598877).jpg)\\n\\nThe [Ringve Museum](./Ringve_Museum \"Ringve Museum\") is a museum devoted to music\\n\\nTrondheim has a broad music scene, and is known for its strong communities committed to rock, [jazz](./Jazz \"Jazz\") and [classical music](./European_classical_music \"European classical music\"). The city\\'s interest in Jazz and classical music are spearheaded by the [music conservatory](./Music_conservatory \"Music conservatory\") at [NTNU](./Norwegian_University_of_Science_and_Technology \"Norwegian University of Science and Technology\") which has been called one of the most innovative in the world,[[94]](./Trondheim#cite_note-94) and the municipal music school, *Trondheim Kommunale Musikk- og Kulturskole*.[[95]](./Trondheim#cite_note-95) The [Trondheim Symphony Orchestra](./Trondheim_Symphony_Orchestra \"Trondheim Symphony Orchestra\") and the [Trondheim Soloists](./Trondheim_Soloists \"Trondheim Soloists\") are well-known. The city hosts a yearly Jazz festival, and is home to [Trondheim Jazz Orchestra](./Trondheim_Jazz_Orchestra \"Trondheim Jazz Orchestra\").[[96]](./Trondheim#cite_note-96) The [Fjordgata Records](./Fjordgata_Records \"Fjordgata Records\") label is also hosted in Trondheim.\\n\\nClassical artists hailing from Trondheim include violinist [Arve Tellefsen](./Arve_Tellefsen \"Arve Tellefsen\"), [Elise Båtnes](./Elise_Båtnes \"Elise Båtnes\") and [Marianne Thorsen](./Marianne_Thorsen \"Marianne Thorsen\"). Also the [Nidaros Cathedral Boys\\' Choir](./Nidaros_Cathedral_Boys\\'_Choir \"Nidaros Cathedral Boys\\' Choir\").\\n\\n[Thomas Bergersen](./Thomas_Bergersen \"Thomas Bergersen\"), a Norwegian self-taught composer, multi-instrumentalist, and the co-founder of the production music company Two Steps From Hell, was born in Trondheim.\\n\\nPop/rock artists and bands associated with Trondheim include [Åge Aleksandersen](./Åge_Aleksandersen \"Åge Aleksandersen\"), [Margaret Berger](./Margaret_Berger \"Margaret Berger\"), [DumDum Boys](./DumDum_Boys \"DumDum Boys\"), [Lasse Marhaug](./Lasse_Marhaug \"Lasse Marhaug\"), [Gåte](./Gåte \"Gåte\"), [Keep Of Kalessin](./Keep_Of_Kalessin \"Keep Of Kalessin\"), [Lumsk](./Lumsk \"Lumsk\"), [Motorpsycho](./Motorpsycho_(band) \"Motorpsycho (band)\"), [Kari Rueslåtten](./Kari_Rueslåtten \"Kari Rueslåtten\"), [the 3rd and the Mortal](./The_3rd_and_the_Mortal \"The 3rd and the Mortal\"), [TNT](./TNT_(Norwegian_band) \"TNT (Norwegian band)\"), [Tre Små Kinesere](./Tre_Små_Kinesere \"Tre Små Kinesere\"), [the Kids](./The_Kids_(Norwegian_band) \"The Kids (Norwegian band)\"), [Bokassa](./Bokassa_(band) \"Bokassa (band)\"), Casino Steel (of [the Boys](./The_Boys_(UK_band) \"The Boys (UK band)\")), Atrox, Bloodthorn, Manes, child prodigy [Malin Reitan](./Malin_Reitan \"Malin Reitan\") and [Aleksander With](./Aleksander_With \"Aleksander With\"). The most popular punk scene is [UFFA](./UFFA \"UFFA\").\\n\\n[Georg Kajanus](./Georg_Kajanus \"Georg Kajanus\"), creator of the bands [Eclection](./Eclection \"Eclection\"), [Sailor](./Sailor_(band) \"Sailor (band)\") and [DATA](./DATA_(band) \"DATA (band)\"), was born in Trondheim. The music production team [Stargate](./Stargate_(production_team) \"Stargate (production team)\") started out in Trondheim.\\n\\nTrondheim is also home to Rockheim, the national museum of popular music, which is responsible for collecting, preserving and sharing Norwegian popular music from the 1950s to the present day.[[97]](./Trondheim#cite_note-97)[[98]](./Trondheim#cite_note-98)[[99]](./Trondheim#cite_note-99)\\n\\n### Film\\n\\nTrondheim features a lively film scene, including three filmfests: Minimalen Short Film Fest and [Kosmorama International Film Fest](./Kosmorama \"Kosmorama\") in March, and [Trondheim Documentarfestival](./Trondheim_Documentarfestival?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Trondheim Documentarfestival\") in November. Trondheim has two cinemas in the center of the city, Prinsen Kino and Nova kino [Prinsen Kinosenter](./Prinsen_Kinosenter?action=edit&redlink=1 \"Prinsen Kinosenter\"), [Nova Kinosenter](./Nova_Kinosenter \"Nova Kinosenter\")\\n\\n### Student culture\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Studentersamfundet_i_Trondhjem_from_South-West.jpg/250px-Studentersamfundet_i_Trondhjem_from_South-West.jpg)](./File:Studentersamfundet_i_Trondhjem_from_South-West.jpg)\\n\\nThe building of the [Studentersamfundet i Trondhjem](./Studentersamfundet_i_Trondhjem \"Studentersamfundet i Trondhjem\")\\n\\nWith students comprising almost a fifth of the population, the city of Trondheim is heavily influenced by student culture. Most noticeable is [Studentersamfundet i Trondhjem](./Studentersamfundet_i_Trondhjem \"Studentersamfundet i Trondhjem\"), the city\\'s student society. Its characteristic round, red building from 1929 sits at the head of the bridge crossing the river southwards from the city centre. As the largest university in Norway, the [Norwegian University of Science and Technology](./Norwegian_University_of_Science_and_Technology \"Norwegian University of Science and Technology\") (NTNU) is the host of some 36,000 students.[[100]](./Trondheim#cite_note-100)\\n\\nStudent culture in Trondheim is characterised by a long-standing tradition of volunteer work. The student society is for example run by more than 1,200 volunteers.[[101]](./Trondheim#cite_note-101) [NTNUI](./NTNUI \"NTNUI\"), Norway\\'s largest sports club, is among the other volunteer organisations that dominate student culture in Trondheim. Students in Trondheim are also behind two major Norwegian culture festivals, [UKA](./UKA_(festival) \"UKA (festival)\") and [The International Student Festival in Trondheim](./Isfit \"Isfit\") (ISFiT). NTNU lists over 200 student organisations with registered web pages on its servers alone.[[102]](./Trondheim#cite_note-102)\\n\\n### In popular culture\\n\\nTrondheim culture is parodied on the [Monty Python](./Monty_Python \"Monty Python\") album *[Another Monty Python Record](./Another_Monty_Python_Record \"Another Monty Python Record\")* in the form of the fictitious Trondheim Hammer Dance.[[103]](./Trondheim#cite_note-103)\\n\\nTrondheim is also a key location in the *[Command & Conquer: Tiberian Sun](./Command_&_Conquer:_Tiberian_Sun \"Command & Conquer: Tiberian Sun\")* universe, as it is a critical battleground for both factions.\\n\\nTrondheim was the name of a planet in the Hundred Worlds of the [*Ender\\'s Game* novel series](./Ender\\'s_Game_(novel_series) \"Ender\\'s Game (novel series)\").\\n\\nTrondheim likely serves as an inspiration for the fictional city Tronjheim in [The Inheritance Cycle](./The_Inheritance_Cycle \"The Inheritance Cycle\").\\n\\nSports and recreation\\n---------------------\\n\\n[Granåsen Ski Centre](./Granåsen_Ski_Centre \"Granåsen Ski Centre\"), a [Nordic skiing](./Nordic_skiing \"Nordic skiing\") venue located in Byåsen, regularly hosts World Cup competitions in [ski jumping](./Ski_jumping \"Ski jumping\"), [biathlon](./Biathlon \"Biathlon\") and [cross-country skiing](./Cross-country_skiing_(sport) \"Cross-country skiing (sport)\"), as well as the [1997](./1997_FIS_Nordic_World_Ski_Championships \"1997 FIS Nordic World Ski Championships\") and [2025 FIS Nordic World Ski Championships](./FIS_Nordic_World_Ski_Championships_2025 \"FIS Nordic World Ski Championships 2025\"). Trondheim [attempted but failed](./Trondheim_bid_for_the_2018_Winter_Olympics \"Trondheim bid for the 2018 Winter Olympics\") to become the Norwegian candidate for the [2018 Winter Olympics](./2018_Winter_Olympics \"2018 Winter Olympics\"). Hiking and recreational skiing is available around the city, particularly in [Bymarka](./Bymarka \"Bymarka\"), which can be reached by the tramway. Trondheim Golfklubb, one of the oldest golf clubs in Norway, has a nine-hole golf course in Byåsen. Byneset Golfklubb has a full 18 hole par 72 course, which has hosted the [Norwegian Challenge](./Norwegian_Challenge \"Norwegian Challenge\") of the [Challenge Tour](./Challenge_Tour \"Challenge Tour\") in 2012, as well as a short and easy 9 hole course, located at Spongdal. Klæbu Golfklubb in Klæbu has another 9 hole course, albeit with artificial greens. [Trondheim Airport, Værnes](./Trondheim_Airport,_Værnes \"Trondheim Airport, Værnes\"), situated in [Stjørdal](./Stjørdal \"Stjørdal\") 32 kilometres (20\\xa0mi) away, which is Norway\\'s fourth largest airport in terms of passenger traffic. Værnes has non-stop connections to cities such as [London](./London \"London\"), [Amsterdam](./Amsterdam \"Amsterdam\"), [Copenhagen](./Copenhagen \"Copenhagen\"), and [Stockholm](./Stockholm \"Stockholm\"), among others. The domestic route Trondheim – Oslo is among the [busiest air routes](./List_of_busiest_passenger_air_routes \"List of busiest passenger air routes\") in Europe with around 2 million passengers annually.\\n\\nTrondheim boasts the world\\'s only bicycle lift, *[Trampe](./Trampe_bicycle_lift \"Trampe bicycle lift\")*.\\n\\n### Bus\\n\\nThe bus network, operated by [AtB](./AtB \"AtB\"), runs throughout most of the city and its suburbs. A new metro line system went public 3 August 2019. The new transportation system covers the Trondheim area (Trondheim, Malvik, and Melhus). The three metro lines and the city lines that link the city across. The new public transport system becomes flexible, with buses running more often and accommodating more passengers. Fewer travelers must take a detour through the center of Trondheim, but relies more on bus transits.\\n\\nIn addition, the Nattbuss (Night Bus) service ensures cheap and effective transport for those enjoying nightlife in the city centre during the weekends. The Nattbus has other and more expensive prices than ordinary buses.\\n\\n### Boats\\n\\nThe Coastal Express ships ([Hurtigruten](./Hurtigruten \"Hurtigruten\"): Covering the [Bergen](./Bergen \"Bergen\")–[Kirkenes](./Kirkenes \"Kirkenes\") stretch of the coast) call at Trondheim, as do many [cruise ships](./Cruise_ship \"Cruise ship\") during the summer season. Every morning the Hurtigruten ships have one southbound and one northbound arrival and departure in Trondheim.\\n\\nSince 1994 there is also a fast commuter boat service to [Kristiansund](./Kristiansund \"Kristiansund\") (via [Brekstad](./Brekstad \"Brekstad\")), the closest coastal city to the southwest; there is also a second commuter boat service to [Vanvikan](./Vanvikan \"Vanvikan\").\\n\\nA [car ferry route](./Flakk–Rørvik_Ferry \"Flakk–Rørvik Ferry\") from the port of Flakk in the northwest of the municipality, connects Trondheim with [Fosen](./Fosen \"Fosen\").\\n\\n### Rail transport\\n\\n[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Trondheim_tram_2.jpg/250px-Trondheim_tram_2.jpg)](./File:Trondheim_tram_2.jpg)\\n\\nA tram in Trondheim in 2006\\n\\nMajor railway connections are the northbound [Nordland Line](./Nordland_Line \"Nordland Line\"), the eastbound [Meråker Line](./Meråker_Line \"Meråker Line\") to [Åre](./Åre \"Åre\") and [Östersund](./Östersund \"Östersund\") in Sweden, and two southbound connections to Oslo, the [Røros Line](./Røros_Line \"Røros Line\") and [Dovre Line](./Dovre_Line \"Dovre Line\").\\n\\nTrondheim also boasts the northernmost (since closure of [Arkhangelsk](./Arkhangelsk \"Arkhangelsk\") tram in 2004) [tramway](./Tram \"Tram\") line in the world: the [Gråkallen Line](./Gråkallen_Line \"Gråkallen Line\"), the last remaining segment of the [Trondheim Tramway](./Trondheim_Tramway \"Trondheim Tramway\"), is an 8.8 kilometres (5.5\\xa0mi) route (which is mostly single-track outside the innermost parts of the city; except the stretch between Breidablikk and Nordre Hoem stations) which runs from the city centre, through the [Byåsen](./Byåsen \"Byåsen\") district, and up to Lian, in the large recreation area [Bymarka](./Bymarka \"Bymarka\").\\n\\n### Roads\\n\\nNorway\\'s longest road, the [European route E6](./European_route_E6 \"European route E6\") north-south [motorway](./Motorway \"Motorway\"), passes through Trondheim mostly southeast of the major districts, except a long section between Tiller and Sluppen just north of Nidelva. The eastern terminus for [European route E39](./European_route_E39 \"European route E39\") is at Klett narrowly within the municipality border, which heads west to [Møre og Romsdal](./Møre_og_Romsdal \"Møre og Romsdal\").\\n\\nThe later built National Road 706, *Nordre avlastningsvei*, is an alternate bypass that heads northwest instead of northeast at Sluppen, passing through Ila, Piren, and northern Strindheim before rejoining European Route E6 northeast of IKEA. This bypass is slower and has various [roundabout](./Roundabout \"Roundabout\") crosses.\\n\\nVarious bridge projects over the Trondheim Fjord to replace the car ferry have been planned, but none have **Dunfermline** ([/dʌnˈfɜːrmlɪn/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [ⓘ](/wiki/File:Dunfermline.ogg "File:Dunfermline.ogg"); [Scots](./Scots_language "Scots language"): *Dunfaurlin*, [Scottish Gaelic](./Scottish_Gaelic_language "Scottish Gaelic language"): *Dùn Phàrlain*) is a city, parish, and former [royal burgh](./Royal_burgh "Royal burgh") in [Fife, Scotland](./Fife,_Scotland "Fife, Scotland"), 3 miles (5 km) from the northern shore of the [Firth of Forth](./Firth_of_Forth "Firth of Forth"). Dunfermline was the de facto capital of the [Kingdom of Scotland](./Kingdom_of_Scotland "Kingdom of Scotland") between the 11th and 15th centuries.[[2]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-2)

To the south of Dunfermline is the town of [Rosyth](./Rosyth "Rosyth"). To the north are the villages of [Townhill](./Townhill,_Fife "Townhill, Fife"), [Wellwood](./Wellwood,_Fife "Wellwood, Fife") and [Kingseat](./Kingseat "Kingseat"). To the west are the towns of [Crossford](./Crossford,_Fife "Crossford, Fife") and [Oakley](./Oakley,_Fife "Oakley, Fife"). And to the east are [Cowdenbeath](./Cowdenbeath "Cowdenbeath") and [Crossgates](./Crossgates,_Fife "Crossgates, Fife").

The earliest known settlements around Dunfermline probably date to the [Neolithic](./Neolithic "Neolithic") period, growing by the [Bronze Age](./Bronze_Age "Bronze Age"). The city was first recorded in the 11th century, with the marriage of [Malcolm III of Scotland](./Malcolm_III_of_Scotland "Malcolm III of Scotland"), and [Saint Margaret](./Saint_Margaret_of_Scotland "Saint Margaret of Scotland") at Dunfermline. As [Queen consort](./List_of_Scottish_consorts "List of Scottish consorts"), Margaret established a church dedicated to the [Holy Trinity](./Trinity "Trinity"), which evolved into [Dunfermline Abbey](./Dunfermline_Abbey "Dunfermline Abbey") under their son [David I](./David_I_of_Scotland "David I of Scotland") in 1128, and became firmly established as a prosperous royal mausoleum for the [Scottish Crown](./Kingdom_of_Scotland "Kingdom of Scotland"). A total of eighteen royals, including seven Kings, were buried here between 1093 and 1420 including [Robert the Bruce](./Robert_the_Bruce "Robert the Bruce") in 1329.

By the 18th century, Dunfermline became a regional economic powerhouse with the introduction of the [linen industry](./Linen "Linen"), and produced industrialists including [Andrew Carnegie](./Andrew_Carnegie "Andrew Carnegie").[[3]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pearson10-3) Dunfermline was awarded city status as part of Elizabeth II's [Platinum Jubilee Civic Honours](./Platinum_Jubilee_Civic_Honours "Platinum Jubilee Civic Honours") in 2022. Today, the city is a major service centre, with the largest employers being [Sky UK](./Sky_UK "Sky UK"), [Amazon](./Amazon.com "Amazon.com"), [Best Western](./Best_Western "Best Western"), [TechnipFMC](./TechnipFMC "TechnipFMC"), [Lloyds](./Lloyds_Banking_Group "Lloyds Banking Group") and [Nationwide](./Nationwide_Building_Society "Nationwide Building Society").[[4]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_Economy_Presentation_p.4-4) Dunfermline sits on the [Fife Pilgrim Way](./Fife_Pilgrim_Way "Fife Pilgrim Way"). In 2020, the [locality](./List_of_towns_and_cities_in_Scotland_by_population#Localities "List of towns and cities in Scotland by population") had an estimated population of 
54,990 and the wider [settlement](./List_of_towns_and_cities_in_Scotland_by_population#Settlements "List of towns and cities in Scotland by population") had a population of 
76,210.[[5]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-5)

History
-------

Main article: [History of Dunfermline](./History_of_Dunfermline "History of Dunfermline")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d4/Malcolm_Canmore%27s_Tower%2C_Dunfermline.jpg/330px-Malcolm_Canmore%27s_Tower%2C_Dunfermline.jpg)](./File:Malcolm_Canmore's_Tower,_Dunfermline.jpg)

Remains of [Malcolm Canmore](./Malcolm_III_of_Scotland "Malcolm III of Scotland")'s Tower

### Early history

There have been various interpretations of the name, *"Dunfermline"*.[[6]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dennison_and_Stronach3–4-6) The first element, *"dun"* translated from [Gaelic](./Scottish_Gaelic "Scottish Gaelic"), has been accepted as a (fortified) hill, and is assumed to be referring to the rocky outcrop at the site of [Malcolm Canmore's Tower](./Malcolm's_Tower "Malcolm's Tower") in Pittencrieff Glen (now [Pittencrieff Park](./Pittencrieff_Park "Pittencrieff Park")).[[7]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Taylor_and_Márkus309–310-7) The rest of the name is problematic.[[7]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Taylor_and_Márkus309–310-7) The second element, the *"ferm"* may have been an alternative name for the Tower [Burn](./Burn_(landform) "Burn (landform)") according to a medieval record published in 1455 which, together with the Lyne Burn to the south, suggests the site of a fortification between these two watercourses.[[6]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dennison_and_Stronach3–4-6)[[7]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Taylor_and_Márkus309–310-7)

The first record of a settlement in the Dunfermline area was in the [Neolithic](./Neolithic "Neolithic") period. This evidence includes finds of a stone axe, some flint arrowheads and a carved stone ball near the town.[[8]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dennison_and_Stronach9-8)[[9]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-9) A [cropmark](./Cropmark "Cropmark") which is understood to have been used as a possible mortuary enclosure has been found at Deanpark House, also near the town. By the time of the [Bronze Age](./Bronze_Age "Bronze Age"), the area was beginning to show some importance. Important finds included a bronze axe in Wellwood and a gold [torc](./Torc "Torc") from the Parish Churchyard.[[8]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dennison_and_Stronach9-8) Cist burials from the [Bronze Age](./Bronze_Age "Bronze Age") have also been discovered at both [Crossford](./Crossford,_Fife "Crossford, Fife") and Masterton, the latter of which contains a pair of armlets, a bronze dagger and a set necklace believed to have complemented a double burial.[[8]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dennison_and_Stronach9-8)[[10]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-10)

The first historic record for Dunfermline was made in the 11th century.[[11]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dennison_and_Stronach15–16-11) According to the fourteenth-century chronicler, [John of Fordun](./John_of_Fordun "John of Fordun"), [Malcolm III](./Malcolm_III_of_Scotland "Malcolm III of Scotland") married his second bride, the Anglo-Hungarian princess [Saint Margaret](./Saint_Margaret_of_Scotland "Saint Margaret of Scotland"), at the church in Dunfermline between 1068 and 1070;[[12]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-12) the ceremony was performed by [Fothad](./Fothad_II "Fothad II"), the last [Celtic](./Celts "Celts") [bishop of St Andrews](./Archbishop_of_St_Andrews "Archbishop of St Andrews").[[11]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dennison_and_Stronach15–16-11)[[13]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunlop44-13) Malcolm III established Dunfermline as a new seat for royal power in the mid-11th century and initiated changes that eventually made the township the de facto capital of Scotland for much of the period until the assassination of [James I](./James_I_of_Scotland "James I of Scotland") in 1437.[[14]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Lamont–Brown178–180-14) Following her marriage to King Malcolm III, Queen Margaret encouraged her husband to convert the small [culdee](./Culdee "Culdee") chapel into a church for [Benedictine](./Order_of_St_Benedict "Order of St Benedict") monks.[[14]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Lamont–Brown178–180-14) The existing culdee church was no longer able to meet the demand for its growing congregation because of a large increase in the population of Dunfermline from the arrival of English nobility coming into Scotland.[[15]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Henderson17-15) The founding of this new church of Dunfermline was inaugurated around 1072, but was not recorded in the town's records.[[15]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Henderson17-15)

### Capital of Scotland

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/52/Scotia_Depicta_-_Dunfermline_Abbey_and_Mill_-Plate-.jpg/330px-Scotia_Depicta_-_Dunfermline_Abbey_and_Mill_-Plate-.jpg)](./File:Scotia_Depicta_-_Dunfermline_Abbey_and_Mill_-Plate-.jpg)

Engraving of Dunfermline Abbey and Mill by [James Fittler](./James_Fittler "James Fittler") in *Scotia Depicta*

King [David I of Scotland](./David_I_of_Scotland "David I of Scotland") (reigned 1124–53) would later grant this church, dedicated to the [Holy Trinity](./Trinity "Trinity"), to *"unam mansuram in burgo meo de Dunfermlyn*" which translates into *"a house or dwelling place in my burgh of Dunfermline"*.[[11]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dennison_and_Stronach15–16-11)[[16]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Fawcett2-16) The foundations of the church evolved into an [Abbey](./Dunfermline_Abbey "Dunfermline Abbey") in 1128, under the reign of their son, [David I](./David_I_of_Scotland "David I of Scotland").[[14]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Lamont–Brown178–180-14)[[17]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Fife_Regional_Council16-17) [Dunfermline Abbey](./Dunfermline_Abbey "Dunfermline Abbey") would play a major role in the general [romanisation](./Liturgical_Latinisation "Liturgical Latinisation") of religion throughout the kingdom. At the peak of its power the abbey controlled four burghs, three courts of regality and a large portfolio of lands from [Moray](./Moray "Moray") in the north down into [Berwickshire](./Berwickshire "Berwickshire").[[14]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Lamont–Brown178–180-14) From the time of [Alexander I](./Alexander_I_of_Scotland "Alexander I of Scotland") (reign 1107–24), the Abbey would also become firmly established as a prosperous royal mausoleum of the [Scottish Crown](./Kingdom_of_Scotland "Kingdom of Scotland").[[18]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Fawcett139-18) A total of eighteen royals, including seven Kings, were buried here from Queen Margaret in 1093 to [Robert Stewart, Duke of Albany](./Robert,_Duke_of_Albany "Robert, Duke of Albany") in 1420.[[19]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Fawcett150-19) During the [Wars of Scottish Independence](./Wars_of_Scottish_Independence "Wars of Scottish Independence"), [Robert The Bruce](./Robert_The_Bruce "Robert The Bruce") insisted as early as 1314 that he wanted to be buried in the royal mausoleum in Dunfermline. This was so he could maintain the legacy of previous Scottish kings interred here, referring to them as our ‘predecessors’.[[20]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Fawcett144-20) Robert The Bruce (reigned 1306–29) would ultimately become the last of the seven Scottish Kings to be given this honour in 1329, although his heart was taken to [Melrose Abbey](./Melrose_Abbey "Melrose Abbey").[[20]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Fawcett144-20)

Dunfermline had become a burgh between 1124 and 1127, if not before this time.[[11]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dennison_and_Stronach15–16-11)[[16]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Fawcett2-16) [Dunfermline Palace](./Dunfermline_Palace "Dunfermline Palace") was also connected to the abbey and the first known documentation of the [Auld Alliance](./Auld_Alliance "Auld Alliance") was signed there on 23 October 1295.

Although the second son of James VI of Scotland and [Anne of Denmark](./Anne_of_Denmark "Anne of Denmark"), [Prince Charles](./Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") was born in Dunfermline Palace, Fife, on 19 November 1600, the [Union of the Crowns](./Union_of_the_Crowns "Union of the Crowns") ended the town's royal connections when [James VI](./James_VI_and_I "James VI and I") relocated the Scottish royal court to [London](./London "London") in 1603.[[21]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Durie17-21) King Charles thus became the last monarch to be born in Scotland. The Reformation of 1560 had previously meant a loss of the Dunfermline's ecclesiastical importance. [David Ferguson](./David_Ferguson_(reformer) "David Ferguson (reformer)") was the town's first reformed minister. On 25 May 1624, a fire engulfed around three-quarters of the medieval-renaissance burgh.[[21]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Durie17-21)[[22]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dennison_and_Stronach35-22) Some of the surviving buildings of the fire were [the palace](./Dunfermline_Palace "Dunfermline Palace"), [the abbey](./Dunfermline_Abbey "Dunfermline Abbey") and the Abbot's House.[[14]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Lamont–Brown178–180-14)[[23]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pride8–10-23)

### Recent history

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Former_St_Leonard%27s_works%2C_Dunfermline.jpg/250px-Former_St_Leonard%27s_works%2C_Dunfermline.jpg)](./File:Former_St_Leonard's_works,_Dunfermline.jpg)

Erskine Beveridge company offices, now converted into flats

The decline in the fortunes of Dunfermline lasted until the introduction of a [linen](./Linen "Linen") industry in the early 18th century.[[3]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pearson10-3) One reason for which the town became a centre for linen was there was enough water to power the mills and nearby ports along the Fife Coast. These ports also did trade with the [Baltic](./Baltic_region "Baltic region") and [Low Countries](./Low_Countries "Low Countries").[[3]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pearson10-3) Another reason was through an act of industrial espionage in 1709 by a weaver known as James Blake who gained access to the workshops of a [damask](./Damask "Damask") linen factory in Edinburgh by pretending to act like a simpleton in order to find out and memorise the formula.[[3]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pearson10-3)[[24]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Lamont–Brown186-24) On his return to his home town in 1718, Blake established a [damask](./Damask "Damask") linen industry in the town.[[3]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pearson10-3) The largest of these factories was St Leonard's Mill which was established by Erskine Beveridge in 1851. A warehouse and office block was later added around 1869. Other linen factories were built on land to both the north and south ends of the burgh.[[25]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Simpson_p85-25) During the mid-19th century, power loom weaving started to replace linen damask. The latter did not survive, going into decline straight after the end of [First World War](./First_World_War "First World War").[[23]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pride8–10-23) In 1909 the [Royal Navy](./Royal_Navy "Royal Navy") established Scotland's only Royal Naval Dockyard at nearby [Rosyth](./Rosyth "Rosyth").
Post-war housing began in the late 1940s with the construction of temporary prefabs and Swedish timber houses around areas such as Kingseat and Townhill. Additional provisions were made for electricity, water and sewage systems. Council housing was focused towards [Abbeyview](./Abbeyview "Abbeyview"), on a 97-hectare (240-acre) site on Aberdour Road; Touch, to the south of Garvock Hill; Bellyeoman and Baldridgeburn. Private housing became focused to the north of Garvock Hill and on the site of West Pitcorthie Farm.[[26]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-McEwan_p87-26)

Dunfermline has experienced significant expansion since 1999, especially in an expansion corridor on the eastern side of the town. This growth has edged the population centre towards the town's boundary with the M90 road corridor; it is planned to continue until 2022. Major developments include the creation of the [Duloch](./Duloch "Duloch") and Masterton neighbourhoods with over 6,000 homes, three new primary schools, new community infrastructure, employment land and the Fife Leisure Park. With the expansion there has been a dramatic rise in the town's population; more than 20% over a 15-year period. [Fife Council](./Fife_Council "Fife Council") have begun drafting plans for an expansion of a similar scale on Dunfermline's south-west,[[27]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-27) west and north sides,[[28]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-28) which will see the creation of 4,000 homes, a new high school and three new primary schools in the first phase.[[29]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-29)

Today, Dunfermline is the main centre for the West Fife area, and is also considered to be a [dormitory town](./Dormitory_town "Dormitory town") for Edinburgh.[[23]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pride8–10-23)[[30]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-30)[[31]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-31) The town has shopping facilities, a major public park, a main college campus at Halbeath and an-out-of-town leisure park with a multiplex cinema and a number of restaurants. The online retailer [Amazon.com](./Amazon.com "Amazon.com") has opened a major distribution centre in the Duloch Park area of Dunfermline.

As part of the [Platinum Jubilee Civic Honours](./Platinum_Jubilee_Civic_Honours "Platinum Jubilee Civic Honours"), it was announced on 20 May 2022 that Dunfermline would be awarded [city status](./City_status_in_the_United_Kingdom "City status in the United Kingdom").[[32]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-32) It was formally awarded the status through [Letters Patent](./Letters_Patent_(United_Kingdom) "Letters Patent (United Kingdom)") on 3 October 2022.[[33]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-33)[[34]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-34)[[35]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-35)

Governance
----------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/08/Dunfermline_City_Chambers_in_Dunfermline.jpg/250px-Dunfermline_City_Chambers_in_Dunfermline.jpg)](./File:Dunfermline_City_Chambers_in_Dunfermline.jpg)

[Dunfermline City Chambers](./Dunfermline_City_Chambers "Dunfermline City Chambers")

Dunfermline retained [royal burgh](./Royal_burgh "Royal burgh") status until this was abolished in 1975, under the [Local Government (Scotland) Act 1973](./Local_Government_(Scotland)_Act_1973 "Local Government (Scotland) Act 1973") in favour of a three-tier [regions and districts](./Regions_and_districts_of_Scotland "Regions and districts of Scotland"). The royal burgh merged into [Dunfermline District](./Dunfermline_(district) "Dunfermline (district)"), which was one of three districts within the [Fife](./Fife "Fife") region serving the town and West Fife from [Kincardine](./Kincardine-on-Forth "Kincardine-on-Forth") to [Aberdour](./Aberdour "Aberdour").[[36]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Post-War_Years_p16-36) The district council was abolished in 1996, under the [Local Government etc (Scotland) Act 1994](./Local_Government_etc_(Scotland)_Act_1994 "Local Government etc (Scotland) Act 1994"),[[37]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Local_Government_Act_1994-37) when the region became a [unitary council area](./Unitary_council_area "Unitary council area"). The new unitary [Fife Council](./Fife_Council "Fife Council") adopted the areas of the former districts as council management areas, and created [area committees](./Area_committee "Area committee") to represent each.

Today, Dunfermline is represented by several tiers of elected government. Abbeyview, Bellyeoman, Carnock and Gowkhall, Central Dunfermline, Izatt Avenue & Nethertown and Touch and Garvock Community Councils form the lowest tier of governance, whose statutory role is to communicate local opinion to local and central government.[[38]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-list_of_community_councils-38) [Fife Council](./Fife_Council "Fife Council"), the unitary [local authority](./Local_authority "Local authority") for Dunfermline, are the [executive](./Executive_(government) "Executive (government)"), [deliberative](./Deliberation "Deliberation") and [legislative](./Legislative "Legislative") body responsible for [local governance](./Local_government_in_Scotland "Local government in Scotland").[[39]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-devolvedmatters-39) Dunfermline has retained some importance as an administrative centre with the council's principal west Fife office based at New City House. Councillor meetings, including the City of Dunfermline Area Committee, take place in the [Dunfermline City Chambers](./Dunfermline_City_Chambers "Dunfermline City Chambers").

Dunfermline forms part of the [county constituency](./United_Kingdom_constituencies "United Kingdom constituencies") of [Dunfermline and West Fife](./Dunfermline_and_West_Fife "Dunfermline and West Fife"). The Dunfermline and West Fife UK (or *Westminster*) constituency, created in 2005 when the previous seats Dunfermline East and Dunfermline West were abolished, elects a [Member of Parliament](./Member_of_Parliament_(United_Kingdom) "Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)") (MP) to the [House of Commons](./House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom "House of Commons of the United Kingdom") of the Parliament of the United Kingdom by the first-past-the-post system. The seat is currently held by [Douglas Chapman](./Douglas_Chapman_(Scottish_politician) "Douglas Chapman (Scottish politician)") MP for the [Scottish National Party](./Scottish_National_Party "Scottish National Party").[[40]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_and_West_Fife-40) For the purposes of the [Scottish Parliament](./Scottish_Parliament "Scottish Parliament"), Dunfermline forms part of the [Dunfermline](./Dunfermline_(Scottish_Parliament_constituency) "Dunfermline (Scottish Parliament constituency)") constituency. The Dunfermline Scottish Parliament (or *Holyrood*) constituency created in 2011, following a [review of Scottish Parliament constituency boundaries](./List_of_Scottish_Parliament_constituencies_and_electoral_regions_(2011–2026) "List of Scottish Parliament constituencies and electoral regions (2011–2026)") is one of nine within the Mid Scotland and Fife electoral region.[[41]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Scottish_Parliament_boundaries-41) Each constituency elects one [Member of the Scottish Parliament](./Member_of_the_Scottish_Parliament "Member of the Scottish Parliament") (MSP) by the first-past-the-post system of election. The seat was won at [2016 Scottish Parliament elections](./2016_Scottish_Parliament_election "2016 Scottish Parliament election") by [Shirley-Anne Somerville](./Shirley-Anne_Somerville "Shirley-Anne Somerville") of the [Scottish National Party](./Scottish_National_Party "Scottish National Party").[[42]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Shirley-Anne_Somerville_MSP-42)[[43]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_Scottish_Parliament_results-43)

Prior to [Brexit](./Brexit "Brexit") in 2020, Dunfermline was part of the pan-Scotland [European Parliament constituency](./Scotland_(European_Parliament_constituency) "Scotland (European Parliament constituency)") which elected seven [Members of the European Parliament](./Members_of_the_European_Parliament "Members of the European Parliament") (MEPs) using the [d'Hondt method](./D'Hondt_method "D'Hondt method") of [party-list proportional representation](./Party-list_proportional_representation "Party-list proportional representation").[[44]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-list_of_MEPs-44)

Geography
---------

Dunfermline is at [56°04′17″N 3°27′42″W﻿ / ﻿56.07139°N 3.46167°W﻿ / 56.07139; -3.46167](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Dunfermline&params=56_04_17_N_3_27_42_W_type:city) on the coastal fringe of Fife.[[6]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dennison_and_Stronach3–4-6) The medieval town rose from approximately 51 metres (167 ft) above sea level in the south, where Nethertown Broad Street can now be found; 69 to 67 metres (226 to 220 ft) west to east along what is now Priory Lane; to 90 to 101 metres (295 to 331 ft) up the High Street, from west to east; to 92 to 105 metres (302 to 344 ft) between Bruce Street and Queen Anne Street from south to north.[[16]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Fawcett2-16)[[45]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dennison_and_Stronach17-45)

[![Dunfermline seen from the town's eastern expansion area. The chimney stacks at Grangemouth and Longanett can be seen in the distance](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/Dunfermline_Panorama.JPG/960px-Dunfermline_Panorama.JPG)](./File:Dunfermline_Panorama.JPG)

Panorama of Dunfermline seen from the town's [Duloch](./Duloch "Duloch") neighbourhood in the east

Temperatures in Dunfermline, much like the rest of Scotland, are relatively moderate given its northern latitude. Fife is a peninsula, between the [Firth of Tay](./Firth_of_Tay "Firth of Tay") to the north, [Firth of Forth](./Firth_of_Forth "Firth of Forth") to the south and the [North Sea](./North_Sea "North Sea") to the east. Summers are relatively cool and the warming of the water over the summer, results in warm winters. Average annual temperatures in Dunfermline range from a maximum of 18 °C (64 °F) to a minimum of 9 °C (48 °F).[[46]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunf_Weather-46)

The town is geologically separated from the area to the north by the [Cleish Hills](./Cleish_Hills "Cleish Hills").

According to the 2001 census, Dunfermline had a total population of 39,229 representing 11.2% of Fife's total population.[[48]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_population-48) By the time of the [2011 Census](./2011_United_Kingdom_census "2011 United Kingdom census"), the population of Dunfermline had risen considerably to 49,706 and has again increased up to 50,380 in 2012.[[49]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-GROS_2012_Table_3a-49)[[50]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Scotland's_Census_2011-50) There are 21,620 households in Dunfermline, 70.7% of which were owned.[[47]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_Profile-47) The demographic make-up of the population is much in line with the rest of Scotland. The age group from 30 to 44 forms the largest portion of the population (23.7%).[[48]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_population-48) The total population in the Dunfermline area was estimated at 55,451 in 2016, with a projected increase of 29% expected by 2026.[[51]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_Area_Local_Strategic_Assessment-51) The number of households in the Dunfermline area in 2016 was recorded at 24,607; 77% of which were owner occupied, 18% social rented and 4% private rented. 30.6% of people live alone and 10.9% are in low income. The median weekly income is calculated at £363 for the area.[[51]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_Area_Local_Strategic_Assessment-51)

Recent [Scottish Index of Multiple Deprivation](./Scottish_Index_of_Multiple_Deprivation "Scottish Index of Multiple Deprivation") (SIMD) figures indicate that the most deprived datazone in Dunfermline is Abbeyview North which is ranked as being one of the 5% most deprived areas in Scotland. The Headwell, Touch and Woodmill areas in Dunfermline fall within the 5–10% banding. Baldridgeburn, Brucefield and Halbeath areas are identified as being within the 10–15%, 15–20% banding of most deprived communities in Scotland.[[52]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-SIMD_Indicators-52)

At June 2017 there was a recorded 539 [Jobseekers Allowance](./Jobseekers_Allowance "Jobseekers Allowance") (JSA) claimants in the Dunfermline area representing a 1.4% rate which was lower than the Fife and Scottish averages.[[53]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Monthly_Economic_Update_June_2017_p4-53)

From about the fifteenth century coal and limestone had been extracted in the area around Dunfermline, at first on a very small and localised scale. As the [Agricultural Revolution](./Scottish_Agricultural_Revolution "Scottish Agricultural Revolution") gathered pace the demand for [lime](./Agricultural_lime "Agricultural lime") (for improving land) increased the requirement for coal to burn it. Salt panning too required coal in large quantities, and the early outcrops near the Firth of Forth became exhausted, forcing the extraction to take place further inland. Many of the sites were within the present-day limits of Dunfermline.

The increasing distance of the pits from the Forth made transport of the minerals an issue, and Dunfermline was a pioneer in the construction of wooden waggonways for the purpose. By the eighteenth century a complex network had developed, and in time many of the lines were converted to railways: the Halbeath Railway, the Fordell Railway, the Elgin Railway and the Townhill Tramway being the most prominent. They generally ran from north to south, still conveying the mineral to the harbours at Charlestown, Limekilns, [Inverkeithing](./Inverkeithing "Inverkeithing") and St David's. From 1848 more modern railways entered Dunfermline, at first on a west to east axis, intersecting the mineral lines. In time the latter were converted to make through running on to the main line network possible.

During the [Industrial Revolution](./Industrial_Revolution "Industrial Revolution") and [victorian period](./Victorian_period "Victorian period") industry in Dunfermline was concentrated to the north of the town centre around Pilmuir Street and to the south along sections of the Lynn Burn at Elgin and Bothwell Streets with textiles being particularly important to the town's economy. After the end of the [Second World War](./World_War_II "World War II") traditional industries, particularly linen and coal mining, declined and eventually became obsolete in the town with many factories ceasing production. Manufacturing in the town rejuvenated by the early 1960s when [Monotype Corporation](./Monotype_Corporation "Monotype Corporation") opened a new factory on Halbeath Road.[[56]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-McEwan_p73-56) The completion of the Pitreavie Industrial Estate (now known as the Pitreavie Business Park) opened in the mid-1970s, following the arrival of [Philips](./Philips "Philips") and the re-location of the offices of the [Dunfermline Press](./Dunfermline_Press "Dunfermline Press"). Smaller industrial estates were focused on Elgin Street, Halbeath Drive and Primrose Lane.[[56]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-McEwan_p73-56)
