The Dunfermline area has Fife's largest concentration of employment providing approximately 26,600 jobs in 2009;[[57]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_Area_Economic_Profile15-57) approximately 16% of the 163,000 jobs in Fife.[[58]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Fife_Economic_Strategy_p6-58) Wholesale and Retail (over 18% of local jobs) Health and Social Work (over 15% of local jobs) and Information and Communication (over 10% of local jobs) are the predominant sectors in the local economy.[[59]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_Economy_Presentation-59) There are also moderate instances of employment in finance, manufacturing, food services and accommodation.[[60]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_Area_Economic_Profile5-6-60)

Key local employers include [Best Western](./Best_Western "Best Western") (hotels), [Sky UK](./Sky_UK "Sky UK") ([home entertainment](./Home_video "Home video") and [communications](./Communications "Communications")), CR Smith (windows manufacturing), [FMC Technologies](./FMC_Technologies "FMC Technologies") ([offshore energy](./Offshore_energy?action=edit&redlink=1 "Offshore energy")), [Lloyds](./Lloyds_Banking_Group "Lloyds Banking Group") and [Nationwide](./Nationwide_Building_Society "Nationwide Building Society") (both financial services).[[4]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_Economy_Presentation_p.4-4) In November 2011 online retailer [Amazon.com](./Amazon.com "Amazon.com") opened a 93,000 m2 (1,000,000 sq ft) fulfilment warehouse in the east of the town adjacent to the M90 motorway. This development has created over 750 jobs and is the company's largest warehouse in the UK.[[61]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Amazon_Dunfermline_Jobs-61)[[62]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Amazon_in_Dunfermline-62) The [Newcastle](./Newcastle_upon_tyne "Newcastle upon tyne") based, Shepherd Offshore Group also plan to erect a [renewables](./Renewables "Renewables") hub near the Halbeath Interchange, off the [M90](./M90_motorway "M90 motorway") on a 6-hectare (15-acre) former [Hyundai](./Hyundai_Group "Hyundai Group")/[Motorola](./Motorola "Motorola") 'white elephant' factory.[[63]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-demolition_of_Hyundai_factory-63)[[64]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Shepherd_Offshore-64) The demolition of the factory began in early 2011 with an expected date for completion at the end of the year. A masterplan is being created for the site identifying significant investment and development opportunities with the potential to create a substantial number of new jobs.[[63]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-demolition_of_Hyundai_factory-63)[[65]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Shepard_Masterplan-65)

Dunfermline is the principal shopping centre serving the western area of Fife and is the region's second largest town centre by floorspace.[[66]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_fact_sheet-66) Retailing accounts for 18% of the total number of jobs in the town.[[60]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_Area_Economic_Profile5-6-60) A [BID](./Business_Improvement_District#United_Kingdom "Business Improvement District") (Business Improvement District) scheme for the town centre has been in operation since 2009.[[57]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_Area_Economic_Profile15-57)[[67]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_BID-67) The majority of shops and retail services in Dunfermline are concentrated in the town centre along a [high street](./High_street "High street"). The [Kingsgate Shopping Centre](./Kingsgate_Centre "Kingsgate Centre") is located on the pedestrianised section of the High Street giving Dunfermline a mix of modern and traditional shops.[[68]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Kingsgate_extension_by_mivan-68)[[69]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Kingsgate_extension_by_Crossland_properties-69) A major extension of the Kingsgate Shopping Centre was completed in 2008 improving and expanding the retail offer in the town by attracting a major department store brand and range of other smaller retailers.[[68]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Kingsgate_extension_by_mivan-68)[[69]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Kingsgate_extension_by_Crossland_properties-69) Other retail areas in Dunfermline exist at Carnegie Drive Retail Park to the north of the town centre and Halbeath Retail Park to the east of the town.[[57]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_Area_Economic_Profile15-57) A large neighbourhood centre with one of the towns major supermarkets was also built as part of the eastern expansion area of Dunfermline. The Fife Leisure Park, constructed in 1999 is adjacent to the [M90](./M90_motorway "M90 motorway") at Halbeath on the eastern outskirts of Dunfermline. The leisure park has a large cinema, a health club, bowling alley and a number of restaurants.[[70]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Fife_Leisure_Park_brochure-70)

Landmarks and notable buildings
-------------------------------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a9/Dunfermline_Abbey_Geograph.jpg/250px-Dunfermline_Abbey_Geograph.jpg)](./File:Dunfermline_Abbey_Geograph.jpg)

Dunfermline Palace and Abbey

The Category A listed[[71]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunf_Abbey_listing-71) [Dunfermline Abbey](./Dunfermline_Abbey "Dunfermline Abbey") on the Kirkgate is one of the best examples of Scoto-Norman monastic architecture.[[72]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Walker_and_Ritchie129-72) The Abbey, built between 1128 and 1150 under [David I](./David_I_of_Scotland "David I of Scotland"), was a reconstruction of the [Benedictine](./Order_of_St_Benedict "Order of St Benedict") chapel dedicated to the [Holy Trinity](./Trinity "Trinity"), founded by his mother, [Queen Margaret](./Saint_Margaret_of_Scotland "Saint Margaret of Scotland").[[17]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Fife_Regional_Council16-17)[[73]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Fawcett89-73) Despite much of the monastic buildings being destroyed by the troops of [Edward I](./Edward_I "Edward I") in 1303, there are substantial remains, with the lower stories of the dormitory and latrine blocks on the east side of the cloister being the earliest surviving parts, dating back to the early 13th century.[[17]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Fife_Regional_Council16-17)[[74]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Lamont-Brown182-74) The Abbey parish church, designed by the architect [William Burn](./William_Burn "William Burn"), was built between 1818 and 1821 on the site of the medieval choir and transepts which had been the eastern part of the abbey.[[17]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Fife_Regional_Council16-17)[[75]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Fawcett59-75)

The main Dunfermline War Memorial on Monastery Street was unveiled by the Lord Lieutenant of Fife, Sir Ralph Anstruther, in 1925. A Second World War Memorial and garden of remembrance were added in 1958 on a site assumed to have been home to the Apiaries of the Monastery. The memorial lists 632 of those killed in the First World War and another 275 in the Second World War.[[76]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Carnegie_Dunfermline_Trust264-265-76)

To the north of the abbey, on the corner of Maygate and Abbot Street, is the Category A listed[[77]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Abbot_House_listing-77) [Abbot House](./Abbot_House,_Dunfermline "Abbot House, Dunfermline").[[78]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Carnegie_Dunfermline_Trust14-78) This is the oldest secular building still standing in Dunfermline.[[79]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pearson19-79)[[80]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Abbot_House_excavations1-80) The house was originally built in the mid-fifteenth century as a residence for Abbot Richard Bothwell and this role continued until Commendator George Durie left to move into new apartments at the [Palace](./Dunfermline_Palace "Dunfermline Palace") in 1540.[[78]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Carnegie_Dunfermline_Trust14-78)[[81]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Durie24-81) Along Abbot Street is the Category B listed[[82]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Carnegie_library_listing-82) [Dunfermline Carnegie Library](./Dunfermline_Carnegie_Library "Dunfermline Carnegie Library") which was built between 1881 and 1883.[[83]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pearson17-83)[[84]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Gifford188-84) This [library](./Carnegie_library "Carnegie library") was the first in the world to be funded via donations by steel magnate and philanthropist [Andrew Carnegie](./Andrew_Carnegie "Andrew Carnegie"). A total of 2,811 free public libraries were eventually built altogether.[[83]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pearson17-83) At the top of Moodie Street is the Category B listed[[85]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Carnegie's_birthplace_listing-85) handloom weavers' cottage, the birthplace of Andrew Carnegie, which dates from the early 18th century.[[86]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pearson13-86)[[87]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-MacKay23-87) An adjacent memorial hall was added to the birthplace in 1928.[[88]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Carnegie_Dunfermline_Trust21-88) Just off East Port between Carnegie Hall and the High Street is [Viewfield House](./Viewfield_House,_Dunfermline "Viewfield House, Dunfermline"), a large square stone [Palladian](./Palladian "Palladian") three storey villa, built in about 1808 for James Blackwood, Provost of Dunfermline, and now a listed building. It served as home to the Carnegie Trust's Craft School from 1920 to 1940.[[89]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-BLB-89)[[90]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-90)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Abbot_House%2C_Dunfermline_Fife.jpg/250px-Abbot_House%2C_Dunfermline_Fife.jpg)](./File:Abbot_House,_Dunfermline_Fife.jpg)

[Abbot House](./Abbot_House,_Dunfermline "Abbot House, Dunfermline") (rear view)

The Category A listed[[91]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Guildhall_listing-91) [Dunfermline Guildhall](./Dunfermline_Guildhall "Dunfermline Guildhall") on the High Street was erected in 1807 by the guilds of the local merchants who were ambitious for Dunfermline to become the county town of Fife.[[79]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pearson19-79) Lack of funds forced the building to be sold, but in 1811 funds were available to add the 40-metre-high (130 ft) steeple.[[79]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pearson19-79) At the west end of the High Street is the Category A listed[[92]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-City_Chambers_listing-92) City Chambers with its 36-metre-high (118 ft) high central clock tower and turrets, designed by [James Campbell Walker](./James_Campbell_Walker "James Campbell Walker") and built between 1876 and 1879 .[[93]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pearson21-93)

In the car park between Bruce Street and Chambers Street is St Margaret's Cave, a place where she would retreat to pray in peace and quiet.[[93]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pearson21-93) The cave was re-opened in 1993 to celebrate the 900th anniversary of her death.[[93]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pearson21-93)[[94]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-McEwan133-94) Forming the main entrance to Pittencrieff Park at the junction of Bridge Street and Chalmers Street are the Category A listed[[95]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Louise_Carnegie_Memorial_Gates_listing-95) Louise Carnegie Memorial Gates, otherwise known as the *Glen Gates*.[[96]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Durie71-96)[[97]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Carnegie_Dunfermline_Trust191-97) The gates, which opened in 1929, were paid for by the Dunfermline Carnegie Trust and named after Louise Carnegie, the wife of Andrew Carnegie.[[98]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-DHCP18-19-98) They lead up a path to a [bronze](./Bronze "Bronze") statue of Andrew Carnegie which was unveiled in 1914.[[93]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pearson21-93)[[98]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-DHCP18-19-98)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/Pittencrieff_House.JPG/250px-Pittencrieff_House.JPG)](./File:Pittencrieff_House.JPG)

Pittencrieff House Museum

In the subsequent development of the modern park, the Category A listed[[99]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pittencrieff_House_listing-99) Pittencrieff House, built around 1610 for Sir William Clerk of Penicuik, was designed as a centre piece.[[100]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Hendrie24-100)[[101]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Durie72-101) Two of the bedrooms were converted to create two long galleries for museum and art exhibition space in a restoration programme undertaken by Sir [Robert Lorimer](./Robert_Lorimer "Robert Lorimer") between 1911 and 1913.[[100]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Hendrie24-100) Work on the building was completed in 2010 to repair and reharl the property, restoring the original ochre-coloured limewash exterior. The project was funded through the £1.7 million Dunfermline Conservation Area Regeneration Scheme (CARS) under a partnership between Fife Council and Historic Scotland.[[102]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pittencrieff_House_revealed-102)

A number of stately homes also exist on the outskirts of the town. The Category A listed[[103]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pitfirrane_Castle_listing-103) Pitfirrane Castle, to the west of Dunfermline, was once the seat of the Halkett family.[[104]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Gifford343-104)[[105]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Carnegie_Dunfermline_Trust168–171-105) The castle, which dates from the 16th century, was purchased by the Carnegie Dunfermline Trust in 1951 for the use as a clubhouse for Dunfermline Golf Club.[[105]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Carnegie_Dunfermline_Trust168–171-105) To the south of Dunfermline is the Category A listed Hill House[[106]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Hill_House_listing-106) and [Pitreavie Castle](./Pitreavie_Castle "Pitreavie Castle").[[107]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pitreavie_Castle_listing-107) Both dating from the mid-17th century, Hill House was built as a residence for William Monteith of Randford and Pitreavie Castle as a manor house by Sir Hendry Wardlaw.[[108]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_Carnegie_Trust168–171-108)[[109]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Carnegie_Dunfermline_Trust17-109) To the south-west of Dunfermline is the Category A listed[[110]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Logie_House_listing-110) Logie House, built as an Edwardian residence and seat for the Hunt family.[[111]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Gifford315-111)

Further Carnegie funded buildings include the Carnegie Leisure Centre, designed by [Hippolyte Blanc](./Hippolyte_Blanc "Hippolyte Blanc") in 1905, and the Carnegie Clinic by [H & D Barclay](./H_&_D_Barclay "H & D Barclay") from 1909 to 1912.[[112]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-112)

Culture
-------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/Glen_Gates%2C_Dunfermline.jpg/250px-Glen_Gates%2C_Dunfermline.jpg)](./File:Glen_Gates,_Dunfermline.jpg)

Louise Carnegie Memorial Gates, leading into Pittencrieff Park

[Pittencrieff Park](./Pittencrieff_Park "Pittencrieff Park") forms the western boundary of the town centre covering 31 hectares (76 acres). It was given to the people of Dunfermline in 1903 by [Andrew Carnegie](./Andrew_Carnegie "Andrew Carnegie").[[98]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-DHCP18-19-98)[[113]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pittencrieff_Park-113) The park is known locally as *the Glen* and was created from the estate of Pittencrieff and the lands of the house, owned by the Lairds of Pittencrieff.[[98]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-DHCP18-19-98)[[113]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pittencrieff_Park-113) A £1.4 million project to regenerate, restore and re-establish the park began in 2009 and is ongoing.[[114]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pittencrieff_for_heritage_lottery_funding-114)[[115]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pittencrieff_regeneration_plans-115) In December 2011 Pittencrieff Park was awarded £710,000 through the [Heritage Lottery Fund](./Heritage_Lottery_Fund "Heritage Lottery Fund")'s *Parks for People* programme for essential maintenance work. A previous award of £27,000 was made under this scheme in 2010.[[114]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pittencrieff_for_heritage_lottery_funding-114) The work included the restoration of historic buildings and bridges; new lighting and the refurbishment of the greenhouse to create a classroom.[[116]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Lottery_funding_boost-116)[[117]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Heritage_Lottery_Fund_good_cheer-117) A separate £1 million project finished in 2012, extending the Glen Pavilion to provide a new 120 seat cafe and linking corridor to the rear of the building.[[116]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Lottery_funding_boost-116)[[118]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-118)

The Bruce Festival is an annual attraction held in Pittencrieff Park every August.[[119]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-festival_fit_for_a_king-119)[[120]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_Area_Economic_Profile20-120) The festival which promotes [Robert The Bruce](./Robert_The_Bruce "Robert The Bruce")'s links to Dunfermline centres on a medieval village and is home to a food fayre, battle reenactments and displays of arts and crafts.[[119]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-festival_fit_for_a_king-119)[[121]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Bruce_Festival-121)

The [Andrew Carnegie](./Andrew_Carnegie "Andrew Carnegie") birthplace museum at the corner of Moodie Street and Priory Lane is dedicated to the well-known businessman and philanthropist.[[122]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Hendrie30-122)[[123]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-DHCP11-123) The museum is made up of two buildings; the weaver's cottage, his birthplace and the memorial hall which tells his life story.[[123]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-DHCP11-123) Annual heritage walks organised by the museum take place each summer.[[122]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Hendrie30-122) The Abbot House on Maygate is the oldest building in the town.

In 2017, Dunfermline Carnegie Library & Galleries opened, an extension of the former Carnegie library building.[[124]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_museum-124)[[125]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-home_to_Scotland's_first_kings-125) This provides the town with museum, art gallery, archive, library, cafe and garden spaces.[[125]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-home_to_Scotland's_first_kings-125) Funders included Fife Council (£6.8 million) and the Heritage Lottery Fund (£2.8 million).[[124]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_museum-124) The building has won architectural awards: EAA Building of the Year and Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland's (RIAS) Andrew Doolan prize.[[126]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-126)

Dunfermline has two theatres, Carnegie Hall on East Port and the [Alhambra](./Alhambra_Theatre,_Dunfermline "Alhambra Theatre, Dunfermline") on Canmore Street. Carnegie Hall hosts a range of theatrical and musical productions including an annual Christmas show. The Music Institute, adjacent to the Hall also provides workshops, classes and children's groups.[[127]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Carnegie_Hall-127) The Alhambra, which opened in 1922, originally served as a dual-purpose role hosting both theatrical productions and films. In 2008, the theatre re-opened as a theatre and live music venue.[[128]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Alhambra_Theatre_history-128) Since 1938, Dunfermline has also been home to the 'Kinema Ballroom' a ballroom/dancehall which has evolved into a famous live music performance venue and nightclub which has hosted many internationally acclaimed artists.[[129]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-KinemaGigz-129)
Local groups include the Dunfermline Folk Club, Dunfermline Abbey Choir and Dunfermline district pipe band. The venue is now a world buffet restaurant.

Dunfermline Fire Station, a category B listed building,[[130]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-130) is an arts venue, cafe and studio space.[[131]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-131)

Media
-----

Television signals are received from either the [Craigkelly](./Craigkelly_transmitting_station "Craigkelly transmitting station") or [Black Hill](./Black_Hill_transmitting_station "Black Hill transmitting station") TV transmitters.[[132]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-132)[[133]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-133)

[Radio West Fife](./Radio_West_Fife "Radio West Fife") is one of the oldest hospital radio stations in Scotland which broadcasts by landline to the [Queen Margaret Hospital](./Queen_Margaret_Hospital "Queen Margaret Hospital") in the city.[[134]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-134)

The town is also served by nation-wide radio stations, [BBC Radio Scotland](./BBC_Radio_Scotland "BBC Radio Scotland"), [Forth 1](./Forth_1 "Forth 1"), [Kingdom FM](./Kingdom_FM "Kingdom FM") and [Greatest Hits Radio Scotland](./Forth_2 "Forth 2").

The [Dunfermline Press](./Dunfermline_Press "Dunfermline Press") is the town's weekly local newspaper.[[135]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-135)

The official guide to Dunfermline looked after by the Local Tourism Association is [Dunfermline.com](https://www.dunfermline.com)

Sports
------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ee/Dunfermline_v_Airdrie_-_Pre_Match_%283%29.jpg/250px-Dunfermline_v_Airdrie_-_Pre_Match_%283%29.jpg)](./File:Dunfermline_v_Airdrie_-_Pre_Match_(3).jpg)

East End Park, the home stadium of Dunfermline Athletic F.C.

Dunfermline is home to a professional [football](./Association_football "Association football") team, as well as [rugby](./Rugby_union "Rugby union") and [cricket](./Cricket "Cricket") teams.[[136]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-McEwan_p97-136) The senior football team, [Dunfermline Athletic](./Dunfermline_Athletic_F.C. "Dunfermline Athletic F.C.") play their games at [East End Park](./East_End_Park,_Dunfermline "East End Park, Dunfermline") in the [Scottish Championship](./Scottish_Championship "Scottish Championship").[[137]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_Athletic-137) The team have become famous for winning the [Scottish Cup](./Scottish_Cup "Scottish Cup") twice in the 1960s (1961 and 1968) gaining a reputation as a side for competitive football in both England and mainland Europe.[[136]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-McEwan_p97-136) The senior rugby team, [Dunfermline RFC](./Dunfermline_RFC "Dunfermline RFC") play their games at McKane Park in [Caledonia League Division 1](./Caledonia_Regional_League "Caledonia Regional League").[[136]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-McEwan_p97-136)[[138]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_RC-138) [Dunfermline Reign](./Dunfermline_Reign "Dunfermline Reign") are a basketball team that competes in the [Scottish Men's National League](./Scottish_Men's_National_League "Scottish Men's National League") Division 1. The team reached the playoffs for the first time in 2017. Dunfermline Tennis Club plays at Bothwell Street, competing in East of Scotland and national competitions. The club's ladies team has won the Scottish Cup a record 18 times since 1988.[[139]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-DTC_Scottish_Cup_Wins-139)

There is also a cricket club based at Carnegie Cricket Ground, an athletics ground at Pitreavie and three golf courses (Dunfermline, Canmore and Pitreavie).[[136]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-McEwan_p97-136) Carnegie Leisure Centre (originally Carnegie swimming baths) is the main sports centre. A £17.2 million major refurbishment and extension to the centre was completed in November 2011. The work has included the conversion of a 25-yard (23 m) Edwardian training pool into a modern 25-metre 6-lane deck-level pool with movable floor; an improved entrance and reception area with a new cafe and a new state-of-the-art gym with 80 stations.[[140]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Carnegie_Leisure_Centre_Refurbishment-140)

The Dunfermline Kings are the town's American football team, playing their games at Duloch Park.

The town's competitive running clubs include Dunfermline Track and Field Club, [Pitreavie AAC](./Pitreavie_AAC "Pitreavie AAC") and PH Racing Club. There are also a number of local jogging groups.

Dunfermline Cycling Club located in the towns Pittencrieff Park was formed in 1935 and is now one of the largest cycling clubs in Scotland. It has members who take part in competition and recreational events.[[141]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-141)

Education
---------

See also: [List of schools in Dunfermline](./List_of_schools_in_Dunfermline "List of schools in Dunfermline")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/NT0986_-_Dunfermline_High_School.jpg/250px-NT0986_-_Dunfermline_High_School.jpg)](./File:NT0986_-_Dunfermline_High_School.jpg)

[Dunfermline High School](./Dunfermline_High_School "Dunfermline High School"), established in 1468, is [one of the oldest schools in the world](./List_of_oldest_schools "List of oldest schools")

Dunfermline has four secondary schools and fourteen primary schools.[[142]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Fife's_primary_schools-142)[[143]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Fife's_secondary_schools-143) Other educational facilities include a private school and Calaiswood ASN School for children with learning difficulties and complex health needs. [Dunfermline High School](./Dunfermline_High_School "Dunfermline High School") is the oldest secondary in the town, having originated in 1816 on what is now Queen Anne Street.[[144]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Henderson588-144) The school which serves both the southern and western parts of the town as well as [Rosyth](./Rosyth "Rosyth") and [Kincardine](./Kincardine-on-Forth "Kincardine-on-Forth") has occupied a site on St Leonard's Street since 1939.[[145]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Guide_to_Dunfermline37-38-145)[[146]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunf._H.S._Inspection-146) A new £40 million Dunfermline High School opened in August 2012.[[147]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-New_DHS-147)[[148]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-school_projects_in_Fife-148) The old school was demolished, allowing new playing fields for the school in 2013.[[148]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-school_projects_in_Fife-148) [Queen Anne High School](./Queen_Anne_High_School_Dunfermline "Queen Anne High School Dunfermline") is located in Wellwood towards the northwest area of the town. [Woodmill High School](./Woodmill_High_School "Woodmill High School"), originally a junior secondary, was upgraded to a High School in 1972.[[149]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-McEwan40-41-149) The school was first established in Priory Lane before moving to a new building on Shields Road in 1960 and serves the eastern side of the town as well as the villages of Crombie, [Limekilns](./Limekilns "Limekilns") and [North Queensferry](./North_Queensferry "North Queensferry").[[149]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-McEwan40-41-149)[[150]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Woodmill_H.S._Inspection-150) [St Columba's High](./St._Columba's_R.C._High_School,_Dunfermline "St. Columba's R.C. High School, Dunfermline"), which opened in 1969 is one of two [Roman Catholic](./Roman_Catholic "Roman Catholic") secondary schools in Fife. The school caters for pupils living in West Fife from [Kincardine](./Kincardine-on-Forth "Kincardine-on-Forth") in the west to [Cowdenbeath](./Cowdenbeath "Cowdenbeath") in the east.[[149]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-McEwan40-41-149) The [SSERC](./SSERC "SSERC") Campus (formerly the Scottish Schools Education Research Centre) is based in Dunfermline and operates nationally to support schools and teachers delivering STEM subjects.[[151]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-151)

Further education is provided by [Fife College](./Fife_College "Fife College"). It was founded as Lauder Technical School in 1899 and funded by Andrew Carnegie who named it after his uncle, [George Lauder](./George_Lauder_(Scottish_industrialist) "George Lauder (Scottish industrialist)") who had been a campaigner for free technical education.[[152]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Durie74-152) A textile school, founded in 1910 and also funded by Carnegie later merged with the technical school in 1927.[[152]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Durie74-152) The school became known as a technical college in 1951 and the name was then shortened to Lauder College in the late 20th century before becoming [Carnegie College](./Carnegie_College "Carnegie College") in 2007.[[152]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Durie74-152)[[153]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Lauder_College_reshaped-153) In 2013 Carnegie became part of Fife College. It is a partner of the Dunfermline Business Centre and provides courses catering to over 10,000 students annually.[[149]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-McEwan40-41-149)[[154]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Carnegie_College-154)

Public services
---------------

Waste management is handled by the [local authority](./Local_authority "Local authority"), [Fife Council](./Fife_Council "Fife Council"). There is a kerbside [recycling](./Recycling "Recycling") scheme in operation in the town. A four-bin collection is in place for the majority of residents living within Fife.[[155]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Four_bin_service-155) Dunfermline has one recycling centre and several recycling points, all operated by the [local authority](./Local_authority "Local authority"), Fife Council.[[156]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Recycling_Centre_in_Dunfermline-156)[[157]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Recycling_Points_in_Dunfermline-157) Non-hazardous waste is sent to [landfill](./Landfill "Landfill") at Lochhead, near the town and Lower Melville Wood, near [Ladybank](./Ladybank "Ladybank").[[158]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Landfill_sites-158)

[Healthcare](./Health_care "Health care") is supplied by [NHS Fife](./NHS_Fife "NHS Fife") who have their headquarters at Hayfield House in [Kirkcaldy](./Kirkcaldy "Kirkcaldy"). The main acute in-patient and accident & emergency services are provided by the [Victoria Hospital](./Victoria_Hospital,_Kirkcaldy "Victoria Hospital, Kirkcaldy"), Kirkcaldy, 13 miles (21 km) to the east. The [Queen Margaret Hospital](./Queen_Margaret_Hospital "Queen Margaret Hospital") provides some long-stay beds but is primarily for out-patient and day care services with a minor injuries unit.

[Statutory emergency fire and rescue service](./Fire_service_in_the_United_Kingdom "Fire service in the United Kingdom") in the town is provided by the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service. The nearest station is at the Pitreavie Industrial Estate.[[159]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_Fire_Station-159) Policing in Dunfermline is provided by Police Scotland. The headquarters of the Dunfermline area is on 2 Holyrood Place, close to the town centre.[[160]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_Area-160) Dunfermline is also served under the East Central Region which covers Tayside, Forth Valley and the Kingdom of Fife of the [Scottish Ambulance Service](./Scottish_Ambulance_Service "Scottish Ambulance Service").[[161]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Scottish_Ambulance_Service-161) There are two ambulance stations in the town; one on Keir Hardie Terrace and the other at the Queen Margaret Hospital on Whitefield Road.[[162]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-ambulance_stations_in_Scotland-162)

Transport
---------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Dunfermline_town_railway_station.jpg/250px-Dunfermline_town_railway_station.jpg)](./File:Dunfermline_town_railway_station.jpg)

[Dunfermline City railway station](./Dunfermline_City_railway_station "Dunfermline City railway station")

Dunfermline is served by the [A907](./A907_road "A907 road") which meets the [M90](./M90_motorway "M90 motorway") and [A92](./A92_road "A92 road") to the east of the city at Halbeath Interchange. This connects the city to [Perth](./Perth,_Scotland "Perth, Scotland") to the north, [Edinburgh](./Edinburgh "Edinburgh") to the south and [Kirkcaldy](./Kirkcaldy "Kirkcaldy") to the east. The main routes through the city are Halbeath Road and Carnegie Drive ([A907](./A907_road "A907 road")) from east to west.[[163]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Nicholson_pp4–7-163)

The main bus terminus [Dunfermline bus station](./Dunfermline_bus_station?action=edit&redlink=1 "Dunfermline bus station") is located to the north of the city centre which provides seating, toilets and a convenience store.[[164]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-DBS-164) In addition to this, there are also two [Park and Ride](./Park_and_Ride "Park and Ride") schemes nearby at Ferrytoll, to the south of [Inverkeithing](./Inverkeithing "Inverkeithing"), and Halbeath. There are plans to create a "park and choose" site at [Rosyth](./Rosyth_railway_station "Rosyth railway station").[[165]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-165) There was formerly a second bus station, called St. Margarets. It is now a car park.[[166]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-166)

Two railway stations serve the city – [Dunfermline City](./Dunfermline_City_railway_station "Dunfermline City railway station") to the south of the city centre and [Dunfermline Queen Margaret](./Dunfermline_Queen_Margaret_railway_station "Dunfermline Queen Margaret railway station") to the east of the city close to [Queen Margaret Hospital](./Queen_Margaret_Hospital "Queen Margaret Hospital"),[[167]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-DQRS-167)[[168]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-DRS-168) with a third proposed to serve Halbeath Park and Ride.[[169]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-169)[[170]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-170) Nearby stations also exist at Rosyth,
[Inverkeithing](./Inverkeithing_railway_station "Inverkeithing railway station") and [Dalgety Bay](./Dalgety_Bay_railway_station "Dalgety Bay railway station") to the south of the town.

The nearest major international airport to Dunfermline is [Edinburgh Airport](./Edinburgh_Airport "Edinburgh Airport"), 13 miles (21 km) south of Dunfermline. Smaller municipal airports are also located nearby at [Glenrothes](./Fife_Airport "Fife Airport") (18 miles [29 km]), [Cumbernauld](./Cumbernauld_Airport "Cumbernauld Airport") (25 miles [40 km]) and [Perth](./Perth_Airport_(Scotland) "Perth Airport (Scotland)") (26 miles [42 km]).

Notable people
--------------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Andrew_Carnegie_tableau.jpg/250px-Andrew_Carnegie_tableau.jpg)](./File:Andrew_Carnegie_tableau.jpg)

Display in the Andrew Carnegie Birthplace Museum

Dunfermline's most famous son is the entrepreneur and philanthropist [Andrew Carnegie](./Andrew_Carnegie "Andrew Carnegie"), who was born in the town in 1835. Among the gifts he gave to his home town are a free library and public swimming baths. Most important of all was the donation of the Pittencrieff Estate which he had purchased in 1903 to be converted into Pittencrieff Park. [George Lauder](./George_Lauder_(Scottish_industrialist) "George Lauder (Scottish industrialist)"), Andrew's "cousin-brother", a leading mechanical engineer, and his partner in the [Carnegie Steel Company](./Carnegie_Steel_Company "Carnegie Steel Company") who would go on to be a board member of [U.S. Steel](./U.S._Steel "U.S. Steel"). In 1888, two Dunfermline men, [John Reid](./John_Reid_(businessman) "John Reid (businessman)") and Robert Lockhart, first demonstrated golf in the US by setting up a hole in an orchard, before Reid set up the USA’s first golf club the same year, [Saint Andrew's Golf Club](./Saint_Andrew's_Golf_Club_(New_York) "Saint Andrew's Golf Club (New York)") in [Yonkers, New York](./Yonkers,_New_York "Yonkers, New York"), with Andrew Carnegie one of the first members.[[171]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-171)

A number of British monarchs were born in Dunfermline Palace. These include [David II of Scotland](./David_II_of_Scotland "David II of Scotland") (reign 1329–71), the son of [Robert The Bruce](./Robert_The_Bruce "Robert The Bruce") in 1324;[[172]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Ashley161-172) [James I of Scotland](./James_I_of_Scotland "James I of Scotland") (reign 1406–37) in late 1394[[173]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Brown9-173) and [Charles I](./Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England"), King of Scotland, England and Ireland (reign 1625–49) in 1600.[[174]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Cavendish322-174)[[175]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Ashley309-175) [James VI and I](./James_I_of_England "James I of England"), the King of Scotland, England and Ireland and his wife, [Anne of Denmark](./Anne_of_Denmark "Anne of Denmark"), the daughter of [Frederick II](./Frederick_II_of_Denmark_and_Norway "Frederick II of Denmark and Norway") of Denmark also lived at the Palace until the [Union of the Crowns](./Union_of_the_Crowns "Union of the Crowns") in 1603.[[176]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Anne_of_Denmark-176)

The 15th-century poet [Robert Henryson](./Robert_Henryson "Robert Henryson"), one of Scotland's most important literary figures during the period of the Northern Renaissance, was based in the town.[[177]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-177)

General [John Forbes](./John_Forbes_(British_Army_officer) "John Forbes (British Army officer)"), who fought the French in the [French and Indian War](./French_and_Indian_War "French and Indian War") to capture [Fort Duquesne](./Fort_Duquesne "Fort Duquesne") and established the city of [Pittsburgh](./Pittsburgh "Pittsburgh"), [Pennsylvania](./Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania"), United States, was brought up in his family's ancestral home of Pittencrieff House (now within Pittencrieff Park).[[178]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Carnegie_Dunfermline_Trust201-178)[[179]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_marks_links_to_Forbes-179)

Sir [John Struthers](./John_Struthers_(anatomist) "John Struthers (anatomist)"), who dissected and drew the [Tay Whale](./Tay_Whale "Tay Whale"), was an anatomist and professor of medicine. He was born and brought up in Brucefield House, now demolished, which gives its name to a district of Dunfermline.[[180]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-LivingInThePast-180) The artist [Sir Joseph Noel Paton](./Sir_Joseph_Noel_Paton "Sir Joseph Noel Paton") was also born in the town.[[181]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-181)

[Ebenezer Henderson](./Ebenezer_Henderson "Ebenezer Henderson") (1784–1858), a minister and missionary, was born at the Linn near Dunfermline. His nephew [Ebenezer Henderson](./Ebenezer_Henderson_(writer) "Ebenezer Henderson (writer)") (1809–1879), a science writer and historian born in Dunfermline, wrote *The Annals of Dunfermline*.

In popular culture, the singer [Barbara Dickson](./Barbara_Dickson "Barbara Dickson");[[182]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-182) actor [Kenneth Cranham](./Kenneth_Cranham "Kenneth Cranham");[[183]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-183) [Dan McCafferty](./Dan_McCafferty "Dan McCafferty")[[184]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-184) and [Pete Agnew](./Pete_Agnew "Pete Agnew") from the Scottish rock band [Nazareth](./Nazareth_(band) "Nazareth (band)");[[185]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-185) [Ian Anderson](./Ian_Anderson "Ian Anderson"), singer and flautist of the progressive rock band [Jethro Tull](./Jethro_Tull_(band) "Jethro Tull (band)")[[186]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-186) and [Moira Shearer](./Moira_Shearer "Moira Shearer"), ballerina and actress[[187]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Moira_Shearer-187) were all born in the town. [Manny Charlton](./Manny_Charlton "Manny Charlton"), the producer of Nazareth, emigrated to the town with his family in the 1940s[[188]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-188) and [Stuart Adamson](./Stuart_Adamson "Stuart Adamson"), rock guitarist with the [Skids](./Skids_(band) "Skids (band)") and frontman with [Big Country](./Big_Country "Big Country"), was brought up in nearby [Crossgates](./Crossgates,_Fife "Crossgates, Fife")[[189]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Stuart_Adamson-189) and moved into the town with his family as a teenager. Film director – and former Skids frontman – Richard Jobson, who grew up in nearby [Ballingry](./Ballingry "Ballingry"), went to school in Dunfermline and during the early part of the Skids' career lived, for a time, in the Pitcorthie area. Big Country's co-founder [Bruce Watson](./Bruce_Watson_(Scottish_guitarist) "Bruce Watson (Scottish guitarist)"), though born in Timmins, Ontario, was also brought up in the town, a few streets away from Pete Agnew and Manny Charlton. Alan Darby, of [Cado Belle](./Cado_Belle "Cado Belle"), also grew up in the town and attended Dunfermline High School.

In literature, the critically acclaimed author, [Iain Banks](./Iain_Banks "Iain Banks"); poet and novelist, [John Burnside](./John_Burnside_(writer) "John Burnside (writer)") and [Robert Gilfillan](./Robert_Gilfillan "Robert Gilfillan") all have links to the town.

In sport, [Caroline Weir](./Caroline_Weir "Caroline Weir") of Real Madrid who was capped 102 times for Scotland national football team, [Harry Lind](./Harry_Lind "Harry Lind") of [Dunfermline RFC](./Dunfermline_RFC "Dunfermline RFC") who was capped sixteen times for the [Scotland national rugby team](./Scotland_national_rugby_union_team "Scotland national rugby union team") and [Jim Greenwood](./Jim_Greenwood_(rugby_union) "Jim Greenwood (rugby union)") who played for [Dunfermline RFC](./Dunfermline_RFC "Dunfermline RFC"), [Scotland](./Scotland_national_rugby_union_team "Scotland national rugby union team") and [British and Irish Lions](./British_and_Irish_Lions "British and Irish Lions") come from the town. [Billy Liddell](./Billy_Liddell "Billy Liddell") who played his entire career with [Liverpool F.C.](./Liverpool_F.C. "Liverpool F.C.") was born in nearby Townhill.[[190]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Billy_Liddell-190)

Twin cities
-----------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/Street_sign_Rua_de_Dunfermline_20_March_2015_%282%29.JPG/250px-Street_sign_Rua_de_Dunfermline_20_March_2015_%282%29.JPG)](./File:Street_sign_Rua_de_Dunfermline_20_March_2015_(2).JPG)

Street sign in the Rua de Dunfermline in the twin town of [Albufeira](./Albufeira "Albufeira"), Portugal

Dunfermline is [twinned](./Twin_towns_and_sister_cities "Twin towns and sister cities") with:

* [Logroño](./Logroño "Logroño"), Spain (since 1990)[[194]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-twin-194)
* [Sarasota, Florida](./Sarasota,_Florida "Sarasota, Florida"), United States (since 23 August 2001)[[194]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-twin-194)
* [Trondheim](./Trondheim "Trondheim"), Norway (since May 1945)[[195]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Trondheim-195)
* [Wilhelmshaven](./Wilhelmshaven "Wilhelmshaven"), Germany (since 24 August 1979)[[194]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-twin-194)
* [Vichy](./Vichy "Vichy"), France (since 1990)[[196]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Vichy_twinnings-196)
* [Albufeira](./Albufeira "Albufeira"), Portugal (since May 1995)[[194]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-twin-194)

Escutcheon  Azure on a rock Proper two lions supporting a tower with four steps Argent masoned Sable windows and portcullis Gules both lions crowned Or.  Supporters  Dexter a lion rampant Argent armed and langued Gules and sinister a unicorn Argent armed maned and unguled Or and gorged with a collar Gules from which is pendent an oval badge Azure fimbriated Or charged with a saltire Argent.  Motto  Esto Rupes Inaccessa |

**Dunfermline** ([/dʌnˈfɜːrmlɪn/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [ⓘ](/wiki/File:Dunfermline.ogg "File:Dunfermline.ogg"); [Scots](./Scots_language "Scots language"): *Dunfaurlin*, [Scottish Gaelic](./Scottish_Gaelic_language "Scottish Gaelic language"): *Dùn Phàrlain*) is a city, parish, and former [royal burgh](./Royal_burgh "Royal burgh") in [Fife, Scotland](./Fife,_Scotland "Fife, Scotland"), 3 miles (5 km) from the northern shore of the [Firth of Forth](./Firth_of_Forth "Firth of Forth"). Dunfermline was the de facto capital of the [Kingdom of Scotland](./Kingdom_of_Scotland "Kingdom of Scotland") between the 11th and 15th centuries.[[2]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-2)

To the south of Dunfermline is the town of [Rosyth](./Rosyth "Rosyth"). To the north are the villages of [Townhill](./Townhill,_Fife "Townhill, Fife"), [Wellwood](./Wellwood,_Fife "Wellwood, Fife") and [Kingseat](./Kingseat "Kingseat"). To the west are the towns of [Crossford](./Crossford,_Fife "Crossford, Fife") and [Oakley](./Oakley,_Fife "Oakley, Fife"). And to the east are [Cowdenbeath](./Cowdenbeath "Cowdenbeath") and [Crossgates](./Crossgates,_Fife "Crossgates, Fife").

The earliest known settlements around Dunfermline probably date to the [Neolithic](./Neolithic "Neolithic") period, growing by the [Bronze Age](./Bronze_Age "Bronze Age"). The city was first recorded in the 11th century, with the marriage of [Malcolm III of Scotland](./Malcolm_III_of_Scotland "Malcolm III of Scotland"), and [Saint Margaret](./Saint_Margaret_of_Scotland "Saint Margaret of Scotland") at Dunfermline. As [Queen consort](./List_of_Scottish_consorts "List of Scottish consorts"), Margaret established a church dedicated to the [Holy Trinity](./Trinity "Trinity"), which evolved into [Dunfermline Abbey](./Dunfermline_Abbey "Dunfermline Abbey") under their son [David I](./David_I_of_Scotland "David I of Scotland") in 1128, and became firmly established as a prosperous royal mausoleum for the [Scottish Crown](./Kingdom_of_Scotland "Kingdom of Scotland"). A total of eighteen royals, including seven Kings, were buried here between 1093 and 1420 including [Robert the Bruce](./Robert_the_Bruce "Robert the Bruce") in 1329.

By the 18th century, Dunfermline became a regional economic powerhouse with the introduction of the [linen industry](./Linen "Linen"), and produced industrialists including [Andrew Carnegie](./Andrew_Carnegie "Andrew Carnegie").[[3]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pearson10-3) Dunfermline was awarded city status as part of Elizabeth II's [Platinum Jubilee Civic Honours](./Platinum_Jubilee_Civic_Honours "Platinum Jubilee Civic Honours") in 2022. Today, the city is a major service centre, with the largest employers being [Sky UK](./Sky_UK "Sky UK"), [Amazon](./Amazon.com "Amazon.com"), [Best Western](./Best_Western "Best Western"), [TechnipFMC](./TechnipFMC "TechnipFMC"), [Lloyds](./Lloyds_Banking_Group "Lloyds Banking Group") and [Nationwide](./Nationwide_Building_Society "Nationwide Building Society").[[4]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_Economy_Presentation_p.4-4) Dunfermline sits on the [Fife Pilgrim Way](./Fife_Pilgrim_Way "Fife Pilgrim Way"). In 2020, the [locality](./List_of_towns_and_cities_in_Scotland_by_population#Localities "List of towns and cities in Scotland by population") had an estimated population of 
54,990 and the wider [settlement](./List_of_towns_and_cities_in_Scotland_by_population#Settlements "List of towns and cities in Scotland by population") had a population of 
76,210.[[5]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-5)

History
-------

Main article: [History of Dunfermline](./History_of_Dunfermline "History of Dunfermline")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d4/Malcolm_Canmore%27s_Tower%2C_Dunfermline.jpg/330px-Malcolm_Canmore%27s_Tower%2C_Dunfermline.jpg)](./File:Malcolm_Canmore's_Tower,_Dunfermline.jpg)

Remains of [Malcolm Canmore](./Malcolm_III_of_Scotland "Malcolm III of Scotland")'s Tower

### Early history

There have been various interpretations of the name, *"Dunfermline"*.[[6]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dennison_and_Stronach3–4-6) The first element, *"dun"* translated from [Gaelic](./Scottish_Gaelic "Scottish Gaelic"), has been accepted as a (fortified) hill, and is assumed to be referring to the rocky outcrop at the site of [Malcolm Canmore's Tower](./Malcolm's_Tower "Malcolm's Tower") in Pittencrieff Glen (now [Pittencrieff Park](./Pittencrieff_Park "Pittencrieff Park")).[[7]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Taylor_and_Márkus309–310-7) The rest of the name is problematic.[[7]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Taylor_and_Márkus309–310-7) The second element, the *"ferm"* may have been an alternative name for the Tower [Burn](./Burn_(landform) "Burn (landform)") according to a medieval record published in 1455 which, together with the Lyne Burn to the south, suggests the site of a fortification between these two watercourses.[[6]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dennison_and_Stronach3–4-6)[[7]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Taylor_and_Márkus309–310-7)

The first record of a settlement in the Dunfermline area was in the [Neolithic](./Neolithic "Neolithic") period. This evidence includes finds of a stone axe, some flint arrowheads and a carved stone ball near the town.[[8]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dennison_and_Stronach9-8)[[9]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-9) A [cropmark](./Cropmark "Cropmark") which is understood to have been used as a possible mortuary enclosure has been found at Deanpark House, also near the town. By the time of the [Bronze Age](./Bronze_Age "Bronze Age"), the area was beginning to show some importance. Important finds included a bronze axe in Wellwood and a gold [torc](./Torc "Torc") from the Parish Churchyard.[[8]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dennison_and_Stronach9-8) Cist burials from the [Bronze Age](./Bronze_Age "Bronze Age") have also been discovered at both [Crossford](./Crossford,_Fife "Crossford, Fife") and Masterton, the latter of which contains a pair of armlets, a bronze dagger and a set necklace believed to have complemented a double burial.[[8]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dennison_and_Stronach9-8)[[10]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-10)

The first historic record for Dunfermline was made in the 11th century.[[11]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dennison_and_Stronach15–16-11) According to the fourteenth-century chronicler, [John of Fordun](./John_of_Fordun "John of Fordun"), [Malcolm III](./Malcolm_III_of_Scotland "Malcolm III of Scotland") married his second bride, the Anglo-Hungarian princess [Saint Margaret](./Saint_Margaret_of_Scotland "Saint Margaret of Scotland"), at the church in Dunfermline between 1068 and 1070;[[12]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-12) the ceremony was performed by [Fothad](./Fothad_II "Fothad II"), the last [Celtic](./Celts "Celts") [bishop of St Andrews](./Archbishop_of_St_Andrews "Archbishop of St Andrews").[[11]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dennison_and_Stronach15–16-11)[[13]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunlop44-13) Malcolm III established Dunfermline as a new seat for royal power in the mid-11th century and initiated changes that eventually made the township the de facto capital of Scotland for much of the period until the assassination of [James I](./James_I_of_Scotland "James I of Scotland") in 1437.[[14]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Lamont–Brown178–180-14) Following her marriage to King Malcolm III, Queen Margaret encouraged her husband to convert the small [culdee](./Culdee "Culdee") chapel into a church for [Benedictine](./Order_of_St_Benedict "Order of St Benedict") monks.[[14]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Lamont–Brown178–180-14) The existing culdee church was no longer able to meet the demand for its growing congregation because of a large increase in the population of Dunfermline from the arrival of English nobility coming into Scotland.[[15]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Henderson17-15) The founding of this new church of Dunfermline was inaugurated around 1072, but was not recorded in the town's records.[[15]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Henderson17-15)

### Capital of Scotland

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/52/Scotia_Depicta_-_Dunfermline_Abbey_and_Mill_-Plate-.jpg/330px-Scotia_Depicta_-_Dunfermline_Abbey_and_Mill_-Plate-.jpg)](./File:Scotia_Depicta_-_Dunfermline_Abbey_and_Mill_-Plate-.jpg)

Engraving of Dunfermline Abbey and Mill by [James Fittler](./James_Fittler "James Fittler") in *Scotia Depicta*

King [David I of Scotland](./David_I_of_Scotland "David I of Scotland") (reigned 1124–53) would later grant this church, dedicated to the [Holy Trinity](./Trinity "Trinity"), to *"unam mansuram in burgo meo de Dunfermlyn*" which translates into *"a house or dwelling place in my burgh of Dunfermline"*.[[11]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dennison_and_Stronach15–16-11)[[16]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Fawcett2-16) The foundations of the church evolved into an [Abbey](./Dunfermline_Abbey "Dunfermline Abbey") in 1128, under the reign of their son, [David I](./David_I_of_Scotland "David I of Scotland").[[14]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Lamont–Brown178–180-14)[[17]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Fife_Regional_Council16-17) [Dunfermline Abbey](./Dunfermline_Abbey "Dunfermline Abbey") would play a major role in the general [romanisation](./Liturgical_Latinisation "Liturgical Latinisation") of religion throughout the kingdom. At the peak of its power the abbey controlled four burghs, three courts of regality and a large portfolio of lands from [Moray](./Moray "Moray") in the north down into [Berwickshire](./Berwickshire "Berwickshire").[[14]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Lamont–Brown178–180-14) From the time of [Alexander I](./Alexander_I_of_Scotland "Alexander I of Scotland") (reign 1107–24), the Abbey would also become firmly established as a prosperous royal mausoleum of the [Scottish Crown](./Kingdom_of_Scotland "Kingdom of Scotland").[[18]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Fawcett139-18) A total of eighteen royals, including seven Kings, were buried here from Queen Margaret in 1093 to [Robert Stewart, Duke of Albany](./Robert,_Duke_of_Albany "Robert, Duke of Albany") in 1420.[[19]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Fawcett150-19) During the [Wars of Scottish Independence](./Wars_of_Scottish_Independence "Wars of Scottish Independence"), [Robert The Bruce](./Robert_The_Bruce "Robert The Bruce") insisted as early as 1314 that he wanted to be buried in the royal mausoleum in Dunfermline. This was so he could maintain the legacy of previous Scottish kings interred here, referring to them as our ‘predecessors’.[[20]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Fawcett144-20) Robert The Bruce (reigned 1306–29) would ultimately become the last of the seven Scottish Kings to be given this honour in 1329, although his heart was taken to [Melrose Abbey](./Melrose_Abbey "Melrose Abbey").[[20]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Fawcett144-20)

Dunfermline had become a burgh between 1124 and 1127, if not before this time.[[11]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dennison_and_Stronach15–16-11)[[16]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Fawcett2-16) [Dunfermline Palace](./Dunfermline_Palace "Dunfermline Palace") was also connected to the abbey and the first known documentation of the [Auld Alliance](./Auld_Alliance "Auld Alliance") was signed there on 23 October 1295.

Although the second son of James VI of Scotland and [Anne of Denmark](./Anne_of_Denmark "Anne of Denmark"), [Prince Charles](./Charles_I_of_England "Charles I of England") was born in Dunfermline Palace, Fife, on 19 November 1600, the [Union of the Crowns](./Union_of_the_Crowns "Union of the Crowns") ended the town's royal connections when [James VI](./James_VI_and_I "James VI and I") relocated the Scottish royal court to [London](./London "London") in 1603.[[21]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Durie17-21) King Charles thus became the last monarch to be born in Scotland. The Reformation of 1560 had previously meant a loss of the Dunfermline's ecclesiastical importance. [David Ferguson](./David_Ferguson_(reformer) "David Ferguson (reformer)") was the town's first reformed minister. On 25 May 1624, a fire engulfed around three-quarters of the medieval-renaissance burgh.[[21]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Durie17-21)[[22]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dennison_and_Stronach35-22) Some of the surviving buildings of the fire were [the palace](./Dunfermline_Palace "Dunfermline Palace"), [the abbey](./Dunfermline_Abbey "Dunfermline Abbey") and the Abbot's House.[[14]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Lamont–Brown178–180-14)[[23]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pride8–10-23)

### Recent history

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/Former_St_Leonard%27s_works%2C_Dunfermline.jpg/250px-Former_St_Leonard%27s_works%2C_Dunfermline.jpg)](./File:Former_St_Leonard's_works,_Dunfermline.jpg)

Erskine Beveridge company offices, now converted into flats

The decline in the fortunes of Dunfermline lasted until the introduction of a [linen](./Linen "Linen") industry in the early 18th century.[[3]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pearson10-3) One reason for which the town became a centre for linen was there was enough water to power the mills and nearby ports along the Fife Coast. These ports also did trade with the [Baltic](./Baltic_region "Baltic region") and [Low Countries](./Low_Countries "Low Countries").[[3]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pearson10-3) Another reason was through an act of industrial espionage in 1709 by a weaver known as James Blake who gained access to the workshops of a [damask](./Damask "Damask") linen factory in Edinburgh by pretending to act like a simpleton in order to find out and memorise the formula.[[3]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pearson10-3)[[24]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Lamont–Brown186-24) On his return to his home town in 1718, Blake established a [damask](./Damask "Damask") linen industry in the town.[[3]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pearson10-3) The largest of these factories was St Leonard's Mill which was established by Erskine Beveridge in 1851. A warehouse and office block was later added around 1869. Other linen factories were built on land to both the north and south ends of the burgh.[[25]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Simpson_p85-25) During the mid-19th century, power loom weaving started to replace linen damask. The latter did not survive, going into decline straight after the end of [First World War](./First_World_War "First World War").[[23]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pride8–10-23) In 1909 the [Royal Navy](./Royal_Navy "Royal Navy") established Scotland's only Royal Naval Dockyard at nearby [Rosyth](./Rosyth "Rosyth").
Post-war housing began in the late 1940s with the construction of temporary prefabs and Swedish timber houses around areas such as Kingseat and Townhill. Additional provisions were made for electricity, water and sewage systems. Council housing was focused towards [Abbeyview](./Abbeyview "Abbeyview"), on a 97-hectare (240-acre) site on Aberdour Road; Touch, to the south of Garvock Hill; Bellyeoman and Baldridgeburn. Private housing became focused to the north of Garvock Hill and on the site of West Pitcorthie Farm.[[26]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-McEwan_p87-26)

Dunfermline has experienced significant expansion since 1999, especially in an expansion corridor on the eastern side of the town. This growth has edged the population centre towards the town's boundary with the M90 road corridor; it is planned to continue until 2022. Major developments include the creation of the [Duloch](./Duloch "Duloch") and Masterton neighbourhoods with over 6,000 homes, three new primary schools, new community infrastructure, employment land and the Fife Leisure Park. With the expansion there has been a dramatic rise in the town's population; more than 20% over a 15-year period. [Fife Council](./Fife_Council "Fife Council") have begun drafting plans for an expansion of a similar scale on Dunfermline's south-west,[[27]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-27) west and north sides,[[28]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-28) which will see the creation of 4,000 homes, a new high school and three new primary schools in the first phase.[[29]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-29)

Today, Dunfermline is the main centre for the West Fife area, and is also considered to be a [dormitory town](./Dormitory_town "Dormitory town") for Edinburgh.[[23]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Pride8–10-23)[[30]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-30)[[31]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-31) The town has shopping facilities, a major public park, a main college campus at Halbeath and an-out-of-town leisure park with a multiplex cinema and a number of restaurants. The online retailer [Amazon.com](./Amazon.com "Amazon.com") has opened a major distribution centre in the Duloch Park area of Dunfermline.

As part of the [Platinum Jubilee Civic Honours](./Platinum_Jubilee_Civic_Honours "Platinum Jubilee Civic Honours"), it was announced on 20 May 2022 that Dunfermline would be awarded [city status](./City_status_in_the_United_Kingdom "City status in the United Kingdom").[[32]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-32) It was formally awarded the status through [Letters Patent](./Letters_Patent_(United_Kingdom) "Letters Patent (United Kingdom)") on 3 October 2022.[[33]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-33)[[34]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-34)[[35]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-35)

Governance
----------

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/08/Dunfermline_City_Chambers_in_Dunfermline.jpg/250px-Dunfermline_City_Chambers_in_Dunfermline.jpg)](./File:Dunfermline_City_Chambers_in_Dunfermline.jpg)

[Dunfermline City Chambers](./Dunfermline_City_Chambers "Dunfermline City Chambers")

Dunfermline retained [royal burgh](./Royal_burgh "Royal burgh") status until this was abolished in 1975, under the [Local Government (Scotland) Act 1973](./Local_Government_(Scotland)_Act_1973 "Local Government (Scotland) Act 1973") in favour of a three-tier [regions and districts](./Regions_and_districts_of_Scotland "Regions and districts of Scotland"). The royal burgh merged into [Dunfermline District](./Dunfermline_(district) "Dunfermline (district)"), which was one of three districts within the [Fife](./Fife "Fife") region serving the town and West Fife from [Kincardine](./Kincardine-on-Forth "Kincardine-on-Forth") to [Aberdour](./Aberdour "Aberdour").[[36]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Post-War_Years_p16-36) The district council was abolished in 1996, under the [Local Government etc (Scotland) Act 1994](./Local_Government_etc_(Scotland)_Act_1994 "Local Government etc (Scotland) Act 1994"),[[37]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Local_Government_Act_1994-37) when the region became a [unitary council area](./Unitary_council_area "Unitary council area"). The new unitary [Fife Council](./Fife_Council "Fife Council") adopted the areas of the former districts as council management areas, and created [area committees](./Area_committee "Area committee") to represent each.

Today, Dunfermline is represented by several tiers of elected government. Abbeyview, Bellyeoman, Carnock and Gowkhall, Central Dunfermline, Izatt Avenue & Nethertown and Touch and Garvock Community Councils form the lowest tier of governance, whose statutory role is to communicate local opinion to local and central government.[[38]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-list_of_community_councils-38) [Fife Council](./Fife_Council "Fife Council"), the unitary [local authority](./Local_authority "Local authority") for Dunfermline, are the [executive](./Executive_(government) "Executive (government)"), [deliberative](./Deliberation "Deliberation") and [legislative](./Legislative "Legislative") body responsible for [local governance](./Local_government_in_Scotland "Local government in Scotland").[[39]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-devolvedmatters-39) Dunfermline has retained some importance as an administrative centre with the council's principal west Fife office based at New City House. Councillor meetings, including the City of Dunfermline Area Committee, take place in the [Dunfermline City Chambers](./Dunfermline_City_Chambers "Dunfermline City Chambers").

Dunfermline forms part of the [county constituency](./United_Kingdom_constituencies "United Kingdom constituencies") of [Dunfermline and West Fife](./Dunfermline_and_West_Fife "Dunfermline and West Fife"). The Dunfermline and West Fife UK (or *Westminster*) constituency, created in 2005 when the previous seats Dunfermline East and Dunfermline West were abolished, elects a [Member of Parliament](./Member_of_Parliament_(United_Kingdom) "Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)") (MP) to the [House of Commons](./House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom "House of Commons of the United Kingdom") of the Parliament of the United Kingdom by the first-past-the-post system. The seat is currently held by [Douglas Chapman](./Douglas_Chapman_(Scottish_politician) "Douglas Chapman (Scottish politician)") MP for the [Scottish National Party](./Scottish_National_Party "Scottish National Party").[[40]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_and_West_Fife-40) For the purposes of the [Scottish Parliament](./Scottish_Parliament "Scottish Parliament"), Dunfermline forms part of the [Dunfermline](./Dunfermline_(Scottish_Parliament_constituency) "Dunfermline (Scottish Parliament constituency)") constituency. The Dunfermline Scottish Parliament (or *Holyrood*) constituency created in 2011, following a [review of Scottish Parliament constituency boundaries](./List_of_Scottish_Parliament_constituencies_and_electoral_regions_(2011–2026) "List of Scottish Parliament constituencies and electoral regions (2011–2026)") is one of nine within the Mid Scotland and Fife electoral region.[[41]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Scottish_Parliament_boundaries-41) Each constituency elects one [Member of the Scottish Parliament](./Member_of_the_Scottish_Parliament "Member of the Scottish Parliament") (MSP) by the first-past-the-post system of election. The seat was won at [2016 Scottish Parliament elections](./2016_Scottish_Parliament_election "2016 Scottish Parliament election") by [Shirley-Anne Somerville](./Shirley-Anne_Somerville "Shirley-Anne Somerville") of the [Scottish National Party](./Scottish_National_Party "Scottish National Party").[[42]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Shirley-Anne_Somerville_MSP-42)[[43]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunfermline_Scottish_Parliament_results-43)

Prior to [Brexit](./Brexit "Brexit") in 2020, Dunfermline was part of the pan-Scotland [European Parliament constituency](./Scotland_(European_Parliament_constituency) "Scotland (European Parliament constituency)") which elected seven [Members of the European Parliament](./Members_of_the_European_Parliament "Members of the European Parliament") (MEPs) using the [d'Hondt method](./D'Hondt_method "D'Hondt method") of [party-list proportional representation](./Party-list_proportional_representation "Party-list proportional representation").[[44]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-list_of_MEPs-44)

Geography
---------

Dunfermline is at [56°04′17″N 3°27′42″W﻿ / ﻿56.07139°N 3.46167°W﻿ / 56.07139; -3.46167](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Dunfermline&params=56_04_17_N_3_27_42_W_type:city) on the coastal fringe of Fife.[[6]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dennison_and_Stronach3–4-6) The medieval town rose from approximately 51 metres (167 ft) above sea level in the south, where Nethertown Broad Street can now be found; 69 to 67 metres (226 to 220 ft) west to east along what is now Priory Lane; to 90 to 101 metres (295 to 331 ft) up the High Street, from west to east; to 92 to 105 metres (302 to 344 ft) between Bruce Street and Queen Anne Street from south to north.[[16]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Fawcett2-16)[[45]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dennison_and_Stronach17-45)

[![Dunfermline seen from the town's eastern expansion area. The chimney stacks at Grangemouth and Longanett can be seen in the distance](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b7/Dunfermline_Panorama.JPG/960px-Dunfermline_Panorama.JPG)](./File:Dunfermline_Panorama.JPG)

Panorama of Dunfermline seen from the town's [Duloch](./Duloch "Duloch") neighbourhood in the east

Temperatures in Dunfermline, much like the rest of Scotland, are relatively moderate given its northern latitude. Fife is a peninsula, between the [Firth of Tay](./Firth_of_Tay "Firth of Tay") to the north, [Firth of Forth](./Firth_of_Forth "Firth of Forth") to the south and the [North Sea](./North_Sea "North Sea") to the east. Summers are relatively cool and the warming of the water over the summer, results in warm winters. Average annual temperatures in Dunfermline range from a maximum of 18 °C (64 °F) to a minimum of 9 °C (48 °F).[[46]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-Dunf_Weather-46)

The town is geologically separated from the area to the north by the [Cleish Hills](./Cleish_Hills "Cleish Hills").

From about the fifteenth century coal and limestone had been extracted in the area around Dunfermline, at first on a very small and localised scale. As the [Agricultural Revolution](./Scottish_Agricultural_Revolution "Scottish Agricultural Revolution") gathered pace the demand for [lime](./Agricultural_lime "Agricultural lime") (for improving land) increased the requirement for coal to burn it. Salt panning too required coal in large quantities, and the early outcrops near the Firth of Forth became exhausted, forcing the extraction to take place further inland. Many of the sites were within the present-day limits of Dunfermline.

The increasing distance of the pits from the Forth made transport of the minerals an issue, and Dunfermline was a pioneer in the construction of wooden waggonways for the purpose. By the eighteenth century a complex network had developed, and in time many of the lines were converted to railways: the Halbeath Railway, the Fordell Railway, the Elgin Railway and the Townhill Tramway being the most prominent. They generally ran from north to south, still conveying the mineral to the harbours at Charlestown, Limekilns, [Inverkeithing](./Inverkeithing "Inverkeithing") and St David's. From 1848 more modern railways entered Dunfermline, at first on a west to east axis, intersecting the mineral lines. In time the latter were converted to make through running on to the main line network possible.

During the [Industrial Revolution](./Industrial_Revolution "Industrial Revolution") and [victorian period](./Victorian_period "Victorian period") industry in Dunfermline was concentrated to the north of the town centre around Pilmuir Street and to the south along sections of the Lynn Burn at Elgin and Bothwell Streets with textiles being particularly important to the town's economy. After the end of the [Second World War](./World_War_II "World War II") traditional industries, particularly linen and coal mining, declined and eventually became obsolete in the town with many factories ceasing production. Manufacturing in the town rejuvenated by the early 1960s when [Monotype Corporation](./Monotype_Corporation "Monotype Corporation") opened a new factory on Halbeath Road.[[56]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-McEwan_p73-56) The completion of the Pitreavie Industrial Estate (now known as the Pitreavie Business Park) opened in the mid-1970s, following the arrival of [Philips](./Philips "Philips") and the re-location of the offices of the [Dunfermline Press](./Dunfermline_Press "Dunfermline Press"). Smaller industrial estates were focused on Elgin Street, Halbeath Drive and Primrose Lane.[[56]](./Dunfermline#cite_note-McEwan_p73-56)
